stories.Headline: Saudi Aramco takes 49% stake in state-backed AI company Humain
stories.Summary:
Saudi Aramco said on Sunday that it was taking a 49 percent stake in the state-backed AI company Humain. The Public Investment Fund, the Saudi sovereign wealth fund, will keep the other 51 percent, the two sides said in a joint statement. Aramco made the move through a wholly owned subsidiary. The oil giant had been planning a significant minority stake in Humain for at least a year, and Humain launched in May 2025.

Aramco will inject about 9.9 billion Saudi riyals, or $2.6 billion, into Humain this year, along with AI, compute and digital assets. The statement said PIF and Aramco are contributing AI assets, capabilities and talent, and that the deal will accelerate Humain's growth and advance its AI capabilities globally. Humain plans to deploy three gigawatts of AI data center capacity by 2030. It is also working on infrastructure and cloud platforms and has developed an Arabic-language LLM.

Amin H. Nasser, Aramco's president and CEO, said AI had helped the oil giant reach $11.3 billion in tech-related value since 2023. The statement said the stake supports Humain's rapid scaling to meet growing regional and global demand for AI compute. Aramco is one of the world's biggest companies by market capitalization. The PIF is driving Saudi economic diversification efforts, and Aramco is the cornerstone of the oil-reliant Saudi economy.

The articles do not say what happens next beyond the companies' plans. Humain intends to keep scaling its AI data center capacity toward three gigawatts by 2030. The joint statement frames the deal as a way to meet rising demand for AI compute. No further steps or approvals are described in the articles.

stories.Headline: 2 Industrial Stocks That Win Whether the AI Bubble Pops or Not
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the U.S. company behind the Claude chatbot, filed for an initial public offering on Oct. 26, 2026, according to a 335-page registration statement. The filing gave the public a first official look at the company's business operations and ownership. The statement did not state a valuation, but some investors have guessed it could be as high as $2 trillion. That would make it the biggest IPO ever, and a large IPO could inflate what is sometimes called an AI bubble.

A bubble is overinvestment in a space that will not see a positive return, eventually creating market instability. Rob May, author of the 2026 book "Investing in AI," pointed to the 19th century railroad infrastructure bubble and the 1990s dot-com bubble as examples. He said people make a mistake when they think of the AI bubble as one consistent thing, because different areas, from data centers to model providers to startups, could see different returns. Dennis Kelleher, CEO of the nonprofit Better Markets, said that if the bubble bursts, companies lose money, debt and loans are not repaid, some companies and banks go bankrupt, stock markets crash and the economy contracts. He compared that to the 2008 economic crash, and said that if it is not a bubble, the economy could benefit depending on which companies win the AI race.

Experts disagree on whether an AI bubble exists. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in August that he is happy to pay hundreds of millions of dollars a year to use AI services. Others worry the money spent on AI is not seeing the expected return, and in 2024 Sequoia Capital estimated that gap at $600 billion. May said he sees pockets of bubbles but does not expect a violent pop, and he predicted that in the next 18 months investors will stop pumping money into startups and model labs. The article says Anthropic is expected to start trading, but it does not say what happens next beyond that.

stories.Headline: Boutique AI firms emerge in India for faster project delivery
stories.Summary:
A new group of small AI consulting firms has emerged in India to deliver enterprise AI projects faster than traditional IT services companies. These firms include Parallel Loop, Krazimo, and Deployment Inc., and they use AI-native engineers and modern tools to embed AI directly into business workflows. Parallel Loop was launched by Prateek Jogani and secured $6.6 million in funding from investors including Paytm CEO Vijay Shekhar Sharma and CRED founder Kunal Shah. Krazimo was co-founded by Akhil Verghese, and Deployment Inc. was spun off by Cars24 after it deployed AI across its operations, with Jayesh Gupta, who led AI at Cars24, as co-founder. Deployment Inc. is an OpenAI Select Partner, giving it access to technical resources and support.

These boutique firms use lean teams and outcome-based pricing, and they deploy AI stacks inside the customer's own infrastructure so enterprises keep control of their data and deployment environments. Krazimo sells outcomes rather than specifications, and its clients typically break even within three to six months, with profits rising by an average of 17%. Krazimo offers a cancellable monthly subscription for exploratory projects and a fixed price tied to delivery milestones for clearly defined work, and clients can exit without payment during the first 30 days. Parallel Loop combines a monthly platform licence fee, packages of forward-deployed engineering hours, one-time software development fees, and recurring maintenance charges, and it secured eight enterprise AI clients within months of incorporation with $2 million in booked revenue. Jogani said one customer received a quote of five months from a services company while Parallel Loop delivered the app in 10 days.

Traditional Indian IT firms such as Tata Consultancy Services and HCLTech are also pursuing AI, with TCS reporting annualised AI revenue of $3.1 billion in the September quarter and HCLTech's annualised advanced-AI revenue rising 28 per cent sequentially to $219 million. Leslie Joseph, VP and Principal Analyst at Forrester, said boutique AI firms are strongest where incumbents would have to cut their own revenue to compete, and that AI shrinks the billable work in these contracts while clients expect the savings passed back. Joseph also said these firms can staff engagements with more senior engineers and that outcome-based pricing is viable in narrow workflows where results are easy to measure, though that model remains unproven for large transformation programs. Verghese said traditional IT services typically deliver against a specification while Krazimo sells an outcome using AI and AI-assisted development, and Jogani said what works in Parallel Loop's favour is that all its engineers are AI native by default.

Outcome-based pricing remains a minority model even as it gains ground, and Indian businesses often demand clear return on investment before committing to AI deployments, with price sensitivity also a factor due to the relatively low cost of human labour. Infosys reported that fixed-price contracts accounted for 58% of its revenue in FY2026, while Wipro derived 45.6% of its revenue from fixed-price and volume-based contracts, with the remaining 54.4% from time-and-materials contracts. In August, Coforge revealed that outcome-based contracts contributed 6-7% of its $2.5 billion revenue run rate, and TCS has reported a shift towards outcome-based commitments, particularly in agentic global business services. Boutique firms also face challenges in talent retention and competition from frontier model companies, and the growth of global capability centres in India takes work away from both large IT firms and smaller consultancies.

stories.Headline: How To Harness Gains Of AI For Devt, By Olaopa
stories.Summary:
Prof. Tunji Olaopa, the Chairman of the Federal Civil Service Commission, proposed measures for governments to harness Artificial Intelligence for development. He spoke on Thursday in Abuja at a stakeholders' dinner on media and information literacy, AI and youth creativity. The dinner was organised by the International Media and Information Literacy Institute with UNESCO to mark the 2026 Global Media and Information Literacy Week. He said proper understanding of media and information literacy builds competences for deploying AI tools well.

Olaopa said generative AI in literacy curricula could reduce cognitive load for younger learners and make complex research easier. He said media and information literacy helps young people detect automated text or graphics, set boundaries, cross-check outputs and counter hidden AI biases. He called for reviewing policy frameworks to blend data literacy and AI ethics into mainstream schools. He also called for institutional hubs like academic libraries and community media networks to give marginalised youth basic AI literacy and to bridge the infrastructural gap.

He said advantaged youth know advanced media and AI while disadvantaged youth lack basic knowledge and access, and he said such youth need internet and AI tools locally for creativity to flourish. He noted that AI and modern media have opened possibilities but also carry bleak implications for humanity. He said the late scientist Stephen Hawking in 2015, with more than 1,000 other experts and researchers, wrote an open letter presented at the International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence in Argentina. He said the letter reflected concern that AI, especially a military AI arms race, could be humanity's biggest existential threat.

Olaopa said Hawking wondered whether the human race could survive the next 100 years, and he said machines are increasingly taking over almost every sphere of human life. He said robotics and intelligent machines have taken over the workplace and are even taking over the role of a wife or husband. He stressed the need for media and information literacy so humanity can navigate modern technology profitably. He said humans created AI as they created the atomic bomb and the Holocaust, so it should not be taken for granted that they know how to tame it. He said humanity should make a determined effort to stop AI from running amok.

stories.Headline: Goldman Sachs has a blunt warning for workers displaced by AI
stories.Summary:
Nate Herk, a 24-year-old Chicago-based AI automation creator and educator and a former business-intelligence analyst at Goldman Sachs, said in an interview with Benzinga that workers displaced by AI need more than the ability to write prompts for a chatbot. He said an AI-ready worker can break a job into tasks, decide which should go to AI, and use their own expertise to check what comes back. He said workers should be able to explain why they used AI for a task and how they know the result is good, adding that you can outsource the thinking but not the understanding. He said that if two people have those qualities and only one knows how to use AI well, he would take that person every time.

The article cites several figures. A 2026 Harris Poll survey for Express Employment Professionals found 93% of U.S. job seekers believe they have the AI skills employers want, while only 35% think companies expect advanced or expert proficiency. Among hiring managers, 41% say candidates need skills at that level and 90% look for at least basic AI proficiency. LinkedIn said U.S. jobs requiring AI-literacy skills grew 70% year over year, and Gallup found in July that 52% of American employees used AI at work by mid-2026, with 30% using it a few times a week or more and 15% daily. Microsoft's 2026 Work Trend Index found 50% of surveyed AI users said quality control of AI output had become more important, 46% pointed to critical thinking, and 86% said they treated AI output as a starting point rather than a final answer.

Herk said the risk goes up exponentially with agents that can send emails, update databases or make purchases, and he recommends narrowly scoped permissions and human approval before actions that are hard to reverse. He said that if you use a hundred agents to build something and it goes well you deserve the credit, and if it goes wrong you do not get to say the AI did it. He also pushed back on claims that one agent can run an entire marketing team, saying he automates tasks, not jobs. The article also cites the Open Worldwide Application Security Project, which warns against giving AI agents excessive functionality, permissions or autonomy, and Yoshua Bengio, who said at the United Nations Security Council in September that capable agents had shown dangerous behavior against instructions.

The article notes a split among experts. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned in 2025 that AI could eliminate as many as half of entry-level white-collar jobs within several years, particularly in technology, finance, law and consulting, while Nvidia's Jensen Huang challenged that outlook and said advances tend to create new work. Anthropic's Economic Index initially found AI usage leaned toward augmenting workers rather than fully automating tasks, while its 2026 research emphasizes substantial uncertainty around how quickly AI will affect employment and wages. Herk advised job seekers to learn to think like a consultant, figure out what is slowing a business down, and solve that problem with as little AI as needed.

stories.Headline: Your writing was flagged as AI. What does that actually mean?
stories.Summary:
Ghostwriter Sally McGraw submitted a writing sample for a book proposal job and received an email saying multiple AI detection tools had flagged her work as machine-generated. McGraw said she had not used AI and had written the text herself, and she had spent more than 20 years as a professional nonfiction writer. She said she assured the client she had written the proposal herself but decided not to press the issue because she considered the job minor. The client confirmed to NPR that she had screened McGraw's work for AI but said the results were not the determining factor in hiring a different writer, citing experience and fit instead. McGraw says she was paid for her samples but believes the detector results cost her the chance to write the full proposal.

Neil Clarke, publisher and editor of Clarkesworld, said a flood of AI submissions has put pressure on the magazine's editing staff. In 2021 the publication received roughly 1,100 submissions a month, and by February 2023, after AI agents like ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini became widely available, that number had doubled, forcing Clarke to temporarily close its submission portal. He estimates his own workload has increased by about 30%, and he said the situation has introduced an element of mistrust into the process. Clarke said he does not personally use AI detectors to screen manuscripts but thinks certain tools could help overwhelmed editors manage the volume if they check the findings. He cautioned that submissions should end in rejection, not an accusation.

A study published in June in the International Journal for Educational Integrity compared four widely used detectors on 160 academic papers across four categories: entirely human-written, entirely AI-written, a combination of the two, and AI material rewritten by a human. Among the four, Pangram was the most consistently accurate, correctly identifying AI use in 37 of the 40 papers with combined text and in 37 of the 40 where a human rewrote AI-generated text. Pangram CEO Max Spero said in an emailed statement that his company's detector can make mistakes, particularly when there is not much writing to evaluate. Chris Callison-Burch, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania, said detectors work by asking a large language model how predictable a passage is, and that language models tend to find text from their training data unusually predictable. Science blogger Janelle Shane encountered this in late 2022 when one detector reported a 98.7% confidence that a passage from her 2019 book was machine-generated, which she called a clear false positive.

Callison-Burch said an unpublished draft like McGraw's could still be falsely flagged based on patterns in writing style, and detectors look for clues in word choice, punctuation and sentence structure. He said words like delve, frequent em dashes and ideas grouped in lists of threes can trigger an AI-positive result, as can opening sentences with adverbs such as notably or crucially, or posing a question and immediately answering it. The Authors Guild said in May that the use of AI detectors creates an environment reminiscent of witch hunts, and that a false positive can cost an author their publishing contract and reputation. McGraw says the fear of another accusation has changed how she writes, and she now avoids certain words and sentence constructions and occasionally leaves out commas she used to include. She said she misses her em dash and worries about facing another accusation when a bigger opportunity is on the line.

stories.Headline: How Can Organizations Combat the AI-Enhanced Threat Actor?
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, Dan Lohrmann moderated a session called "Combatting the Artificially Enhanced Threat Actor" at the Secure Delaware conference, which is hosted by Government Technology. The two expert panelists were Dovid Clarke, Chief Executive Officer of RedShield, and Amad Sheikh, Chief Information Security Officer at the University of Delaware. Lohrmann asked the packed audience two yes or no questions, one about whether AI-enabled attackers are already changing the cybersecurity risk their organizations face and one about whether their organizations had adjusted priorities because AI can speed up vulnerability discovery or exploitation. Most hands went up to answer yes. The panelists described growing cyber threats driven by AI, alongside growing use of AI in governments and universities worldwide, with examples ranging from Hugging Face and poorly governed AI to shadow AI and a rising number of ransomware and other AI-powered attacks from bad actors.

The panel said AI genuinely scales phishing and speeds up social engineering, which lowers the barrier for low-skill attackers, while hype exceeds reality on autonomous zero-day discovery and fully self-driving complex breaches remain rare. The real threat is volume and velocity, and total autonomous orchestration is exaggerated. AI compresses the time from vulnerability disclosure to weaponized exploitation from weeks down to hours, because attackers automate exploit generation instantly while defenders are held back by manual testing and change windows. Traditional patching cycles are too slow, turning disclosure into an immediate race against machine-speed attacks. Rigorous asset management and strict identity access controls become even more important because they prevent automated lateral movement and shrink the attack surface, and rapid patch management with continuous backup verification supports recovery when machine-speed exploits get past perimeter defenses.

On prioritization, the panel said organizations should move from static CVSS scores to threat-informed prioritization based on active exploitation data, aiming automated patching and isolation at high-risk external assets first. Combining contextual threat intelligence with continuous attack surface management lets large public-sector and university security teams outpace machine-speed scans, use limited resources efficiently and protect critical infrastructure from automated exploitation waves. Information sharing through groups like REN-ISAC and MS-ISAC lets universities and local governments pool threat intelligence instantly, and turning individual detections into automated collective blocklists and defensive playbooks helps public-sector organizations neutralize machine-speed threats together faster than any single entity could alone. On communicating with executives, the panel said leaders should ground discussions in business risk and operational impact rather than technical hype, frame AI threats as faster velocity and scale on existing vulnerabilities such as automated phishing and quicker exploit delivery rather than speculative sci-fi scenarios, and use objective threat intelligence to separate proven adversary tactics from vendor marketing. Presenting AI as a risk multiplier rather than a new paradigm keeps leadership focused on funding baseline controls like asset visibility, identity control and rapid patching.

Lohrmann wrote that what he enjoyed most were the practical stories and real-life impacts from the experts and the audience questions, most of which covered awareness and helping enterprise business leaders and government leaders understand the risks and benefits of AI. He said it was clear at the session that personal roles still have a huge impact and that the basics can never be dropped. In his view it still comes down to people, process and technology solutions, and people problems and solutions are the most important piece. The articles do not say what specific follow-up actions, deadlines or policy changes come next.

stories.Headline: Veterans Affairs Ridesharing Program: Utilizing Artificial Intelligence for Optimal Rideshare Requests
stories.Summary:
In 2017, Charles Franklin was working as a community employment coordinator at the VA in Boston, where rising housing costs pushed veterans to seek affordable housing outside the city. Limited public transportation made it hard for those veterans to find and keep jobs. In 2018, Franklin piloted a program that gave 10 veterans in the VA homeless program a vehicle for the first four weeks of their new jobs. All 10 veterans kept their employment and later moved into more fulfilling and higher-paying positions.

The pilot's success brought additional funding, and the effort grew into what is now the VA Rideshare Program, with a platform where veterans can request and schedule rides. The service is free, since the VA covers all expenses and handles payment, and rides can be booked through the app or the customer service center up to 30 days in advance or on demand. Customer service is available 24/7 to address safety concerns and help with rescheduling. In 2021 the program was approved for national expansion, and it now covers same-day mental health appointments, medical appointments, help reaching safe destinations when stranded, and more recently food service delivery.

The platform is driven by artificial intelligence, which analyzes each ride based on ZIP code, day of the week, hour, and cost. Using historical data, the AI calculates the most efficient rideshare company for the request, considering time and location, and then schedules the ride. The VA is working on features that use AI to adapt to market changes, including new vehicle emission regulations set by states and localities, so the algorithms can select electric vehicles or vehicles meeting required emission standards based on location. The program operates in all 50 states plus 3 U.S. territories and has provided more than 700,000 rides, and 1,270 participating veterans kept employment for at least one year.

The platform has 92 transportation company APIs built in, including taxi services for areas not served by Lyft or Uber. The average cost per ride is $31.55, or $2.39 per mile, including software development fees, and 93% of every dollar spent supports veterans in accessing transportation services. The article also notes that the General Services Administration has a blanket purchase agreement for rideshare services with Lyft and Uber, which could be a viable solution for federal sites, though the VA did not use this agreement. Rideshare services may be able to replace employee shuttle buses, reduce rental vehicle requests, or decrease fleet vehicle numbers.

stories.Headline: Researchers Create Tool to Detect AI-Hallucinated Legal Citations
stories.Summary:
Georgia Tech researchers have created a tool to detect legal citations that artificial intelligence has made up. Master's students Adrian Lozada and Di Wu were selected as fellows to build it, through a fellowship competition run by the Center for Scientific Software Engineering and the Open Source Program Office with a donation from IBM. The tool is called the Mellea Legal Requirements Checker, or Mellea-LRC. It uses large language models and IBM's Mellea open-source framework to verify and repair prompts.

The team tested the tool on 26 public court-filing documents that contained falsified citations. Mellea-LRC can process a document in about eight minutes. It first extracts the case law citations from the document, then checks that each citation is authentic and supports the document's content. The team also released a new test and validation dataset on Hugging Face for future benchmarking studies, and the tool's code is open source.

Wu said IBM's Mellea framework was the foundation the team built on, and that Mellea's job is to make model calls predictable by letting you write the rules the output must satisfy as ordinary code, with the framework retrying until the output meets them. Lozada said agentic AI is growing quickly and much of that growth happens in open-source projects, where anyone can read, use and improve the work. Jeff Young, OSPO director and principal research scientist, said the framework's instruct, verify, repair approach allows reliable LLM loops and the use of small language models such as IBM's Granite, which can run on a laptop. He said the project shows the power of open-source models and the importance of novel software engineering and algorithmic techniques for improving reliability, and that Mellea-LRC shows AI's potential to evolve from a source of error in the legal profession into a trusted ally that helps lawyers work faster and cite precedents more accurately.

stories.Headline: Auburn Engineering artificial intelligence and aquaculture research projects part of $8.1 million statewide investment
stories.Summary:
Auburn University researchers in artificial intelligence and aquaculture will receive nearly $1.3 million in research grants, Gov. Kay Ivey announced this week. The funding is part of a combined $8.1 million investment from the Alabama Research and Development Enhancement Fund, which is administered by the Alabama Department of Economic and Community Affairs (ADECA). Three Auburn projects were included among the grants, which are being issued to provide practical solutions to emerging challenges and to promote economic growth in the region. The Auburn research projects are expected to run for two years.

One project will receive $600,000 to develop an AI platform that can aid law enforcement, first responders and veterans in recognizing post-traumatic stress disorder. That project is led by Xiao Qin, a professor in the Department of Computer Science and Software Engineering. A second project will receive $277,240 to enhance AI technology and make AI easier to use for the public and organizations, and its lead investigator is Jiaqi Wang, an assistant professor in the same department. A third project will receive $387,658 to study the use of microalgae to convert aquaculture wastewater and paper mill emissions into protein-rich fish feed, with Jin Wang, a professor in the Department of Chemical Engineering, as principal investigator.

Steve Taylor, senior vice president for research and economic development, said the investment confirms Auburn's position as a trusted partner in improving quality of life for the citizens of Alabama. He said the funds will be used to leverage Auburn researchers' expertise in AI technology development and chemical engineering processes. According to Taylor, the work aims to make AI tools easier to use, to enhance community safety and to help farmers ensure a cost-effective agricultural supply chain. The projects align with Auburn's Strategic Plan 2035 goals for doubling its research activity through impactful scholarly work that enhances economic prosperity and solves problems through collaborative team science.

stories.Headline: AI Infrastructure on DOE Lands Request for Information
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Department of Energy released a Request for Information on October 29, 2026, through its Office of Policy. The request asks data center developers, energy developers, and the broader public for input on using DOE land for artificial intelligence infrastructure. The department said the goal is to help America lead the world in AI while helping to lower energy costs. It wants to co-locate data centers and new energy infrastructure on DOE lands.

DOE has identified 16 potential sites that it says are uniquely positioned for rapid data center construction. These sites have in-place energy infrastructure and the ability to fast-track permitting for new energy generation such as nuclear. The information collected will be used to inform development, encourage private-public partnerships, and enable construction at select DOE sites. The department set a target of commencing operation by the end of 2027. Publicly available information about each site, including location and available acreage, is provided in appendices to the RFI.

The RFI also aims to gather information on potential development approaches, technology solutions, operational models, and economic considerations for establishing AI infrastructure. The sites offer industry a chance to partner with DOE's world-class research facilities co-located there. DOE said such partnerships could further advancements in power systems design needed to run the centers and in developing next-generation data center hardware. The department framed the effort as helping ensure America leads the world in AI while helping to lower energy costs.

The articles do not say who else is responsible or what happens next beyond the request for information. The full RFI is available as a PDF, and a related notice is posted in the Federal Register. The articles do not give a deadline for responses or a date for announcing site selections. More to follow.

stories.Headline: UNESCO and Chile’s Supreme Court Explore Artificial Intelligence Training for Judges
stories.Summary:
UNESCO representatives met with the President of Chile's Supreme Court, Gloria Ana Chevesich, on 26 October to discuss artificial intelligence and its growing presence in the judicial sphere. The meeting let the two sides exchange experiences and explore possible cooperation on how the technology relates to the work of courts. Discussions covered training, knowledge sharing and the opportunities artificial intelligence could offer for justice. Esther Kuisch Laroche, Director of the UNESCO Regional Office in Santiago, attended alongside Guilherme Canela, Director of UNESCO's Division for Digital Inclusion and Policies and Digital Transformation in Paris.

The UNESCO representatives shared the experience of UNESCO's Global Initiative for Judges, which has supported judicial professionals across different regions since 2013. The initiative has helped strengthen the capacities of more than 39,000 judicial actors in over 160 countries. The conversation builds on a relationship between UNESCO and the Chilean judiciary that began in 2014. Both institutions discussed possible areas of collaboration based on their respective experience, areas of work and shared interest in examining artificial intelligence's role in justice.

Kuisch Laroche said UNESCO greatly values the chance for dialogue with the Supreme Court of Chile, which allows the two sides to share experiences and explore new possibilities for collaboration in an area of growing importance. She said UNESCO hopes to keep strengthening the exchange, making its international experience available while also learning from the perspectives and progress of the Chilean judiciary. She described cooperation as a mutual exchange and stressed the value of learning from Chilean judicial perspectives and developments. The conversation established areas for further consideration without announcing a new training programme or formal agreement.

Cooperation between UNESCO and the Chilean judiciary dates to Chile's hosting of the 17th Ibero-American Judicial Summit in Santiago from 2 to 4 April 2014. The relationship also included a meeting hosted by the Supreme Court during the 2024 World Press Freedom Day Conference. That discussion focused on crimes against the environment and the role of judicial systems in protecting journalists and other critical voices. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the areas marked for further consideration.

stories.Headline: Not Your Mama’s SaaS: AI Didn’t Change Your SaaS Contract. It Changed What It Means.
stories.Summary:
A law firm article published on October 30, 2026, describes how generative AI is changing the meaning of ordinary software contract terms. The article comes from BakerHostetler and is based on a presentation called "Not Your Mama's SaaS: Same Clauses. New Consequences," given during Atlanta Technology Week 2026 at Render(ATL). It says many organizations are finding that their AI governance problems did not start with an AI agreement but with a SaaS agreement signed years earlier. The article is the first part of a three-part series.

The article gives no specific dates, numbers or names beyond those. It explains that provisions drafted long before generative AI became mainstream now carry new consequences even though the language has not changed. It gives the example of a CRM vendor releasing an AI assistant through a routine product update, with no new agreement, no procurement involvement and no legal review, while a foundation model provider may now process company data. It says standard update clauses, de-identified data clauses, feedback provisions and product improvement clauses may now permit AI training, model improvement or long-term retention. It also says protections may not cover prompts, outputs and information derived from customer data, and that a restriction on training does not resolve questions about fine-tuning, evaluation, safety review or retrieval.

The article is written by attorneys and is aimed at legal teams and procurement professionals. It says the challenge is not simply understanding AI but understanding how AI changes the practical meaning of contract language that already exists. It advises organizations to stop asking whether their contracts mention AI and start asking whether existing language already permits it. It says legal teams should identify precisely which activities are permitted, prohibited or subject to separate approval, and should address the permitted use, retention and deletion of retrieval indexes and embeddings. It also notes that customers often warrant their inputs while vendors may give no comparable assurance about outputs, and it says part two of the series will address how to allocate that risk.

The article presents itself as analysis and does not report any enforcement action, court decision or regulatory change. It says the highest-risk provisions are often familiar ones negotiated years ago and long treated as routine. It does not say what happens next beyond noting that part two will address the asymmetry between customer warranties on inputs and vendor assurances on outputs. It ends with a disclaimer that the information may not apply in all situations and should not be acted upon without specific legal advice.

stories.Headline: AI data centers could be raising your electric bill — even if there's not one in your town
stories.Summary:
The articles describe how the growth of AI data centers is affecting electricity bills and local politics in the United States. Data centers consumed about 4.4% of all U.S. electricity in 2023, up from 58 terawatt-hours in 2014 to 176 terawatt-hours in 2023, according to the Yahoo article. The Department of Energy's Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory projects that share could reach between 6.7% and 12% of the country's total electricity consumption by 2028. The NPR article reports that this midterm election, voters in more than 40 cities and towns across eight states will decide ballot measures on data center bans, moratoriums and requirements that residents get a vote before one is built.

The Yahoo article says utilities may need to build new power plants, substations and transmission lines when a large data center connects to the grid, and depending on local regulations some of that expense can be passed to everyone who pays an electric bill. PJM Interconnection, which manages the grid for 67 million people across 13 states and Washington, D.C., saw auction prices rise roughly 1,000% in two years, reaching a record $333.44 per megawatt-day in December 2025, with its July 2026 auction slightly lower at $325. PJM's independent market monitor estimated that data center demand contributed $29.4 billion to capacity auction costs across four auctions. In Maryland, households are estimated to be paying an extra $168 to $216 a year, primarily because of growing data center demand, and a 2026 study from NC State, Carnegie Mellon and other universities projected wholesale electricity prices could rise between 6% and 29% nationally by 2030, with some regions seeing increases as high as 57%.

Ari Peskoe, director of Harvard's Electricity Law Initiative, told NPR that those costs can be spread across businesses and households throughout the region. Ohio approved rules in July 2025 requiring large data centers to pay for most of the electricity capacity they reserve, even if they don't use it all, and Virginia has considered a similar approach. In June 2026, New Jersey passed a law requiring large data centers to pay for the infrastructure they need instead of passing those costs on to residents, and Wisconsin regulators ruled that people who already pay electric bills shouldn't have to help cover the cost of new data centers. Several tech companies have signed a federal pledge to cover their own power needs, and Anthropic, the company behind Claude, has said it will cover any electricity price increases caused by its data centers, but consumer advocates are skeptical. Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, discussed the backlash with NPR's Fresh Air, and the article notes that in Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown, who is challenging Republican Senator Jon Husted, accuses Husted of aggressively courting data centers and backing corporate tax breaks while residents face rising electricity bills.

A Consumer Reports survey of more than 2,000 adults released in October 2026 found that 81% of people who had stayed in the same home for at least three years had seen their electricity bills rise, with 28% reporting increases of 20% to 49%, and 84% said they would support their utility creating a separate rate category for large users like data centers. A Gallup survey earlier in the year found that seven in 10 Americans oppose building AI data centers in their area. Most major data center projects go through a state's public utility commission, where regulators decide who pays, and residents in Wisconsin and Kentucky have already submitted thousands of comments about proposed data center rates. The Yahoo article says AI data centers aren't going away anytime soon, but who ends up paying for all that power is still being worked out, and in many cases homeowners can weigh in before the decision is made.

stories.Headline: Opsera relaunches as AI-native software factory with Forge at core
stories.Summary:
Opsera has relaunched as an AI-native software factory, with its Forge factory at the centre of the new approach. The company announced the relaunch in late October 2026, and Forge had been released in April of that year. Opsera said the move aims to change how software is delivered and how legacy systems are modernised. Forge was built as an AI-SDLC that enforces context, spec-based development and guardrails.

Forge is designed to help organisations move faster from idea to production while supporting any coding assistant. It works as an AI harness that provides the context, specifications and traceability needed to create specs from existing logic, architecture and business intent. Forge also includes ForgeScore, a modernisation assessment tool that evaluates legacy codebases for security, maintainability, cognitive load, semantic quality and future-proofing. That evaluation produces a modernisation blueprint based on technical risk, architectural complexity and AI readiness. Opsera's Unified Insights gives engineering, security and finance leaders one view of AI investment, tracking spending across tools, teams and workflows.

Kumar Chivukula, CEO of Opsera, said AI has changed how code gets written but not yet how software gets delivered, how legacy systems get modernised or how AI investment gets measured. He said the company rebuilt Opsera to solve those three problems. He also said enterprises keep their code, models and tools, while the AI-native software factory gives them the context, specifications and guardrails to turn AI-generated or legacy code into applications they can ship, trust and measure. The company said Unified Insights connects AI spend to results such as lower operating expenses and leaner token usage through tokenomics and token mapping.

Opsera was long known for its continuous orchestration platform for DevOps before the relaunch. The articles describe the change as a shift toward an AI-native software factory built around Forge. The company said the relaunch addresses challenges in software delivery, legacy system modernisation and the measurement of AI investment. The articles do not say what happens next beyond pointing readers to opsera.ai for more information.
