stories.Headline: AI Nuclear Push: $4.6B Raised, 2 Reactors Building [2026]
stories.Summary:
US nuclear startups have raised $4.6 billion so far in 2026, up from $3.8 billion in all of 2025, according to a Bloomberg report carried by EnergyNow.com. The money is driven by tech companies that want carbon-free power around the clock for their AI data centers. The hardware does not exist yet, though. The same report says only two new commercial reactors are under construction in the US and Canada, and no other project has won approval from regulators. Bloomberg first published the piece on Sept. 25, and it was still circulating through energy and finance outlets as of Oct. 31, 2026.

The gap between cash and kilowatts is the core of the story. Bloomberg Intelligence senior analyst Scott Levine does not expect widespread commercialization until around 2035. A Carnegie Endowment study by John Pendleton and Mackenzie Schuessler, dated June 2, says hyperscalers spent $443 billion on data centers in 2025 and are on track for more than $700 billion in 2026. An Energy Transitions Commission report dated Oct. 6 puts early US small modular reactor cost estimates at roughly $140 to $270 per megawatt-hour, while large reactors fall in a range of $40 to $190 per megawatt-hour. The same summary says US SMR capital cost estimates have climbed from $3,000 to $10,000 per kilowatt to $12,000 to $15,000 per kilowatt.

Carnegie counts about 13 gigawatts of potential nuclear capacity tied to hyperscaler commitments by the mid-2030s, roughly 6.9 GW from power purchase agreements and roughly 6.1 GW from direct partnerships with reactor developers. The deals that deliver soonest involve existing plants, including Microsoft with Constellation Energy on an 835 MW Three Mile Island Unit 1 restart in 2027 and Amazon with Talen Energy on 1.9 GW at Susquehanna by 2032. New-reactor deals cluster in the 2030 to 2039 window. Carnegie estimates projected hyperscaler nuclear output at 102 terawatt-hours a year against mid-range 2035 data center demand of 560 terawatt-hours a year, which works out to about 18% coverage.

Washington has tried to speed things up. Executive Order 14300, signed in May 2025, told the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to decide new reactor applications within 18 months and renewals within 12 months. Carnegie reports the commission completed more than 700 licensing actions in 2025, 90% of them ahead of schedule, and in March 2026 the NRC finalized Part 53, a risk-informed framework written for advanced reactors. Bloomberg frames regulators as only one of three bottlenecks, alongside cost and supply chain. Capital can accelerate paperwork and fund engineering teams, but it cannot compress the time needed to pour concrete, forge pressure vessels, and fuel a core.

stories.Headline: AI risks to the Sec. 7525 practitioner privilege
stories.Summary:
A federal district court has ruled that a criminal defendant’s use of a consumer AI chatbot to research his defense was not protected by attorney-client privilege or the work-product doctrine. The case involved Bradley Heppner, the former CEO of GWG Holdings, who faced charges of securities fraud, wire fraud, conspiracy, false statements to auditors, and falsifying corporate records. After receiving a grand jury subpoena and retaining defense counsel, Heppner used a consumer version of Anthropic’s Claude without his counsel’s guidance to research legal matters, develop defense strategies, and draft analyses. He produced 31 prompt-and-response documents and shared them with his counsel, and federal agents later seized the devices containing them during a search warrant execution. The court’s privilege holding rested on two independent grounds and a third, closer alternative ground, each of which the court considered sufficient on the facts presented.

First, the court ruled that Claude was not an attorney, so communications with the application were not client-attorney communications, and it rejected analogies to other internet-based software. Second, the court determined that there was no reasonable expectation of confidentiality in the material. The article says the decision in Heppner, if followed by other courts, would leave CPA-controlled AI work structurally exposed under Sec. 7525. Sec.

7525 was enacted as part of the IRS Restructuring and Reform Act of 1998, P.L. 105-206, and extends common-law confidentiality protection to communications between taxpayers and federally authorized tax practitioners. The protection has three structural limitations: it applies only in federal noncriminal tax matters, it excludes communications connected with promotion of participation in a tax shelter under Sec. 6662(d)(2)(C)(ii), and it inherits all the limits of the attorney-client privilege. The article says the IRS has shown renewed interest in pursuing practitioner workpapers, drafting memoranda, and contemporaneous communications documenting the analytical history of aggressive return positions. It argues that prudent practice now requires routing privilege-sensitive AI work through a Kovel-mediated architecture, imposing operational discipline at the AI prompt and verification layers, and adopting four engagement-letter provisions.

The article describes three groups of AI tools used in CPA practice: general-purpose large language models such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Copilot, tax-specialized platforms such as Blue J, Thomson Reuters’s Checkpoint Edge with CoCounsel, and Wolters Kluwer’s CCH AnswerConnect AI, and embedded features in workpaper, audit, and practice-management software. It says the AICPA’s revised Statements on Standards for Tax Services, effective Jan. 1, 2024, address technology competence and reliance on tools in SSTS No. 1, Section 1.4. Treasury Circular 230 lacks a dedicated AI provision, but the article says the duties of diligence under Section 10.22, competence under Section 10.35, and care in written advice under Section 10.37 extend to AI-assisted work. It also cites ABA Formal Opinion 512 as analogous guidance for CPAs operating under Kovel arrangements.

Articles.Title: AI risks to the Sec. 7525 practitioner privilege - The Tax Adviser

stories.Headline: PrivacyEvalClaw: A Tool-Augmented Deliberative Agent for Auditing Privacy Leakage in LLM Jailbreak Responses
stories.Summary:
A paper posted on arXiv on November 1, 2026 describes a new tool for checking whether responses from large language models leak personal information when users try to jailbreak them. The authors are Krishna Kanth Nakka, Yujun Wang, Shijie Zhou, Tu Nguyen, Gabriele Gelardi and Xuebing Zhou. They first studied existing privacy evaluators and found that these tools often disagree, especially on ambiguous cases that need more evidence or targeted analysis. The paper is titled PrivacyEvalClaw: A Tool-Augmented Deliberative Agent for Auditing Privacy Leakage in LLM Jailbreak Responses.

The authors introduce PrivacyEvalClaw, which they describe as a training-free deliberative agent for evaluating privacy leakage in jailbreak responses. Instead of relying on isolated single-pass judgments, it treats evaluators and analysis modules as tools, gathers evidence adaptively, investigates uncertain disclosures and reconciles conflicting signals before giving a final judgment. The primary experiments use pairwise LLM-as-Judge evaluation of complete trajectories. According to the abstract, PrivacyEvalClaw achieves favorable win rates against competing baselines across outcome, process and overall quality, and it produces explicit reasoning traces that make the evaluation process more transparent and auditable.

The paper attributes the work to the six named authors and presents the findings as their own study and experiments. It says existing approaches increasingly rely on guard models and LLM-as-Judges, and that these evaluators may interpret the same response differently. The authors state that their systematic study found substantial disagreement among privacy evaluators, particularly in ambiguous cases. They present PrivacyEvalClaw as a response to those findings, with the aim of making privacy evaluation of jailbreak responses more reliable and auditable.

The articles give no information beyond the paper's abstract and listing page, so no further context or next steps are reported. The page notes that arXivLabs is a framework for collaborators to develop and share features on the site, and that partners in it accept values including openness, community, excellence and user data privacy. It also invites ideas for projects that would add value for the arXiv community. More to follow.

Articles.Title: PrivacyEvalClaw: A Tool-Augmented Deliberative Agent for Auditing Privacy Leakage in LLM Jailbreak Responses

stories.Headline: Tech services firms face a talent decision, not a shortage, in $100-200 billion AI race, says Boston Consulting Group
stories.Summary:
Boston Consulting Group released a report on Thursday, October 29, 2026, saying technology services firms do not face an AI talent shortage but a talent decision. The report says AI-led services are expected to add $100-200 billion of net new work by 2030. It says firms can staff much of that work from people they already employ. The findings draw on more than 2,500 AI-tagged job postings and over 50,000 professional profiles across more than 15 firms, plus BCG's own skills database.

BCG identified 40 distinct Applied AI roles, each linked to an existing technology role. A data scientist or full-stack developer can grow into a forward-deployed engineer, a DevOps engineer into an AI Ops engineer, and a data engineer into a semantic engineer. Moving a data scientist into a forward-deployed engineer role takes roughly three times the upskilling effort of moving a data engineer into an AI data engineer role. Firms that hire against the new titles pay up to roughly 35% over the comparable traditional role.

Sreyssha George, Managing Director and Partner at BCG and a co-author of the report, said the people who can deliver Applied AI are largely already on the payroll. She said clients are moving from paying for hours to paying for outcomes, which changes how work is staffed and rewarded. The report sorts the 40 roles into four groups, with a distinct action for each: buy the scarce anchor roles, build the scale drivers at volume, retain the delivery core, and watch the early signals. It also proposes five career tracks from a single role, with lateral moves between them and progression tied to demonstrated capability.

The report says the decision that turned existing talent into supply was role architecture, including a skill taxonomy, proficiency gates, bands and a dedicated job family, so each Applied AI role has a title, a level and a band attached. It closes with five questions for leaders to answer this quarter, including whether pay bands and career paths would hold against an AI-native offer. The global services market is projected to grow from roughly $1.6-1.7 trillion in 2025 to $2.2-2.4 trillion by 2030. AI-led services contribute $300-400 billion of that growth through building and running agentic solutions, work that becomes outsourceable as agentic tooling matures, and the human oversight and governance clients may not hand to a model.

Articles.Title: Tech services firms face a talent decision, not a shortage, in $100-200 billion AI race, says Boston Consulting Group

stories.Headline: EU DMA [2026]: 10% Revenue Fines Hit Big Tech Cloud, AI
stories.Summary:
The European Commission is pushing on three fronts at once to rein in U.S. tech giants as of November 1, 2026. It is weighing a cloud gatekeeper decision that would pull Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure under the Digital Markets Act. It has a draft AI Office rulebook open for feedback. It also just finished a Digital Markets Act review that left the law mostly intact. Bloomberg reported on October 2 that the Commission plans to name AWS and Azure as gatekeepers as soon as November, though the decision is still a draft and could slip.

On June 25, 2026 the Commission told Amazon and Microsoft it had reached a preliminary view that their cloud services should be designated under the Digital Markets Act. It called AWS the largest and Azure the second largest cloud computing service in the EU. Its reasoning rested on lock-in effects, high switching costs, large ecosystems and entrenched positions that have lasted for years. It also said AI tools and partnerships have become a decisive factor when companies buy cloud services. The cloud designation decision is due in November 2026, and the cloud investigation that could add interoperability and data portability duties runs to May 2027.

If the designation goes through, both companies get six months to bring the designated cloud services into line with the Digital Markets Act. The Register reported that the penalty ceiling for non-compliance is 10 percent of worldwide annual turnover. The obligations reporters described include interoperability, data access, rules against favoring a provider's own services, and limits on lock-in tactics. The AI Office feedback window closes on November 9, 2026, and adoption of the AI Office rules is planned for the fourth quarter of 2026. The draft AI Office rules would take effect 20 days after publication in the Official Journal.

Microsoft told reporters it was in a productive dialogue with regulators, while according to The Register it also argued that ignoring the growing power of Google Cloud and Gemini would tilt the market in a harmful way. AWS said European customers already enjoy an unusually wide choice of cloud options and, per The Register, argued the findings disregard the breadth of services on offer and could deter investment. Neither company confirmed the designation was coming. The Commission said the assessments were ongoing and no final decision had been taken, and it had already shared its preliminary assessments with both companies in June.

stories.Headline: S. Korea mulls over longer bans, criminal complaints for use of AI glasses in college entrance tests
stories.Summary:
South Korea’s Education Ministry announced on Oct 29 that it plans to step up enforcement against students who use smart glasses to cheat on the country’s annual college entrance exam. The measures include filing criminal complaints or requesting investigations. The ministry is also considering extending the ban on repeat test-takers caught cheating from one year to up to three years. The announcement follows rules made in July that list smart glasses as prohibited items for the 2027 academic year’s Suneung, the College Scholastic Ability Test.

Under current regulations, wearing or using the glasses invalidates a student’s results and bars them from taking the following year’s exam. Students found with the devices who fail to surrender them before the first session can have their current-year results invalidated. Refusing a proctor’s request to inspect a smart device may also lead to invalidation of the current results and disqualification from the following year’s exam, after a review. The authorities will assign one staff member to each of the 1,312 test sites nationwide to help identify smart glasses and other prohibited devices during this year’s exam.

The ministry said it will urge universities to adopt similarly strict penalties for their own admissions tests in 2026. It also plans to assess radio-signal detectors being developed by specialist institutions, and if deemed feasible, the devices could be distributed to test sites starting in 2027. The ministry said it would protect teachers who diligently supervise exams from being held responsible or disadvantaged when cheating involves smart glasses or other devices. The report came from The Korea Herald and Asia News Network.

stories.Headline: James Gallagher's Bill Targets AI-Driven Trafficking
stories.Summary:
James Gallagher introduced the Countering Online Trafficking Act in Washington, D.C., according to a report published on October 31, 2026. Gallagher has served as California Assembly Republican leader. The bill targets traffickers who use artificial intelligence to find and groom children online. It would require the State Department to evaluate whether its Office to Monitor and Combat Trafficking in Persons has the expertise to identify and respond to these evolving threats.

Under the bill, the office's ambassador-at-large would assess whether existing personnel have the technical background to address AI-facilitated trafficking. If the assessment finds gaps, the ambassador-at-large would then have to develop a plan to close them. The articles cite a State Department warning that AI can automate and expand grooming, letting traffickers reach far more targets than human recruiters could alone. The department's 2025 Trafficking in Persons Report said AI systems can automate and scale grooming through chatbots that optimize manipulation tactics using natural language processing and sentiment analysis.

Gallagher framed the legislation around the concern that criminals are moving faster than the institutions meant to stop them. He said human traffickers use new technology to prey on children and that the federal government must keep pace. He added that human trafficking is a horrific crime demanding action, and that the responsibility to protect the innocent remains constant even as technology changes. The articles also note that Gallagher previously helped secure passage of California's SB 14, which made qualifying child sex-trafficking offenses serious felonies under the state's three-strikes law.

The articles cite United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime figures showing detected trafficking victims worldwide rose 25% in 2022 compared with pre-pandemic 2019. Detected child victims rose 31% over the same period, girls accounted for a 38% rise among child victims, and children made up 38% of all detected victims by 2022. Victims trafficked for forced labor rose 47% between 2019 and 2022, while trafficking for forced criminality, including online scams, went from 1% of detected victims in 2016 to 8% by 2022. Women and girls made up 61% of detected victims in 2022, drawn from the 2024 Global Report on Trafficking in Persons covering 156 countries. The articles say the bill is framed as a diagnostic step rather than a sweeping overhaul, and whether the assessment finds serious gaps, and what any resulting plan would look like, remains to be seen.

stories.Headline: ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization
stories.Summary:
Ning Yang, Bohan Cui, Zhuowen Liu and Yuting Wang posted a paper on arXiv on November 1, 2026 describing a method called ResCom. The work addresses low-bit weight and activation quantization, which cuts the memory and computation needed to deploy large language models. The authors note that activation rounding can still degrade accuracy after calibration, because reconstruction from rounded inputs cannot tell activations within the same quantization bin apart. Their proposal is a low-rank correction that uses the activation rounding residual to compensate for the resulting layer-output error.

The method relies on an output-aware calibration procedure that picks residual directions by how much they contribute to output reconstruction. It computes the correction in closed form, with no gradient training and no updates to the calibrated weights. On Llama-3-8B with 4-bit weights and activations, rank-32 attention corrections lowered WikiText-2 perplexity from 7.708 to 7.147. The same setting improved MMLU by 2.89 percentage points and raised five-shot GSM8K accuracy from 23.96 to 36.16 percent. The authors also evaluated models from 1B to 70B parameters and a held-out C4 set to test the method beyond this setting.

The evaluated FP32 implementation adds 2.25 percent to 4K prefill time, according to the abstract. A separate compact-storage implementation keeps a 27.7 percent peak-memory reduction relative to FP16. The paper is listed on arXiv with a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source, and the page also describes arXivLabs, a framework for collaborators to develop and share features on the site. The abstract does not say what happens next beyond the reported evaluations.

Articles.Title: ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization

stories.Headline: Amplify, Locate, Estimate (ALE) on Rare-Failure Rates of Fine-Tuned LLMs
stories.Summary:
Patrick Reichherzer, Jonathan Evertz and Thorsten Holz posted a paper on arXiv on October 31, 2026 describing a method called Amplify, Locate, Estimate, or ALE. The method is meant to estimate rare failure probabilities in fine-tuned large language models. Safety fine-tuning can make undesirable behaviors so rare that measuring their frequency by direct sampling becomes very expensive. The paper is listed as arXiv 2610.35472.

ALE uses the change in token log-probabilities caused by safety fine-tuning to define an amplification direction. Along that direction the failure rate is raised so it can be measured cheaply. The authors develop a score-function estimator that uses the amplified batch to recover the local slope of the log failure rate from the token probabilities of sampled failures, which allows extrapolation back to rare target rates. They also use the amplified batch to get an importance-sampling estimate. Across 41 evaluation targets, the median of ALE's estimate-to-reference ratios is close to one, and 37 ALE estimates fall within a factor of three of reference values from independent direct measurements.

Ablation tests show that with a budget of up to about 1000 labeled rollouts, plus a cheap unlabeled scan, ALE estimates failure probabilities for Qwen3-8B fine-tunes down to about 10 to the minus 5. Direct measurement at that level can require hundreds of thousands of rollouts. The required sampling budget scales inversely with failure probability at fixed relative precision. The paper does not say who will use the method or what happens next.

Articles.Title: Amplify, Locate, Estimate (ALE) on Rare-Failure Rates of Fine-Tuned LLMs

stories.Headline: Pope says 'most urgent' challenge facing AI race is need for institutional ethical framework - The Tribune-Democrat
stories.Summary:
Pope Leo XIV spoke on Friday at a Vatican gathering of artificial intelligence researchers and experts. He told the meeting that the most urgent challenge in the AI race is to identify international institutions that will put ethical principles into practice. The American pope has made AI a key priority. The gathering was held in the Vatican and was co-sponsored by the Pontifical Academy of Life, the Vatican's bioethics think tank, and the Future of Life Institute.

The pope said the principles are already known, but what is missing are the institutions that can effectively safeguard the global common good. He called for shared standards, independent oversight and clear mechanisms of accountability, so that decisions on the development and use of AI can be examined, challenged when necessary, and met with appropriate remedies for any harm caused. Leo's 2026 AI encyclical, "Magnificent Humanity," called for robust regulation of AI and for its developers to work for the common good rather than profit. On Friday he highlighted many of the encyclical's key points, especially that the future of AI is not predetermined and that much will depend on the choices developers and political leaders make today.

He also stressed that machines are tools, not persons, and should not be granted legal status or be delegated to make life-or-death decisions. He said that among all the challenges facing the AI field, the institutional ethical framework was the most urgent. The gathering was a chance for the Vatican's in-house AI commission to engage with experts in the field. The articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: Ftc Investigates Major Companies Over Personalized Pricing And Ai - News12
stories.Summary:
The Federal Trade Commission is investigating how major companies use artificial intelligence and consumers' personal data to set prices and determine worker compensation. Delta, United, JetBlue, Lyft, Uber, DoorDash, Instacart, Target and Walmart are among the companies named in the investigation. The agency is seeking information about how these businesses use consumer data to determine what customers pay for products and services. The investigation was reported by News 12 on October 30, 2026, with an update that afternoon, and in a Bronx report on October 31, 2026.

The FTC's request focuses on the use of personal data and AI in pricing and in setting worker pay. The agency wants to learn how consumer information shapes the prices customers are charged for products and services. Companies that fail to provide the requested information could be required to answer questions in federal court, according to the FTC. The articles do not give further details on the scope of the requests or a deadline for the companies to respond.

Consumers like Jasmine Edwards raised concerns about being charged different prices based on their online activity. She said that if she is looking for a plane ticket on her phone, which she does constantly because she likes to travel, being charged a different price every time she looks is ridiculous. stories.Headline: Foxconn working on a new tie-up with OpenAI, says there is no AI bubble
stories.Summary:
Foxconn said on Oct 30 that it is working on a new collaboration with OpenAI, the leading US artificial intelligence developer. Chairman Young Liu told reporters at the company's annual technology showcase in Taipei that he had met OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman earlier that day. Liu said an announcement would come once details were confirmed, and he did not elaborate further. Foxconn is formally called Hon Hai Precision Industry and is the world's biggest contract electronics manufacturer. Any new deal would build on an agreement the two firms made in 2025 to work together on designing and engineering data-centre racks, components and other AI hardware.

Foxconn is Nvidia's biggest AI server maker and has six factory buildings in Houston, Texas, where it makes AI servers for Nvidia. Liu said the company sees a need for further expansion there. Foxconn said in August that its cloud and networking products segment, which includes AI servers, accounted for 51% of second-quarter revenue, exceeding 50% for the first time. Liu said the AI industry was not in a bubble and that Foxconn expects to maintain double-digit growth in 2027. He spoke as AI-sector stocks have been hit hard by concerns that relentless heavy investment is not sustainable amid climbing borrowing costs.

Separately, Brand Cheng, chairman of Foxconn unit Foxconn Industrial Internet, told Reuters that more than 10 humanoid robots had been deployed at its Texas facilities for internal use. He said Foxconn plans to extend deployment beyond the state. According to presentation materials seen by Reuters, FII introduced two wheeled models in October, one that lifts things vertically and one that can bend at the waist for assembly as well as loading and unloading tasks. The unit is developing AI models for humanoid robots based on Nvidia's GR00T foundation model. The articles do not say when the OpenAI tie-up details will be announced or what the collaboration will involve.

stories.Headline: Lao Gan Ma faces backlash over AI automation claims, company denies mass layoffs
stories.Summary:
Lao Gan Ma, one of China's best-known chili sauce brands, faced public criticism after comments about its use of artificial intelligence in quality inspection were seen as evidence of large-scale job cuts. The controversy began after Li Xin, executive vice-president and chief quality officer of the Guiyang-based company, spoke at the 2026 Guizhou provincial quality development conference. Li said an AI-powered visual inspection system had significantly reduced product defect rates and helped the company reach a record-high revenue of 5.4 billion yuan in 2025. According to a report by China Business Herald, Li said more than 600 workers were involved in sorting chili peppers on the production line before the AI system was introduced, compared to just 48 after it was deployed.

The remarks were quickly amplified on social media, where headlines claiming Lao Gan Ma laid off more than 500 workers after adopting AI sparked widespread criticism. Some consumers threatened to boycott the brand, with comments saying that if the company replaced workers with AI, they would get its products taken off the shelves. Lao Gan Ma denied the reports, and a staff member from its human resources department told local media on Oct 26 that claims of mass layoffs were false. According to Phoenix News, the company confirmed it uses AI inspection technology but said it had never employed that many workers on the production line.

Public records added to the debate, as Jimu News reported that data from Tianyancha and Qichacha showed the number of employees covered by social insurance at Guiyang Nanming Laoganma Flavor Food declined from 2,912 in 2022 to 1,783 in 2023, then to 941 in 2024 and 740 in 2025. The articles said changes in insured headcount do not necessarily indicate layoffs, because retirements, staff turnover, outsourcing arrangements, or changes in the legal entity responsible for social insurance can also affect the figures. Jason Yu, general manager of CTR Market Research, said the controversy reflects growing public concern about the human impact of AI. He said people are not rejecting technology but a mindset that calculates efficiency while ignoring people, and that companies should explain how workers are supported through the transition.

Lao Gan Ma's business performance has remained resilient, with revenue of 5.26 billion yuan in 2022, 5.38 billion yuan in 2023, and 5.39 billion yuan in 2024, according to the 2025 Guizhou Top 100 Enterprises ranking. Sixth Tone reported that Lao Gan Ma's founder, Tao Huabi, was herself a laid-off worker who sold cold rice noodles from a street stall before founding the brand in 1997. As of Wednesday, a hashtag related to the scandal had garnered more than 120 million views on Weibo, with some users defending automation as part of industrial upgrading and others arguing the company should consider its responsibilities to workers. The debate comes as China seeks to expand AI adoption while curbing its potential negative effects on employment, and on Oct 23 the State Council issued guidelines calling for maximizing AI's potential to create jobs while slowing the impact of AI-related job replacement.

stories.Headline: Behind every screen is a face: FABC communication chair urges Asian Church to humanize AI
stories.Summary:
Bishop Marcelino Antonio “Junie” Maralit Jr. of the Diocese of San Pablo, Philippines, who chairs the FABC Office of Social Communication, gave an address titled “The Face Behind the Screen” on October 29, 2026. He spoke in the conference hall of St. Jose Villa in Macau during the annual FABC-OSC Assembly. The assembly runs from October 27 to 31 and brings together Asian bishops, priests, religious, and lay media leaders. Its theme is “Magnifica Humanitas and the Synodal Ways of Evangelization in Asia: Communicating Christ in the Age of Artificial Intelligence.” The meeting coincides with preparations for the 450th anniversary of the Diocese of Macau, the oldest diocese in the Far East.

Bishop Maralit said two-thirds of the world’s six billion internet users live in Asia, yet the continent also has the world’s largest offline populations. Catholics make up just 11 percent of Asia’s population, so millions may first meet the Church on a screen rather than in a building. He warned of digital wounds such as human trafficking in cyber-scam compounds, online child exploitation, state surveillance, deepfakes, and the loss of interior prayer life. He urged clergy never to pass off AI-generated homilies as their own or hand spiritual care to algorithms. He called for transparency, data privacy, formation of Asian seminarians, who are nearly 29 percent of the world’s total, solidarity with marginalized data workers, and interreligious partnerships against digital abuse.

The bishop said the fundamental challenge of AI is not technological but anthropological, quoting Pope Leo XIV. He said God did not save us by sending information but sent a Person with a face, a voice, and hands. He described the digital world in Asia as the main square and the Areopagus of our time. He concluded that behind every screen in Asia there is a face, and that machines can carry words faster than ever but only persons can carry presence.

Dr. Levi Checketts of Hong Kong Baptist University gave a keynote on the human costs of technology, including environmental damage from mining and electronic waste and poorly paid, psychologically demanding data work. Professor Leo-Martin Angelo R. Ocampo of Manila’s University of Santo Tomas contrasted Babel and Jerusalem, saying algorithms reflect human priorities. Bishop Stephen Lee Bun-sang of Macau told communicators at the opening Mass on October 28 to listen before speaking and accompany before judging. Gethsemani Cindy Gorospe of Radio Veritas Asia reported on the First Asian Catholic Digital Missionaries Assembly, held in Manila from September 10 to 13 with more than 100 creators from 17 Asian countries. She proposed a dedicated FABC-OSC committee and urged support for young communicators ahead of World Youth Day 2027 in Seoul.

stories.Headline: Oracle Introduces AI Agent-Ready Fusion Applications Setup and Configuration to Speed Implementations - Engineering / Artificial Intelligence - Oracle Corporation
stories.Summary:
Oracle announced the Oracle Fusion Setup and Configuration Registry, or FSCR, on October 30, 2026, at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas. The registry is a public Git repository that makes Oracle Fusion Cloud Applications setup and configuration machine-readable and executable by AI agents. Oracle built the registry and maintains it continuously. It captures Oracle product expertise and best practices as reusable AI skills.

The registry lets agents plan, execute, test, and validate setup and configuration directly in Oracle Fusion Applications. It covers configuration options, dependencies, sequencing, execution, testing, and validation. AI assistants and coding agents from OpenAI and others can turn business requirements, process documents, policies, and existing configurations into implementation runbooks and then do the work. Expert reviewers can examine completed configurations, request adjustments, and approve them for deployment. Systems integrators can extend the open foundation with their own methodologies, accelerators, automations, and industry solutions.

Chris Leone, executive vice president of Applications Development at Oracle, said customers and partners often have to rebuild critical setup knowledge for every implementation or rely on static documentation and one-time guides that go out of date. He said the registry is like having an expert Oracle product manager guide teams through the whole setup and configuration process. DK Sinha, CEO of Accenture Edge, said FSCR gives an AI-ready foundation that helps organizations move beyond manual, repetitive configuration work. Chris Rapp, CEO of Apex IT, said the registry lets partners extend Oracle's authoritative foundation with automation and resources for specific customer and industry needs.

Swami Rajagopalan, global Oracle offering leader at Deloitte Consulting LLP, said FSCR gives the Oracle network a common foundation for configuring and implementing Fusion Applications. Brandon Johnson, Oracle practice leader at Grant Thornton, said implementation teams should not have to recreate the same foundational setup logic on every project. Kevin Sullivan, Global and US alliance leader at PwC, said the open-source foundation lets the firm invest more in industry insight and differentiated services. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the registry being continuously maintained alongside Oracle Fusion Applications.

stories.Headline: Humans are still doing the work behind some AI agents
stories.Summary:
AI agents still cannot reliably handle many real-world tasks, especially phone calls, so people are being used to finish the work. CNBC reported on October 31, 2026, that foundation models from companies like Meta and OpenAI can browse the web but often fail at tasks such as negotiating a cable bill, booking a doctor's appointment or reserving a cleaning service. Startups including Marissa Mayer's Dazzle AI, Duckbill and Wajo AI are building human workers into their services for when the software fails. Meta's Muse, OpenAI's Dots and other agents can do many web-browsing tasks, but the technology is still early and often hits digital roadblocks.

Duckbill recently launched an application programming interface, or API, that lets companies building personal agents connect to human contract workers. Duckbill's CEO, Meghan Joyce, said the company breaks tasks into small pieces that an average adult can do reliably, and it tracks what happens. Duckbill uses 1099 contractors, compares them to Uber and DoorDash drivers, does full background checks and also uses workers from contact center businesses. Mayer said Dazzle checks contractors for discretion, good taste and good judgment, and she described the market as being in a transitionary period. Meta said testing with human contractors is core to product development, and a spokesperson said Meta currently does not use humans to complete users' Muse requests.

Mayer said AI models can lack common sense. She described a Dazzle user who asked the agent to handle a roof replacement, a broken window and a glass tabletop purchase at once, and the agent confused window glass with tabletop glass. Dazzle flagged the task and sent it to a person, who sorted it out within seconds, while an agent might have burned many tokens or never found a good solution. Wajo AI's CEO, Shivani Poddar, said her startup uses human workers for phone calls and CAPTCHA tests, and she argued that AI plus humans is what gets the job done. Mayer said Dazzle is not trying to hide the human role and called the human in the loop a benefit.

A separate article in ET CIO, published October 29, 2026, said human skills are becoming more valuable as AI takes on routine work. It cited the World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025, based on more than 1,000 employers representing over 14 million workers across 22 industry clusters and 55 economies. Analytical thinking was the most sought-after core skill, with seven out of 10 companies calling it essential, followed by resilience, flexibility and agility, leadership and social influence, creative thinking, and motivation and self-awareness. The report projected that 39% of key skills will change by 2030, down from 44% in 2023, and that 170 million new jobs will be created globally over the next five years, a net increase of 78 million. The author, Kshama Singh, HR Head at Powerweave, said organizations should hire for curiosity, judgment and collaboration, train people to work with AI and develop leaders who guide teams with empathy.

stories.Headline: Andy Jassy Says West Is 'Very Hungry' For More Western Open Source AI Models as Amazon Adds China's Kimi and GLM to Bedrock
stories.Summary:
Amazon.com Inc. added China's Kimi and GLM open models to its Bedrock AI platform, the company said during its third-quarter earnings call on Thursday. The additions join Bedrock's mix of proprietary and open models. CEO Andy Jassy said Bedrock now offers closed models from Anthropic and OpenAI alongside open models such as Moonshot's Kimi K3 and Z.ai's GLM 5.3. He also referenced SpaceXAI's Grok 4.7 model on Bedrock. Earlier in October, Bedrock added Z.ai's GLM 5.3 open-weight model, which the company said offers enhanced capabilities for agentic coding and complex software engineering with AWS security and compliance protections.

Jassy said the Western world is very hungry for additional Western open models, and that he believes this will happen over time. He called Bedrock's potential gigantic and suggested the platform could ultimately become comparable in scale to AWS's EC2 cloud computing offering. He emphasized Bedrock's security structure, saying customer inputs and outputs are not shared with model providers or used to train their foundational models. He expects six to eight models to handle more than 95% of workloads within two to three years.

The expansion follows the broader rise of Chinese-developed open AI systems. Last week, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt said China was roughly six months behind the U.S. in AI, but warned that free products could still give China a strategic advantage. He said China's cheaper, often free and open-weight models could gain traction in developing markets, and attributed the country's progress partly to access to restricted advanced chips and the use of distillation to replicate Western AI capabilities. In July, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang called Chinese models excellent and argued Washington should use rather than ban high-quality open-source technology. He dismissed fears that Chinese open models pose security risks or threaten U.S. tech firms, arguing wider adoption of models like DeepSeek and Kimi will boost demand for Nvidia chips and infrastructure.

stories.Headline: AI-fueled hacking spree ‘Black October’ culminates with $6.3B Binance hack
stories.Summary:
In late October 2026, a month-long wave of cyberattacks that experts called Black October hit hundreds of companies and institutions worldwide. The spree ended on Thursday, October 29, when hackers stole an estimated $6.3 billion from Binance, the largest crypto heist in history. On Saturday the FBI confirmed that TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking unit, was behind the theft. The attackers got in through several breach points, including one engineer's computer, and took the funds in about 20 minutes.

The month's targets included the Federal Election Commission, Sony, John Deere, Oracle Health, Burger King Japan, the coding agent OpenCode, the State Bank of India and French grocery stores. At least nine AI developer platforms also disclosed incidents: Fireworks AI on October 6, Andromeda on October 9, Zeabur on October 14, Lightning AI on October 15, OpenCode on October 16 and 17, Railway on October 20, Warp on October 23, CommandCode on October 28 and Northflank on October 30. Fireworks, OpenCode and Warp reported signs of an agent swarm attack, and OpenCode and CommandCode blamed attempts at distillation. On October 21 the NSA warned of two vulnerabilities in PHP, which powers more than 70% of websites, that could let attackers take over servers without prior access or authentication, and said the risks required immediate patching across US government agencies. The FEC took its electronic filing system offline on Tuesday for about 41 hours after suspicious activity, disrupting mandatory 24-hour and 48-hour campaign spending reports ahead of the November 3 midterms, and declined to comment.

Binance said on Saturday that it had already covered 90% of the lost customer funds and would fully cover the financial impact, citing measurable progress, transparent reporting and concrete actions. Dr. AK Pradeep, founder and CEO of Sensori.AI, told the Post that every hack is concerning but Binance is most concerning, and that banks would be next, followed by individual payment mechanisms, because the world has never been prepared for super-intelligence thieves. Zeabur shared a full write-up and said it will shut down because of its incident. Railway released a preliminary report and timeline, saying it believed initial access came through privilege escalation in its build infrastructure. Warp suggested a third-party vendor dependency, and OpenCode pointed to a legacy system.

The articles tie the volume of attacks to AI models such as Claude Code, which have lowered the skill barrier so that less-skilled actors can let AI agents find flaws for them. Wiz Research linked stolen keys from the vendor breaches to resale operations, including one around the address 23.106.46.239 that appears to call itself momo and runs the site llm-routing.com, and a second at xingjiabiapi.org. In two cases Wiz documented, abuse of enterprise keys ran up likely over $100,000 in usage at list price, with about 800,000 and 1.7 million Bedrock calls before the keys were remediated. The articles do not say what happens next beyond Binance's reimbursement pledge, Zeabur's shutdown and the ongoing analysis of the incidents.

stories.Headline: AI Balloon in China Deflates by Half a Trillion Dollars
stories.Summary:
China's AI and semiconductor stock index, the STAR50, fell 40 percent over four months, wiping out 480 billion dollars in market value, according to Reuters reporting cited by Futurism and CleanTechnica. The drop hit shares of Unitree, a robotics company whose stock has halved since its much-hyped IPO in August. The chipmaker CXMT lost more than a quarter of its value in the past month. A Beijing fund manager, Dong Baozhen, told Reuters that the market had turned into a speculative craze and that the bubble was now bursting.

The decline followed a viral claim that 55 percent of China's AI tokens went to short dramas and video generation, a figure that COL Group, a digital-content company, gave at a June 3 investor event. Caixin reported that the company's investor record put e-commerce and marketing at 24 percent and software development at 15 percent. ByteDance, maker of the Seedance 2.5 video model, publicly disputed the figure, saying video generation was only about 10 percent of its own computing. Three state-affiliated outlets, including the People's Daily on October 21, pushed back on the claim, and the People's Daily rejected the simple comparison and listed AI uses in research and industry.

The People's Daily commentary was titled "Turning 'Gunpowder' into 'Fireworks'? Beware the Claim That China's AI Has Gone Astray." Nanfang Commentary asked readers not to judge AI by its tokens, and Beijing News questioned whether the contrast between American and Chinese AI was a false proposition. ByteDance challenged the numbers directly. Caixin traced the 55 percent figure to COL Group's roadshow and conference call, and noted that a CAICT report said to support it can no longer be found on the institute's website.

The debate reflected anxiety about how AI should be used, with entertainment ranked below productivity and coding. China had 851 million micro-drama viewers as of May 2026, about three-quarters of its internet population, and more than 90 percent of the roughly 430,000 micro-dramas released in the first eight months of 2026 were AI productions. A rough calculation in the ChinaTalk article put AI micro-dramas at about 7.4 percent of token use, far below 55 percent. The articles say it remains to be seen whether this is the start of a much larger deflation of AI bubbles.

stories.Headline: Two Chipmakers to Account for 73% of Q4 Profit at Korean Listed Firms
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics and SK hynix reported record quarterly operating profits, but their shares still fell on October 30, 2026. Samsung posted 107.4405 trillion won in operating profit, up about 783%, and SK hynix posted 83.3338 trillion won, up about 632.1%. Their shares dropped 3.02% and 7.08% respectively. The KOSPI closed down 206.92 points, or 3.48%, at 5,730.74 that day, after falling as low as 5,599.42 during the session and triggering a sell-side sidecar. Foreign investors sold a net 1.6169 trillion won worth of KOSPI shares, including 429 billion won of SK hynix and 213.4 billion won of Samsung Electronics.

For the fourth quarter, 188 KOSPI-listed companies are forecast to post 296.4814 trillion won in combined operating profit. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix account for 73.4% of that, or 217.7417 trillion won. Forecasts for the remaining companies have been cut by about 2.0% over the past month, including Hyundai Motor at minus 14.47%, LG Electronics at minus 38.59%, LG Innotek at minus 39.59% and Hanwha Ocean at minus 17.38%. Of the 76 companies that reported third-quarter results, combined operating profit beat forecasts by 3.38%, but excluding the two chipmakers it came in 1.09% below estimates, with 42 companies, or 55.3%, falling short.

The market decline followed weak results from Alphabet, Amazon and Intel. Amazon put $77.3 billion into data center facilities in the third quarter, pushing free cash flow to minus $42.4 billion, six times worse than the minus $7.6 billion in the second quarter. Alphabet's third-quarter free cash flow fell to minus $9.07 billion, and its shares plunged 12.64% after its earnings release, erasing about $500 billion, or 700 trillion won, in market value in a single day. Intel's chief financial officer said positive free cash flow would be difficult to achieve next year as well.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics announced an 879.3 billion won supply contract for MLCCs used in AI servers, yet its shares slid 7.50%. Kia's third-quarter operating profit rose 24.3% from a year earlier but came in 22.9% below the market forecast of 2.3574 trillion won, sending its shares down 11.73% to a 52-week low. With investor deposits falling to the 88 trillion won range, whether buying spreads to non-semiconductor sectors has emerged as the key test for a market rebound. China's CXMT saw third-quarter revenue surge 613% from a year earlier to 118.7 billion yuan, about 23.812 trillion won, and swung to a net profit of 54.4 billion yuan, though growth from the previous quarter was just 19.3%, down from 95.9% between the first and second quarters.

stories.Headline: The Tangled Web of AI Bets Is Reason to Fear Tech Stocks
stories.Summary:
Tech shares fell across Asia on Friday, the yen rose and bonds headed for their biggest monthly gain in nearly three years, as investors moved to safety on worries that huge and rising AI spending may not deliver sufficient returns. In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng Index opened up 52 points, or 0.23 percent, at 23,011. The China enterprises index rose 23 points, or 0.31 percent, to 7,779, while the tech index fell 23 points, or 0.63 percent, to 3,720. In Shanghai, the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index opened down 45 points, or 1.25 percent, at 3,605, and the blue-chip CSI300 headed for its largest monthly fall in a decade after nearly four months of AI stocks tanking on fears that a slowdown in demand for chips and other data centre equipment could crush revenues. The Shenzhen Component Index fell 267 points, or 2.4 percent, to 10,871, while the ChiNext Index plunged 3.29 percent to 2,434.

In Tokyo, the Nikkei opened 315 points, or 0.49 percent, down at 64,344 and was 1,742 points lower at one stage before noon, tracking overnight losses on Wall Street and weighed down by late earnings from Amazon.com and Intel that showed massive cash burns. In Seoul, the Kospi dived 177 points, or 2.99 percent, to open at 5,760 before falling further to be 313 points down at one stage before noon, at one point triggering a sidecar trading curb that halted algorithmic trading for five minutes. The weakness came as shares in Google parent Alphabet fell 12.6 percent on Wall Street and slid a little further after hours, wiping out US$500 billion in market value, as massive AI spending turned the company's cash flow negative. An aftermarket plunge of 23 percent in Intel shares and a drop of seven percent in Amazon stocks, as they too burn through cash, drove Nasdaq 100 futures down 1.4 percent and sent stocks of chipmakers around Asia into a tailspin.

Pepperstone analyst Chris Weston said the market is not necessarily questioning whether the AI buildout can be financed, but is increasingly questioning whether shareholders will earn an adequate return on the enormous capital being deployed. Nerves were also frayed by a potentially record-breaking hack at Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, which drove down bitcoin, other cryptocurrency prices and stocks including rival exchange Coinbase. Investors' rush into bonds was further spurred by the Federal Reserve's Wednesday decision to keep US interest rates on hold, with no firm projection of when it might need to hike next. Benchmark 10-year US Treasury yields fell by more than seven basis points in Tokyo trade on Friday to 4.91 percent, a fall of some 37 bps through October and the largest one-month drop since December 2023. The risk-averse mood strengthened haven currencies such as the yen, pushing the currency up about 0.2 percent to 157.47 per US dollar.

stories.Headline: Chinese Spy Targeted Nvidia's Jensen Huang, U.S. Officials Say
stories.Summary:
U.S. intelligence agencies believe a Chinese national known as Alice Huang, also called Huang Le, built a close relationship with Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang and passed information to China, The New York Times reported on the 19th, according to the Seoul Economic Daily. She was a former senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company that buys Nvidia chips and leases computing capacity to Chinese companies. U.S. authorities placed her under electronic surveillance and found she was in contact with a U.S. citizen, and a procedure to unmask the person revealed it was Jensen Huang. Photos posted online in June 2024 showed the two at a bar in Taipei, Taiwan, after a local tech show, and they were also seen together in May 2025 leaving a restaurant after a business dinner. President Donald Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings about a year ago but took no action.

Megaspeed is listed by Nvidia as a cloud partner, and a Malaysian affiliate of the company bought at least $4.8 billion worth of AI equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February this year. U.S. authorities have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 on suspicion it smuggled Nvidia chips barred from export to China, and a Commerce Department site inspection found some equipment still in its packaging rather than installed in data centers. Nvidia is the world's most valuable publicly traded company, with a market capitalization of roughly $5.2 trillion. The Times reported that Jensen Huang personally lobbied Trump in 2025 when the administration was considering a ban on AI chip sales to China, and that Nvidia donated at least $20 million to Trump's White House ballroom fund and pledged to invest $500 billion in U.S. manufacturing. The Times said it could not determine what information Alice Huang passed along, and that it remains unclear which agency monitored her.

Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo said meeting customers is part of a chief executive's job and that Jensen Huang speaks with thousands of customer executives every year, adding that he was confident the U.S. government would have told the company if it had determined a particular individual posed a threat to American industry. Nvidia said Jensen Huang and Alice Huang had a routine business relationship. Liu Chang, a spokesman for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, dismissed the reports as groundless slander and defamation. Megaspeed said it was taking the matter extremely seriously and doing its utmost to establish the relevant facts, and that it was cooperating actively with the U.S. government investigation.

U.S. officials concluded that Jensen Huang did not know Alice Huang was a Chinese government spy, but some senior figures in the Trump administration question whether he could have been unaware of it, the Times reported. Authorities did not give Jensen Huang a defensive briefing alerting him that he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence service, and intelligence agencies sometimes skip such briefings when doing so could expose their surveillance to the spy. The White House is on alert that Alice Huang may have learned not only about Nvidia's technology but also about Trump's views on U.S.-China relations through Jensen Huang, and the Times said the issue is likely to come up when Trump visits China next month. Current and former U.S. officials told the Times that the close relationship between Trump and Huang is obstructing enforcement against chip transfers abroad, and that sanctions proposals involving Nvidia and China have been halted within the Commerce Department.

stories.Headline: Copilot AI Predicts Solana Could Hit $2,500 if This Landmark Event Happens
stories.Summary:
On November 1, 2026, Microsoft Copilot AI predicted that Solana could reach between $1,000 and $2,000 by January 1, 2027, with a stretch target toward $2,500 or more. Alex Ioannou reported the prediction for 99Bitcoins, and Yahoo Finance republished it. Solana was trading near $95 at the time. The forecast assumes a full crypto bull market returns and is boosted by a landmark event, which the article describes as a major global consortium adopting Solana as its blockchain for consumer applications and real-time payments.

The article says Solana had been recovering and consolidating in the $115 to $125 region after reclaiming key levels from earlier lows, and that it was holding above important intermediate moving averages. It says a sustained break above $130 to $150 would open the path toward the prior all-time high near $296, and that clearing that high could trigger measured-move extensions and multi-cycle Fibonacci projections. It lists nearer-term support zones at $110 to $115 and $100 to $105, and says the RSI was in neutral-to-constructive territory with room to run. It also says only an extraordinary surge in real-world, high-throughput adoption could justify the multi-thousand-percent move the targets imply. The article lists five catalysts: scrutiny of traditional banking products, geopolitical instability, interest rate cuts, Bitcoin's next rally and institutional investment.

A separate NTT DATA article by Sandeep Kaushik, published August 21, 2026, says AI agents are moving from emerging technology into everyday enterprise use and are becoming part of how companies operate. It says agents need identities, defined access, governance, policies, observability, accountability and lifecycle management, much like employees. It describes Microsoft tools including Copilot Chat, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Cowork and Microsoft Scout, and says the opportunity is to redesign work itself rather than just save time per user. It says the risks change once agents take action, such as retrieving sensitive information, triggering workflows or updating business systems, and it distinguishes agents that borrow a person's identity from agents with their own managed identity.

The NTT DATA article says CIOs, CISOs and other business leaders must answer who owns an agent, what data it can access, what actions it can take, how it is monitored and how its behavior is stopped or changed. It says organizations should extend their existing trusted infrastructure rather than build a new governance model, using tools such as Microsoft Entra, Defender, Purview, the Microsoft 365 admin center and Microsoft Agent 365. It recommends assessing AI readiness, prioritizing use cases with measurable value, building a secure foundation with least-privilege access and agent registries, scaling through a repeatable agent factory, and treating AI as an ongoing transformation. It says a partner can shorten the path from experimentation, and the text ends there. The Solana article does not say what happens next beyond its price scenarios.

stories.Headline: DoorDash's CEO: Don't be 'delusional' after just a few hundred AI agent orders
stories.Summary:
DoorDash has received only "several hundred" orders in total from third-party AI agents such as Meta's Muse, Instinct, and Fo, CEO Tony Xu said on the company's earnings call. The call covered the third quarter, and Business Insider reported on it on November 1, 2026, while TechCrunch reported on it on October 30, 2026. By comparison, DoorDash delivered 3.2 billion orders worldwide in 2025, and the company said in its 2025 report that it completes an average of 3 million deliveries daily. Xu said customers still mostly come to DoorDash's app and website to place orders.

DoorDash is nonetheless changing its own AI tools. The company said in September that it was testing a text-to-order feature with an interface reminiscent of Instinct, and it launched a command-line agent in July. A chatbot called Ask DoorDash, launched in June, creates an order from a recipe or shopping list, can adjust the contents to match customers' preferences, and lets users order through prompts and photos. DoorDash also released an MCP to enable ordering from other chatbots for corporate ordering. Xu said those AI tools could eventually generate new orders on DoorDash.

Xu said the use of agents to order is still a very dynamic area. He said his take on all things technology is that you never want to fight gravity, but at the same time you do not want to be delusional, referring to the low number of agent-placed orders. He said the company wants to learn more about agentic use cases and develop a healthy relationship with third-party agent makers. He added that in the future there could be an opportunity for DoorDash to advertise within these agents.

Users told Business Insider earlier in October that agents can be useful for tracking the prices of holiday gifts or airline tickets. Many are hesitant to let agents make the purchases themselves, and they use more secure payment options, such as single-use credit cards, in case the agents make a mistake. The space of agent-based ordering is evolving, as websites are still deciding whether to allow agents to access their content. Amazon has been blocking such personal agents, while Walmart has laid out a red carpet for them in order to snag some business from its competitors.

stories.Headline: U.S. Justice Department Probes Nvidia's Hugging Face Deal Over AI Competition
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Justice Department has opened a wide-ranging review of how Nvidia operates, including the possible effect of its acquisition of Hugging Face on competition in artificial intelligence. Justice Department officials are examining whether the $12.9 billion purchase of Hugging Face would give Nvidia control of a key distribution hub in AI, Reuters reported on the 28th. The main lines of questioning concern whether Nvidia could use Hugging Face, a platform for sharing open-source AI models, to harm rivals in the AI market, and whether it could use the platform as leverage in negotiations. Officials also asked about Hugging Face's competitors. Nvidia agreed to buy Hugging Face in September, paying almost $13 billion, and the deal is expected to close in the first half of next year.

The review is broad in scope, covering Nvidia's acquisitions, investments, sales practices and whether it has pressured customers. It extends earlier scrutiny of Nvidia that began under former President Joe Biden and carried into the administration of Donald Trump, and Reuters said there was no indication that Trump had intervened. The department has also looked at whether Nvidia allocated more AI chips to customers that bought networking equipment together with Groq processors, following a deal in which Nvidia licensed technology from the chip startup Groq and hired its key engineers. Nvidia's acquisitions of SchedMD and Run:ai, completed in December 2025, are also under review. Reuters said a Justice Department investigation is not evidence of wrongdoing and does not necessarily lead to litigation.

In announcing the Hugging Face acquisition last month, Nvidia said the platform would continue to support partnerships with a range of chip, cloud and AI companies and would remain open to the entire AI ecosystem. Nvidia has declined to comment on the Reuters story, according to Tom's Hardware. Hugging Face offers an open-source platform for the hosting and testing of new AI models, and that appears to be behind the department's concerns. The move could be seen as a way for Nvidia to lock in a key distribution channel for its own products, and Hugging Face also sells AI infrastructure.

This is not the first time Nvidia has found itself in the department's crosshairs. As Nvidia becomes more vital to the tech industry as a whole and to AI technologies specifically, the company has come under increasing scrutiny within the U.S. government, stretching back to the Biden administration. Things did not improve when the Trump administration took over, with the U.S. president reportedly tempted to break the company up despite being unfamiliar with what it was. More recently, Nvidia and other AI hardware makers found themselves under export controls. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the review and the expected timing of the deal's close.

stories.Headline: Ear infection? A new AI model may have the diagnosis
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Turku University Hospital in Finland trained a computer model to sort images from a digital otoscope into two groups, abnormal or normal. The classifier identified more than 750 eardrum photos of children between six months and three years old. The study was reported on October 31, 2026. The tool is meant to help rule out ear infections in young children and support doctors in diagnosis.

To check the model, the researchers set a gold standard of three physicians, two ENT specialists and one pediatrician, who reviewed the same images. The physicians agreed on their diagnoses, and against their standard the classifier was 92% accurate at identifying acute otitis media. The classifier first had 96% accuracy for abnormal ears, but this fell to 92% after multiple images were too unclear for the device. The model needs a clear image to work accurately, which is hard with children who rarely sit still.

Pediatrician Dr. Simo Nuuttila, one of the lead authors, said around 70% to 80% of children get otitis media at least once in their life, and some susceptible kids may get it five to six times a year. He added that for young children who cannot express ear pain, an infection can get bad and potentially puncture or rupture the eardrum. He said the model relies on the images it was trained on, so angled or outdated images could lead to an inaccurate diagnosis. He said the tool cannot fully replace a doctor but can serve as a rule-out if image quality is good.

Dr. Matthew Crowson, a surgeon at Mass General Brigham Eye and Ear in Boston and a professor at Harvard Medical School, is developing other AI models to address that limitation. He said his team intentionally included poor-quality photos, programming the model to prompt the user to retake a photo or clean the ear. He said labels of just abnormal or normal are not as clinically useful, because an abnormal ear does not necessarily need antibiotics for an infection. Nuuttila's research is now expanding to 40 families in Finland, half of whom received digital otoscopes for home use, and Crowson said parents should confirm all diagnoses with telehealth physicians.

stories.Headline: Anthropic set to make stock market debut as questions swirl about safety of AI | CNN Business
stories.Summary:
Anthropic filed paperwork with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, October 26, 2026, to sell shares to the public for the first time, in what could become one of the largest stock market debuts in history. The San Francisco company says trading could begin as soon as November 16, under the ticker ANT on the Nasdaq exchange. It has not said how many shares it plans to sell or at what price, and those details are expected to be settled in the coming weeks. The offering could reportedly value the company at up to $2 trillion, which would place it among the biggest public companies in the world.

The filing lays out a business that is growing fast but losing money on paper. Revenue rose 1,300% from a year earlier in the first six months of 2026, reaching $16.3 billion, and most of it depends on businesses using the Claude AI system. Anthropic reports more than 14,000 enterprise customers, with about 250 of them paying $10 million or more a year. Its net loss topped $80 billion, but just under $9 billion came from spending on AI infrastructure and computing, while more than $72 billion came from changes in the fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities and SAFEs. Results for the quarter that ended September 30 were not included, and the company was last valued at $965 billion after raising $65 billion in May.

The filing runs 93 pages on risk factors, far more than Snap, which had around 30, or Uber, which had about 50. Anthropic sorts the dangers of AI into four groups: misuse, such as designing bioweapons or launching cyberattacks, loss of human control, authoritarian abuse, such as building surveillance states, and economic disruption. It warns that its models could act in misaligned ways and take harmful actions that no user directed, and that damages from extreme harm could exceed its insurance. The company's founders also wrote to prospective shareholders that frontier AI firms must invest in safety and alignment. Jacob Bourne, an analyst at Emarketer, said the decision to proceed shows a willingness to face heightened public scrutiny, and Dan Ives of Yorkville & Ives Co. said growth will likely overshadow concerns about losses and risks.

The listing arrives as a wave of expected fall public offerings has not materialized, and rival OpenAI has reportedly pushed its own IPO to next year, according to Bourne, amid worries about debt-fueled infrastructure spending and AI safety. Gartner expects global AI spending to reach roughly $3.6 trillion in 2027, up from $1.8 trillion in 2025. Fintech firm Ramp found that 43.8% of US businesses paid for Anthropic in September, against 40.6% for OpenAI, and Sensor Tower estimates the Claude app has more than 67 million monthly active users, up from 9.4 million a year ago. Last month, CEO Dario Amodei called for an industry-wide slowdown so safety research and regulation could catch up, and the company has had a rocky relationship with the White House, including a temporary cutoff of access to its most capable models in June after the Trump administration ordered it to keep foreign nationals from using the technology. The offering will test Wall Street's appetite for AI, with pricing and share details still to come before the November debut.

stories.Headline: SK Hynix taps HBM veteran to lead new American unit
stories.Summary:
SK Hynix appointed its AI memory development chief, Ahn Hyun, to lead a newly established Americas unit based in the United States, according to a report dated Oct. 30, 2026. The unit places a technology veteran closer to major US customers. The move comes as the industry shifts toward customized high-bandwidth memory and deeper ties with buyers. The report did not give further details on the unit's size or start date.

The articles give several figures on SK Hynix's business. The company posted third-quarter revenue of 104.6 trillion won and operating profit of 83.3 trillion won, up 327.9% and 632.1% from a year earlier, with an operating margin of 79.7%. Yuanta Securities projected fourth-quarter revenue of 147.1 trillion won and operating profit of 118.2 trillion won, raising its price target 12.1% to 3.7 million won from 3.3 million won, while Shinhan Securities forecast revenue of 126.1 trillion won and operating profit of 101.5 trillion won, lifting its target 11% to 3 million won. SK Hynix has signed long-term supply agreements with 14 customers, and the contracted volumes cover more than 50% of its total production capacity for 2027-2028.

Yuanta analyst Baek Gil-hyun said that counting volumes still under negotiation, DRAM and HBM output through 2029 has effectively all been sold, and that earnings visibility is far higher than in past semiconductor cycles. He said the demand confirmed so far is volume within the company's available supply range, and that investment is diversifying beyond companies to their own AI infrastructure and state-led AI investment. Shinhan analyst Kim Hyung-tae estimated fourth-quarter DRAM and NAND shipments would rise 24% and 5%, with average selling prices for both rising around 10%, above the market's 5% expectation. He also said the 12-month forward price-to-book ratio is 1.7 times, the cheapest valuation among DRAM peers.

The forecasts rest on record third-quarter results, with all-time highs for six consecutive quarters, as rising memory prices and expanded sales of high-value products offset a currency headwind of 5 trillion to 6 trillion won from a stronger won. HBM4 is seen as the key driver of fourth-quarter results, with Baek expecting it to surpass HBM3E in both shipment volume and revenue share. SK Hynix shares rose as high as 1.536 million won on the morning of Oct. 29, up 3.30% from the previous session. stories.Headline: AI-accelerated exploits outpace patch cycles, eBPF shields cloud workloads
stories.Summary:
AI-assisted vulnerability research is now producing exploits within hours, shrinking the time between disclosure and attack, according to TechGig. Attackers use large language models to trace exploit paths and generate proof-of-concept variants quickly. Four years after Log4Shell, vulnerable instances of that library are still found in production, the report said. Modern applications rely on hundreds of transitive open-source dependencies, which makes inventory and fast patching hard.

Sweet Security launched Virtual Patching for running cloud and AI workloads on 31 October 2026, according to IT Brief Australia. Security teams pick a vulnerability from Sweet's catalogue, choose an enforcement option and deploy a policy to nodes running the affected workload. Sweet's sensor then blocks requests that try to exploit the weakness while letting normal traffic through, and the protection stays attached as the workload scales or restarts. Sweet pointed to a recent Atlassian flaw that drew exploitation attempts within hours of a proof of concept becoming public, while many fixes take days or weeks to reach production. The feature also links with Sweet Attack, the company's autonomous AI red-team agent, which can suggest a virtual patching policy for immediate enforcement.

James Berthoty, Chief Executive Officer and Founder of Latio Tech, said AI is speeding up vulnerability discovery and exploitation so much that exploits appear days before patches, and faster patching alone is not enough. He said Sweet's Virtual Patching gives teams protection immediately while they fix vulnerabilities at the source. Dror Kashti, Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder of Sweet Security, said that when a team knows an application can be exploited, waiting is not an option. He said the feature lets security teams protect production immediately while engineering finishes the permanent fix, and that it changes the economics of cloud security by cutting the time and effort between identifying a risk and acting on it.

TechGig reported that eBPF lets small verified programs attach to kernel events without changing application code or the kernel, giving deep observability and low-overhead enforcement of process, network and file activity. Cilium's Tetragon sub-project uses eBPF for runtime security, enforcing policy in real time without in-process agents. Compensating controls should observe before enforcing, roll out gradually, keep an audit trail and be retired once the permanent patch is verified, the report said. Isovalent is extending Tetragon to provide verifiable eBPF-based protection. Sweet said its virtual patching is available for cloud and AI applications in production and is meant to work alongside standard remediation, as vendors move from detection into direct intervention in production.

stories.Headline: Is AI slipping beyond human control?
stories.Summary:
In March 2026, Admiral Brad Cooper, head of US Central Command, described how AI tools helped his personnel sort through large amounts of information during Operation Epic Fury against Iran, cutting task time from hours or days to seconds. He also said humans will always make the final decisions on what to shoot, what not to shoot and when to shoot. The article says the key challenge is not whether humans stay involved in military decision-making but how that involvement is designed and governed so it remains meaningful rather than nominal. It gives an example of an operator deciding whether to authorize a strike on a building, with one version of the system showing its reasoning, confidence and limits, and another version hiding the evidence under time pressure.

The article says keeping humans in the loop is a good first step but should not be the whole of responsible integration. It says militaries must ensure responsible procurement, training and structures, and should secure and test AI systems that let personnel scrutinize recommendations, recognize uncertainty and understand the limits of their use. Training must prepare personnel to seek corroboration, challenge recommendations and disregard outputs when warranted, and organizations must provide the time and authority to exercise that judgment, opportunities for independent verification and incentives that reward scrutiny. It says meaningful human control is a continuous responsibility for the whole military organization, extending beyond the individual making the final decision.

The article says private sector actors develop or supply many military AI capabilities, so states need to engage with industry to set clear requirements for the systems they acquire. It says commercial incentives and proprietary development practices do not always align with military operational, legal and accountability requirements, and developers should design systems that enable meaningful oversight before they reach militaries. It cites NATO's acquisition of Palantir's Maven Smart System in just six months as raising concerns that pressure to adopt may come at the expense of rigorous scrutiny. It says procurement should mandate clear, intuitive interfaces that communicate the rationale behind outputs and the associated uncertainty and limitations, and testing should examine whether operators can critically evaluate recommendations under realistic conditions.

The article cites the Saker Scout, a Ukrainian AI-powered drone that can recognize military equipment but cannot distinguish Ukrainian from Russian targets. Rostyslav Olenchyn of Twist Robotics, the Kyiv-based defense-technology company that developed the drone, warns that you should be sure there are no civilians and not your own people. The article says suppliers should disclose such limitations, and militaries should test whether the proposed safeguard works. It adds that embedding or deploying engineers alongside military personnel, where appropriate, can help developers understand the challenges operators face, and that procurement should establish not only what a system can do but also where its capabilities stop.
