The products shown cover several areas.

Hikvision demonstrated its Guanlan large-scale AI models, which go beyond basic object detection to scenario-specific analytics, and operators can set automated alerts by describing what matters to their site. Its AcuSeek tool lets users find footage after an incident with a typed or spoken query. The company introduced new Pro-Series UHD cameras, including 16 MP dual-lens models for a seamless wide-angle view, and highlighted Guanlan Encoding to offset the extra storage that higher resolution requires. It also showcased Quick Pass access control for people and vehicles, with AI face recognition and license plate recognition working with automatic gates and barriers, plus eight converged SMB solutions that link two or more types of security systems.

Hikvision described how these systems work together. In one demonstration, a camera recognizes a trespasser's attributes, AI turns what it sees into a description, and an IP speaker plays a voice warning addressed to that person. The company said HIKO, the AI engine in Hik-Connect 7 and HikCentral Professional, cuts down the manual configuration and searching that SMB operators have to do. It also showed AI tools in Hik-Partner Pro for installers, where HPP Designer reads an uploaded floor plan, recommends devices, and places them automatically with coverage simulation.

Hik Chatbot answers questions about product selection, technical support, and solution design around the clock. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the event itself. stories.Summary:
Overseas companies and institutions raised a record amount of yen-denominated debt in the April to September half of 2026, according to Nikkei Asia. The total reached $16bn as foreign borrowers joined a global fundraising push driven by AI hyperscalers. Alphabet raised funds in May, and Hon Hai and Zurich Insurance followed. The offerings were reported on November 1, 2026, in a story by Seiichiro Takita and Takuro Hosoda.

It describes the borrowing as yen-denominated debt issuance by foreign entities. It says the money is being raised from Japanese investors.

The context is a worldwide race to finance AI buildouts, with hyperscalers raising money across markets. The article links the yen bond record to that broader fundraising wave. It does not say what happens next for the issuers or the market. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Google Public Sector Summit 2026: AI Moves From Possibility To Mission
stories.Summary:
The Google Public Sector Summit 2026 took place on October 20 in Washington, DC. Forrester noted that no single major announcement defined the day. Instead, federal, state, local, and education leaders showed how they are applying AI to government missions. The conversation has changed since Forrester wrote about the creation of Google Public Sector in 2022, when the question was whether Google could build the industry credentials to compete for government business.

The Department of War discussed putting Gemini into the hands of more than 3 million personnel. The Army showed how AI could make fragmented logistics data accessible, and Iowa discussed using Gemini and its data cloud for child welfare case histories. At the US Patent and Trademark Office, thousands of highly specialized patent examiners face a roughly 700,000-application backlog. Executive Order 14249, Protecting America’s Bank Account Against Fraud, Waste, and Abuse, was signed on March 25, 2025, and elevated fraud prevention and better use of government data as administration priorities.

A panel including Justin Fanelli, CTO of the US Navy, James Wolff, CIO of the US DOE’s National Nuclear Security Administration, Vice Admiral (Ret.) TJ White, chief of Texas Cyber Command, and Thomas Browning of Rhombus Power discussed what security means when technology and threats change faster than traditional processes can accommodate. The discussion focused on human on the loop, or humans in the lead, rather than human in the loop for risk management. Barry Schindler, the USPTO’s acting commissioner for patents, brought props tracing technology in his lifetime from the slide ruler to the calculator to AI. He joked that each leap felt a little like cheating, but that you would be a fool not to take advantage of it.

Google showed early experimentation using Gemini to recommend model-routing and architecture choices, forecast spend, reuse agent skills, and apply runtime spend caps. Forrester described this as a glimpse of FinOps shifting further left, with AI helping optimize the cost and efficiency of AI itself. Another panelist observed that vibe coding quickly separated the strongest talent from the weakest. Forrester said AI can amplify expertise but cannot replace the expertise needed to know when an answer is wrong.

stories.Headline: 'The reality is that not every task requires the most advanced or expensive model available': Snowflake explains why finding the right AI model can make all the difference in helping your business succeed
stories.Summary:
Snowflake recently launched new capabilities that let customers automatically select the best AI model based on quality, speed and preferences, while tracking AI spend with greater control. The company says the tool is meant to help organizations get more from their AI investment at a time when budgets are tighter than ever. TechRadar spoke to Grace Adamson, AI Product Marketing Manager at Snowflake, about the approach. The article was published on 1 November 2026.

Adamson said the first wave of generative AI focused heavily on model power, with an experimental race to reach the highest quality outputs or solve the most complex tasks. She said organizations are now shifting from AI experimentation to driving real business outcomes. She said not every task requires the most advanced or expensive model available, since some workloads need sophisticated reasoning while others involve repetitive classification, summarization or extraction that more efficient models, including the latest open source models, can handle at a fraction of the cost. Snowflake calls this idea intelligence efficiency, meaning how effectively organizations turn models, data and compute into measurable outcomes and value.

Adamson said this is possible through dynamic model routing, native governance, and having AI built directly alongside an organization's trusted data so it understands the business context behind every request. She said this means organizations can run their AI workloads on the most suitable model while better managing AI costs. The article presents this as a way to solve what it calls the AI economics problem. The article does not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: 'The reality is that not every task requires the most advanced or expensive model available': Snowflake explains why finding the right AI model can make all the difference in helping your business succeed

stories.Headline: The AI-Generated Airbnb Scam That Left Me Stranded Outside an Empty Lot in Rome
stories.Summary:
Reports from 2024 and 2025 describe a surge of fake rentals across Europe, in which tourists in Paris, Rome and Prague were left stranded after booking nonexistent apartments, often lured by cheap deals and asked to pay upfront. In Rome, dozens were reportedly tricked by fake hosts using stolen listings. In August 2026, Euro Weekly News described a case in which criminals allegedly took control of the online profile of a legitimate property in the Siena area and used it to sell bookings for a fictitious apartment in Rome. The report said the apartment looked real on a screen, yet nothing was waiting for the guests on arrival.

Italy now requires a national identification code, known as the CIN, for short term rentals, and it must be displayed on all online listings and on the property itself. It became compulsory on January 1, 2025, and hosts who lack one face fines of €800 to €8,000 per violation. According to The Local, the code means the property is registered with the tourism ministry, meets fire safety standards and the owner is paying tax on the rental income. Airbnb has said it would verify listings in its top five markets, and the company said in 2023 that it had blocked 157,000 fake listings from joining the platform and removed 59,000 fraudulent listings. Airbnb's April 2026 terms update banned AI generated evidence in host damage claims.

Airbnb's own research, as reported by travel outlets, found that nearly two thirds of British travelers struggled to tell AI generated property images from real ones, and more than a third mistook fakes for genuine photos. One 2026 guide notes that Airbnb's AirCover doesn't cover payments made outside the platform, and that if payment goes through the platform and the listing proves fraudulent, AirCover should provide recourse. The guide advises guests to document everything, report the listing through the in-app reporting function and contact Airbnb support right away so a rebooking or refund request is on record. It also says to call your bank or card issuer quickly if money moved outside the platform. In one Rome case reported in 2025, local police received many complaints and eventually had a fake listing removed, and reports from Rome's tourism department and police in summer 2025 indicate that scam alerts for incoming tourists have been issued.

Articles.Title: The AI-Generated Airbnb Scam That Left Me Stranded Outside an Empty Lot in Rome

stories.Headline: Phenom Gains Top Rankings as AI Expands Across HR Operations
stories.Summary:
Phenom received the highest classification in two Everest Group assessments of artificial intelligence used in recruiting and human resources, the Philadelphia-based software company announced on November 1, 2026. Everest Group named Phenom a Luminary in its Agentic AI in Talent Acquisition 2026 and Agentic AI Applications in HR 2026 Innovation Watch assessments. The evaluations looked at 31 providers of AI recruiting technology and 25 providers offering AI applications across human resources. The Luminary classification recognizes providers based on market performance and demonstrated customer value.

The recognition reflects Phenom's strategy of connecting recruiting, onboarding, employee development and workforce planning through one common data platform instead of separate AI tools for each HR function. Its recruiting technology uses AI agents to handle candidate sourcing, screening, interview scheduling and fraud detection, and its WorkOps platform applies business-specific requirements based on industry, position and location. Phenom reported that at a major airline its technology scheduled 96% of interviews within 24 hours and cut hiring event cycle times from 182 days to 29 days. A large health system reduced its time to offer by 21%, increased applications by 15% and eliminated more than 8,200 hours of scheduling coordination, while a major bank scheduled 76% of interviews within eight hours for more than 11,000 hours in reported time savings and mapped employee skills across a workforce of 39,000. The company did not identify those customers, and the figures are company-reported results rather than independently detailed findings from the Everest Group assessments.

Phenom is extending its AI agents into employee onboarding, internal career development and workforce planning, with tools that coordinate documentation and compliance reviews, recommend training and internal job opportunities, and provide attrition analysis and staffing projections. A unified employee and candidate profile carries information from recruiting into later employment processes, and the company maintains integrations with major human capital management, human resources information and applicant tracking systems. Phenom also supports Agent-to-Agent and Model Context Protocol connectivity so its AI agents can interact with other enterprise software. John Deal, Phenom's senior director of product marketing, said the company's AI is purpose-built to solve customer problems and that its impact is measured in value and outcomes.

The broader HR assessment considered supported functions, maturity of AI technology, production deployments, integration capabilities, measurable customer outcomes and platform investment. Phenom emphasized its deployment process, which includes AI bootcamps, and reported that one financial institution deployed operational AI agents within three days of initial discussions while a diversified conglomerate reduced time to hire by 10 days after its bootcamp. The recognition comes as enterprise HR software providers increasingly compete to automate interconnected business processes rather than offer AI assistance limited to recommendations or administrative tasks. The announcement did not disclose revenue growth, contract values or new customer commitments.

Articles.Title: Phenom Gains Top Rankings as AI Expands Across HR Operations

stories.Headline: Spewing US election falsehoods, AI chatbots face scrutiny
stories.Summary:
AI chatbots are spreading misleading voter information, misidentifying candidates and repeating Russian propaganda ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3, researchers say. This is the first federal election in which millions of voters are actively relying on AI tools for political information. Experts say the trend is playing a key role in shaping the information ecosystem before the polls. While chatbots can help debunk conspiracies and educate voters, multiple studies show they often draw on unreliable sources on the open web.

A study by Forum AI, a start-up that evaluates AI models, found that almost 40 percent of chatbots’ answers to election-related queries contained at least one factual error. The study examined eight models and found that chatbots answered questions about voting logistics incorrectly more often than questions about candidates. When researchers asked Anthropic’s Claude why voters should elect Representative Don Davis from North Carolina, it listed “former school superintendent” among his credentials, confusing him with a different person. When Google’s Gemini 3.6 Flash was asked about voting in Pennsylvania, it gave November 3 as the deadline to request a mail-in ballot, when the actual deadline was a week earlier.

Forum AI said chatbots also put wrong words in the mouths of candidates, officials and observers hundreds of times, and often cited poor quality sources such as Reddit threads. Anthropic did not respond to AFP’s request for comment. Google said it was focused on helping voters find reliable information across its platforms and added that it had strict quality and policy protections across its AI products on election topics. In late October, AFP’s fact-checkers debunked a likely AI-altered clip that purported to show a former student of Texas Senate candidate James Talarico accusing him of sexual misconduct, an allegation that bore the hallmarks of a Russian disinformation campaign.

Google’s AI Overview repeated the allegation when prompted by the disinformation watchdog NewsGuard, and Google’s Gemini and Microsoft’s Copilot also repeated the false claim. NewsGuard said in a separate study of 10 AI tools that chatbot users are at risk of being fooled by foreign influence operations and other bad actors. Google said the issue was addressed as its systems quickly updated to surface the latest reporting on the topic. Microsoft said it was a rapidly developing situation with limited reliable information at the time of the initial query, and that Copilot later reflected the updated context and identified the claim as fabricated.

The November 3 vote marks the first US election with AI tools built into every major tech platform, according to the London-based Institute for Strategic Dialogue. In a recent survey by the nonpartisan National Conference on Citizenship, two in five Americans said they had used AI tools to search for election information, including candidates or ballot measures. Only 40 percent trust the tools with logistical information such as when, where and how to vote, and 60 percent said they trust it only a little or not at all to be unbiased about candidates. Research by the nonpartisan Brennan Center for Justice found that leading chatbots pushed back against common election conspiracy theories, including claims that voting machines were rigged, even when repeatedly challenged.

Articles.Title: Spewing US election falsehoods, AI chatbots face scrutiny

stories.Headline: Building CRM Automations That Don't Break: APIs, Webhooks, and AI Validation
stories.Summary:
The article is a technical guide published on SitePoint on October 27, 2026, and updated on November 1, 2026, by an author listed as Jane digital. It explains how to build CRM automations that do not break, using GoHighLevel as the running example because it combines native workflows with a public API and webhooks. The piece describes the platform's three layers: data collection through forms, funnels and API requests, workflow processing that evaluates conditions and starts actions, and external integrations for tasks beyond native capabilities. It also walks through a lead management workflow in five stages, from capturing and normalising a lead to updating reporting.

The article says GoHighLevel's REST API uses JSON and supports token-based authentication, including OAuth 2.0 for delegated access, with Private Integration Tokens suited to internal integrations. Its sample contact-creation request sends a POST to the contacts endpoint with a bearer token, a location ID, and fields for first name, last name, email and phone, and it checks the response before reading the result. It advises treating a 429 rate-limit response as a normal control signal, backing off exponentially and respecting any retry-after value rather than retrying in a tight loop. It also recommends upserts keyed on a stable identifier such as a normalised phone number or email address instead of blind creates, so a retried request cannot spawn a duplicate contact.

On webhooks, the article says a publicly accessible endpoint should not trust every request, and where signature verification exists developers should compute an HMAC over the raw request body with the shared signing secret and compare it in constant time. It warns that deliveries can be repeated, so handlers should store each event's unique ID or a payload hash in a processed-events table and check it before any side effect, making a duplicate a cheap no-op. It recommends separating reception from processing: validate the event, record it, acknowledge with a 2xx response within a second or two, and place substantial work on a queue. Failed jobs should retry with exponential backoff and, after a set number of attempts, land in a dead-letter queue for a human to inspect.

The article lists common mistakes developers should avoid, including building everything in one enormous workflow, ignoring API rate limits, failing to handle duplicate contacts, storing credentials insecurely and automating without adequate testing. It says AI fits into CRM automation only with structured outputs, that AI should not control every decision, and that human escalation still matters. It frames the choice between native workflows and custom development as an architectural decision about which tasks belong inside the CRM and which should be handled externally. The patterns it describes, data normalisation, idempotent event handling, queue-based processing and validated AI outputs, are presented as applying to any CRM, and its closing advice is to build for reliability rather than complexity.

Articles.Title: Building CRM Automations That Don't Break: APIs, Webhooks, and AI Validation

stories.Headline: Enterprise voice AI tools provider Deepgram acquires Daily, which has raised $62M+ and develops open-source voice AI framework Pipecat, for an undisclosed sum (Ivan Mehta/TechCrunch)
stories.Summary:
Deepgram, an enterprise voice AI tools provider, said on Thursday that it is acquiring Daily, the maker and maintainer of the open source voice AI framework Pipecat. The companies did not disclose the deal amount. Both companies were reportedly in the same Y Combinator batch in 2016. Daily has raised over $62 million in funding to date from investors including Tiger Global, Highfield Capital, Nat Friedman, Lachy Groom, and Kevin Weil, according to PitchBook data. Earlier this year, Deepgram reached unicorn status with a $130 million Series C round.

The companies said they will keep Pipecat open source. Pipecat is a framework that manages voice and video streams along with other pipeline pieces such as speech-to-text, large language models, and text-to-speech models while reducing latency. Daily provides hosted infrastructure for voice and video calls of any kind. Deepgram is also launching the Real-Time Context Standard, an open protocol for voice agents that it co-developed with the Pipecat team. The protocol defines metadata such as context from the audio, like a whisper, instructions for a language model on how it can use those signals, and guidance on how the response should sound.

Kwindla Kramer, Daily's co-founder, said the company began experimenting with AI-to-human communication over voice and text around the time GPT-4 came out, which eventually resulted in Pipecat. He said there had been a lot of acquisition interest, but he favored Deepgram CEO Scott Stephenson's commitment to keeping Pipecat open source forever. Kramer said the engineering cultures of both organizations matched, giving Daily's team the freedom to work on different parts of the stack within a bigger organization. He also said Pipecat was never thought of as a voice toolkit but as the toolkit needed to build a new kind of AI-native software, and that the company always assumed real-time because of where it came from.

Stephenson said Deepgram had wanted to work in open source for a long time and realized an orchestration framework for agents was a potential area, which drove the decision to partner with Daily. He said the aim is to open up the ecosystem so everybody can build voice agents, and that it is fine if people use the best models for their use case rather than only Deepgram's. He said that if Deepgram notices it has ground to catch up on in some area for its own models and products, that is great, and that the company wants developers to use partners while it also works on becoming better in those areas. Stephenson said the acquisition lets developers build agents with expressivity and end-to-end speech systems by plugging in different models and a context bus that connects all parts, and that the deal also lets Deepgram explore areas beyond voice through Pipecat.

Articles.Title: Enterprise voice AI tools provider Deepgram acquires Daily, which has raised $62M+ and develops open-source voice AI framework Pipecat, for an undisclosed sum (Ivan Mehta/TechCrunch)

stories.Headline: Sydney council proposes AI-powered security cameras to monitor city streets
stories.Summary:
The City of Sydney has proposed a major upgrade to its street surveillance network that would add artificial intelligence to monitor for suspicious activity across the CBD and inner-city suburbs. More than 100 cameras already watch the streets, and the changes would let the network look much more closely at what is happening on the ground. Under the plan, the AI would scan footage for unusual activity such as crowds gathering, vehicles travelling in the wrong direction or suspicious items left behind. The proposal was reported by 7NEWS in a story by Emily Francis.

The City of Sydney has ruled out facial recognition technology, and human operators would keep control of the cameras and check any alerts that come through. Descriptions of people's appearance could still be used to help police pick up persons of interest. A similar trial in Western Australia led to 79 wanted people being picked up in the first three months, with eight false alarms. The City of Sydney says privacy would be protected under the proposal, but the idea has already raised questions about how much AI should be involved in surveillance.

The council is responsible for the plan, and it will be put to the public before any final decisions are made. The articles do not say what happens after that public consultation or when any decision would be made. They also do not give a date for when the cameras would be upgraded if the plan goes ahead. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Sydney council proposes AI-powered security cameras to monitor city streets - 7NEWS

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence, plans for the future discussed at 2026 State of the Valley
stories.Summary:
Members of local city and county government, schools and citizen ballot issue committees took part in the 2026 State of the Valley luncheon on Wednesday. One of the topics they discussed was Artificial Intelligence, or AI, and how their organizations are dealing with or using it. Scottsbluff Public Schools Superintendent Dr. Andrew Dick said AI is a hot topic in education and can be beneficial for both staff and students. The annual event was sponsored by the Government Affairs Committee of the Scottsbluff-Gering Chamber of Commerce.

Dr. Dick said a Board policy does not allow students to use an AI tool unless their respective teacher gives permission. He said one of his fears is that AI takes away the opportunity for students to develop critical thinking skills and their ability to write. As one small example, he said teachers may assign more in class writing instead of a five-page research paper done at home, where students run the risk of using ChatGPT or another comparable tool. He said in class writing requires a student to demonstrate those skills.

Other topics covered included measures and races on the November ballot and the importance of getting out to vote this year. They also discussed what needs to happen to keep young people in the valley and how to ensure the area remains vibrant. The cities and schools of Gering and Scottsbluff also discussed what projects or plans they have on tap in the future. On that last topic, Gering City Council member Susan Wiedeman pointed to completion of the city's electric system upgrade project.

Wiedeman said three of the new substations have already been built, and a good portion of the city has already been converted to the higher voltage. She said the last substation to be built is on 21st Street, and it takes basically most of the west side from 10th Street west, which is a big portion of the city. She said the city is hoping to have that substation built and online by the end of 2027, and she asked Domingo Palomo, the Electric Utilities Superintendent, to confirm. The articles do not say what happens next beyond that hoped-for completion date.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence, plans for the future discussed at 2026 State of the Valley - Rural Radio Network

stories.Headline: Three Takeaways from Wednesday’s Board Study Session on AI - M-A Chronicle
stories.Summary:
The District Board of Trustees held a special study session on Wednesday afternoon, the M-A Chronicle reported on October 31, 2026. The Board reviewed the use of artificial intelligence and its AI policy drafts. The drafts would rewrite three District policies and would give students suspected of cheating with AI a chance to explain their work. The Board took no action on the drafts, which are expected to be finalized this winter.

The Academic Honesty draft requires a teacher who suspects a student of misusing AI to give the student an opportunity to demonstrate understanding of the content through other methods the teacher deems suitable. A University of Maryland study of a dozen AI detectors found that detectors wrongly flagged human writing as AI-generated about 7% of the time. Under the California Education Code, a teacher's grade is final unless the student can prove a clerical error, fraud, bad faith, or incompetence. If a teacher allows AI, the draft says it should support a student's own thinking, and students must cite their usage. The draft lists what counts as misuse, including passing off AI work as original and generating answers on math, science, or analytical problems.

Trustee Mary Beth Thompson said parents had complained repeatedly about children who failed after a teacher said they used AI. She said a teacher cannot just say a student used AI or that a detector said so, and she pointed to the fact that detectors often make mistakes. Trustee Sathvik Nori said there should be some formal process outside of a teacher that a student can appeal to if they think they are being falsely accused. Thompson also questioned why the District policy would create different rules for math and science when similar concerns exist in other areas, such as music composition. On the item allowing any AI use a teacher has not specifically prohibited, Thompson said it needs to default one way or the other, and that it needs to default to not using it, and Solutionary Advisors, the consulting firm that led the session, agreed to rework that section.

Staff would face AI rules of their own, and employees who use AI must check its output and are prohibited from entering personally identifiable information into tools not expressly allowed by the District. The Employee Use of Technology draft would let teachers use District-approved AI to give feedback on or even grade student work, while California's model policy calls for both consent and notification whenever AI is used for grading or feedback. The District has not committed to adding consent, and in written answers to the working group it stated that consent would be discussed further, calling the state's principles recommendations but not mandates. Nori wanted trustees to review the guidance, a staff document separate from the policies, and the working group will look it over in November and December. Superintendent Crystal Leach said that if the Board really wants to enforce an implementation, it needs to be in a policy, describing guidance as staff's work, and the Board will reconvene for its next regular meeting on Nov. 18.

Articles.Title: Three Takeaways from Wednesday’s Board Study Session on AI - M-A Chronicle

stories.Headline: District outlines policy for responsible AI use
stories.Summary:
South Washington County Schools adopted ISD Policy 625 on the Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence earlier in the fall, and the policy was explained in more detail at the Oct. 8 board workshop meeting. Assistant Superintendent Kelly Jansen introduced the presentation by School Tech Integration Coordinator Dr. Amber Sorenson and Tech Director Bob Berkowitz. Jansen said the district had passed Policy 625 in August and had promised to come back and talk about what it looks like in practice. The policy is supported by three documents, a board approved policy setting what and why as well as values, guardrails and accountability, a procedures document owned by administration that spells out how staff apply the policy, and staff guidance on how the policy is used.

The policy permits AI but regulates it, uses it as a supplement rather than a replacement, and keeps teacher control over classroom use. It authorizes AI but does not require anyone to use it, and it follows an H-AI-H model that begins with human input, then AI, then returns the end result to human agency. The policy defines terms including personally identifiable information, hallucinations, deep fakes, agentic AI, autonomous AI and district-approved tool. Expectations differ by age, with use highly restricted for grades K to 3, a structured introduction for grades 4 to 8, and broader access with increased expectations for transparency and accountability for grades 9 to 12. The four levels of acceptable use are AI free, AI assisted, AI enhanced and AI empowered, and teachers determine the appropriate level for each assignment.

Sorenson said the purpose of the policy is to state that AI is here, that people are using it, and that the district wants to make sure it is used safely, responsibly and as a supplemental tool. She said the policy authorizes AI but does not require anyone to use it, and that the human owns the outcome, noting that AI can be wrong and can be very confident about being wrong. Berkowitz said that without an agreement, AI use should be assumed to be public. The policy addresses student privacy, academic integrity and human oversight, and it includes commitments to original thinking, transparent use with attribution, reviewed privacy controls, fair access to approved tools, training on bias and misinformation, and preserving human decision making.

Vendor contracts for AI tools go through an approval process of request, review, contract and listing, and vendors must disclose their data practices, deletion rights and procedures for reporting security breaches. The District Technology Advisory Committee will provide opportunities for families and community members to comment on AI guidance, digital literacy and other technology-related decisions. The policy provides for staff, student and family training and planned annual reviews of data safeguards, with a three tier system for reporting violations, from minor matters escalated to a principal or program lead, to serious matters escalated to an assistant superintendent, to critical matters escalated to law enforcement, appropriate agencies and legal counsel. Families are notified as appropriate for minor incidents, as soon as possible for serious incidents, and as soon as legally permissible for critical incidents, while administrators will update procedures as technology changes and staff guidance will be reviewed yearly.

Articles.Title: District outlines policy for responsible AI use - Cottage Grove Journal

stories.Headline: AMZN Q3 deep dive: cloud surge and AI investments drive mixed market reception
stories.Summary:
Amazon reported third quarter 2026 results on October 31, 2026, with revenue up 12.1% year on year to $201.9 billion. That figure was in line with S&P analysts' estimates of $202.3 billion. GAAP earnings per share came in at $1.89, which was 3.4% below the consensus estimate of $1.96. The operating margin was 13.9%, up from 9.7% in the same quarter last year, and the company's market capitalization stood at $2.63 trillion.

Amazon guided next quarter's revenue to around $243.5 billion, close to analysts' estimates. AWS grew 39.3% year over year, accelerating for the sixth straight quarter, and its backlog grew in the triple digits year over year. Customers using custom silicon such as Trainium and Graviton saved more than $2 billion in the quarter, and revenue commitments for these chips rose over 20 times year over year. Prime members ordering groceries with same-day delivery tripled year over year, and pharmacy users increased over 60% year over year.

CEO Andy Jassy said AWS accelerated for the sixth consecutive quarter and that the company believes AWS can grow north of 40% in each of 2027 and 2028 and become a trillion-dollar revenue business in the next five to 10 years. CFO Brian Olsavsky said ongoing capital expenditures in AI and cloud are expected to drive long-term revenue and free cash flow, though near-term profitability may fluctuate. He also said the outsized growth of AI puts margin pressure on the business as a whole because those margins are lower. Management expects advertising growth to return to the high teens with the rollout of the Amazon Ads Agent.

The stock traded at $239.15, down from $244.45 just before the earnings, and the report said the profit miss prompted a significant negative market reaction. Management pointed to a sizeable AWS backlog and growing adoption of new AI services as support for its outlook. The report said the team will watch AWS adoption of new AI offerings, the effectiveness of robotics and automation in cutting fulfillment costs, and retail cross-selling in grocery and pharmacy. It also said integration and monetization of new advertising and AI services will be crucial signposts for Amazon's execution.

Articles.Title: AMZN Q3 deep dive: cloud surge and AI investments drive mixed market reception

stories.Headline: Kayakers bring 'Power for People, Not for Tech' protest to Washington's AI Week kickoff
stories.Summary:
Members of the Seattle climate activism group Troublemakers interrupted the opening panel of Seattle AI Week several times before security escorted them out, according to GeekWire. The panel focused on AI and economic growth and took place at the Washington Technology Industry Association's third annual event. While the panel was underway, kayakers on Elliott Bay displayed a banner reading "Power for People, Not for Tech." The panel included Beau Perschbacher, a senior policy advisor to Gov. Bob Ferguson, Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce leader Joe Nguyen, and Mattie Zazueta, OpenAI's global head of community programs. OpenAI was also the event's presenting sponsor.

The group wants green jobs and clean energy to be Washington's investment priorities, and it describes the expansion of data centers and the deployment of AI as threats to the state's environment, jobs, and communities. The action was the latest in the group's efforts against data center expansion, after members blocked access to Amazon's Seattle headquarters in 2024 over a plan to use natural gas for Oregon data centers. Washington AI Resistance coordinated 19 or more demonstrations across Washington in October to seek a statewide moratorium. In June, Seattle's City Council unanimously approved a yearlong halt on new large data centers, according to GeekWire. Ferguson's administration established a working group to examine data centers' effects.

Perschbacher acknowledged that the facilities use a really significant amount of electricity, according to GeekWire, and he said ensuring an adequate power supply is a major challenge with demand from electric vehicles and heat pumps also growing. He said the state's review found data centers' water consumption was not out of line with a typical industrial user. He said Washington won't allow the facilities to operate diesel generators continuously and that lawmakers would likely reconsider legislation addressing ratepayer protections. During a later panel, State Sen. Marko Liias, who sponsored legislation on high-risk AI uses, said that when energy becomes scarce, communities deserve access to that energy before the data centers do. GeekWire described his other expectations for facilities seeking to locate in Washington as supplying the grid with additional clean energy, reusing water, and abandoning nondisclosure agreements that leave communities uninformed.

Articles.Title: Kayakers bring 'Power for People, Not for Tech' protest to Washington's AI Week kickoff

stories.Headline: Trump says AI leaders signed a 'constitution' to police themselves - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that technology leaders he met at the White House had signed a "constitution" to police themselves on artificial intelligence. The meeting took place on September 29, 2026, and followed warnings from AI leaders about the technology's risks. House Speaker Mike Johnson said the accord is voluntary for the companies, and Trump stressed the industry would be self-policing. When asked whether the agreement is binding, Trump said it is "morally" binding.

The document is called "The White House Accord on Superintelligence: A Joint Commitment on Frontier SI Responsibilities." Johnson described it as a statement of principles, standards and voluntary commitments that sets out robust internal controls and layers of internal and external review. The screenshot Trump shared says signatories believe each AI company should implement a series of controls and audits, and it recognizes the steps are not codified into laws or regulations. Trump said officials are thinking about forming a committee of maybe 10 people to watch over the enterprise, though it is unclear who would serve or whether its decisions would be binding.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg attended along with Elon Musk, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Nvidia's Jensen Huang, Palantir's Alex Karp and Shyam Sankar, Amazon's Jeff Bezos and OpenAI's Greg Brockman. Zuckerberg called the agreement a start that the whole industry could come to, and said it covers principles and commitments around building multiple layers of auditing and controls. He said companies' boards would independently review reports from auditors. Johnson said Congress would continue to guide the industry's development safely but stopped short of announcing any enforcement action.

Trump has opposed guardrails and regulations on the technology or anything that would stifle its growth, and last week at the United Nations General Assembly he said the U.S. rejects a global attempt to regulate AI. When a reporter asked why there should not be more stringent guardrails than the voluntary document, Trump said the AI CEOs love America, and when pressed on whether it requires more than love, he pointed to his head and said it requires this. Johnson said two weeks ago there would be a deliberate discussion about the companies' responsibility for safety and what role, if any, government has to play. On Monday, Johnson said fears of the threat of AI are a Chinese psychological operation and are politically motivated.

Articles.Title: Trump says AI leaders signed a 'constitution' to police themselves - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos

stories.Headline: NYSBA Releases In-Depth Guidelines To Advise Attorneys on Ethical Use of AI - New York State Bar Association
stories.Summary:
The New York State Bar Association's House of Delegates adopted a report titled "Legal Ethics Guidelines for Lawyers' Use of Artificial Intelligence" on Saturday, October 31, 2026. The report was written by the association's Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technologies. The committee is chaired by Vivian Wesson, who is executive vice president, general counsel, and chief compliance officer of The Board of Pensions of the Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.). The article was published by Rebecca Melnitsky on October 31, 2026.

The guidelines aim to help attorneys avoid the unauthorized practice of law, keep legal decisions in human hands, and reduce bias in legal proceedings. The association urges attorneys to check that AI results do not reflect biased input from training data, design, and deployment, with particular concern about tools used in ways that could affect a person's rights, access, opportunity, or treatment. Attorneys may charge fees for time spent verifying an AI tool's output but not for learning how to use it, and they must keep fees reasonable and disclose specific charges to clients. Acquiring an AI tool is an overhead expense that may not be billed to a client unless it is for a service specially incurred for that case. The report also covers conflicts of interest, notifying all parties when AI is used for recording and summaries, disclosing AI use for court submissions, and reviewing the output of agentic AI systems.

Taa Grays, president of the association, said generative AI is indelibly changing the practice of law and that the guidelines are meant as a resource so attorneys can use AI responsibly and ethically. She said the guidelines can help attorneys avoid perils such as inadvertently practicing law in a jurisdiction where they are not licensed or failing to notify clients or the courts of AI use. Wesson said that while technology keeps evolving, it is important to still follow the ethical principles of the law. She said the committee developed the report to aid attorneys using AI tools and systems, aiming to help lawyers use the technology while fulfilling their responsibility to clients, the courts, and the administration of justice.

The New York Rules of Professional Conduct do not specifically address AI-generated legal work, but the association's guidelines extrapolate that an attorney is still responsible for ensuring a non-lawyer's work is up to standards, even if the "non-lawyer" is an AI tool or system. Attorneys are also responsible for carefully supervising non-lawyers and vendors who use AI tools. The report notes that disclosing AI use for court submissions is a policy many courts already have in place. The association is holding its Annual Conference in 2027, with registration open and early bird pricing ending November 2.

Articles.Title: NYSBA Releases In-Depth Guidelines To Advise Attorneys on Ethical Use of AI - New York State Bar Association

stories.Headline: Two US senators write letter to Google CEO Sundar Pichai asking 9 questions as company pushes for AI in classrooms
stories.Summary:
Two US senators, Richard Blumenthal and Josh Hawley, sent a letter to Google CEO Sundar Pichai asking nine questions about the company's push of AI products into schools. The letter followed an investigation into how Google's AI tools affect schoolchildren. The senators gave November 2, 2026 as the deadline for Google to respond. They wrote that they had grave concern that Google's aggressive push of AI products to children in schools is threatening the academic success and wellbeing of an entire generation. The letter asks what Google knows about the impact of its AI products on children's mental health and educational development.

It asks what research Google has conducted on Gemini, AI Overviews, AI Mode and other AI products, and requests that research. It asks why Google set AI product integration as the default and in some cases made it impossible to disable these features on licensed education devices. It also asks about promotional programs, how much money Google has spent on them, what resources Google has given to school districts, and what steps Google took after its researchers published a paper titled "The Ethics of Advanced AI Assistants." The senators cited a Wall Street Journal article that interviewed more than 60 teachers, parents, students and clinicians. They said test scores on national exams have declined and many students are increasingly unable to think critically or complete assignments independently after AI was introduced to the classroom.

They said Google is forcing its AI products into classrooms across America and children are paying the price. They also said the country cannot repeat the mistakes of social media platforms, where products were pushed onto children with profit put ahead of young people's best interests. The questions also ask whether Google has identified cases where its classroom AI tools encouraged a minor to engage in harmful behavior or emotional dependence, or failed to detect signs of suicidal or self-harm ideation. They ask what Google has done to prevent its AI chatbots from engaging in sycophantic or emotional conversations with children, including in light of failures to protect the Maryland student who was hospitalized after developing an intense dependence on Google's AI. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the November 2 deadline for Google's response.

Articles.Title: Two US senators write letter to Google CEO Sundar Pichai asking 9 questions as company pushes for AI in c - The Times of India

stories.Headline: Indices Weekly Outlook: S&P 500 breaks support as wobbling AI trade weigh on stocks
stories.Summary:
The S&P 500 broke support between 7,620 and 7,632 and closed below its 21-day exponential moving average, Fawad Razaqzada of StoneX wrote on Sunday, 1 November 2026. The index had bounced off its session lows on Friday after a bruising day but kept much of its weakness into the close. A 30% drop in Intel shares after its earnings results triggered the latest leg lower. Renewed weakness in technology shares put the AI trade back under the microscope.

The article says a daily close below that zone, which was previously resistance, is another technically bearish sign. It also says the index took out a short-term bullish trend line, so the path of least resistance is to the downside for now. If selling continues, 7,500 could be the next stop, followed by the 200-day moving average around 7,325. On the upside, the broken support around 7,620 is the first resistance, followed by Thursday's low at 7,675.

Razaqzada wrote that without a convincing recovery in the big technology names, it is hard to see the index regaining its footing in a hurry. He said a lot will depend on the direction of the AI trade and upcoming earnings releases. He noted that the tech sell-off pushed investors toward Treasuries, dragging yields and the dollar lower. He also said the near-term forecast remains tilted to the downside.

Tuesday's midterm elections and Friday's non-farm payrolls report are the main event risks, according to the article. It says a Democratic clean sweep is increasingly likely and could revive concerns over government shutdowns and the debt ceiling. The Federal Reserve kept rates unchanged last week, but a December hike is highly likely, with third-quarter GDP up 3.4% and core PCE inflation up 0.3% month on month in September. The Bank of England is expected to raise rates to 4% on Thursday, and a strong payrolls print would cement expectations for a December hike.

stories.Headline: Energy Leaders Move AI From Pilots to Core Operations: ADNOC-Backed Report - News and Statistics
stories.Summary:
The third edition of the annual Powering Possible report was released by ADNOC, XRG and Microsoft ahead of the fourth ENACT Majlis in Abu Dhabi and ADIPEC 2026, which is scheduled in Abu Dhabi from November 2 to 5. The report, subtitled Energy Resilience in the Intelligence Era, draws on a survey of close to 400 senior energy and finance leaders. It found that AI now ranks among the two highest corporate priorities for 62 per cent of energy leaders, up from 42 per cent in 2025. Take-up of agentic AI more than doubled in the last twelve months.

Spending rose at 89 per cent of respondents over the past year, and 63 per cent expect returns from current investments to match or surpass their outlay. The share of organisations running integrated agentic AI workflows climbed from 15 per cent to 33 per cent, while the share still testing isolated applications fell from 35 per cent to 15 per cent. Within the industry, 60 per cent of respondents are already trialling or rolling out autonomous and robotic systems in physical operations, from infrastructure inspection to hazardous tasks. Supply stability and reliability became the most cited gauge of AI's contribution, rising from 26 per cent to 39 per cent, while cost reductions as the principal contribution fell from 19 per cent to 13 per cent.

Dr Sultan Al Jaber, ADNOC Managing Director and Group CEO and Executive Chairman of XRG, said AI is opening substantial new possibilities for the sector to generate greater value, reinforce resilience and enhance safety and reliability. He said ADNOC is integrating AI, robotics and advanced technology across its operations to optimise every barrel, molecule and megawatt produced, and that energy and technology need to progress in tandem. Brad Smith, Vice Chair and President of Microsoft, said progress should be judged not merely by uptake but by whether it produces enduring value while securing public confidence. He said energy's reliance on reliability and security demands robust governance, clear accountability and continuing investment in people and skills.

Seventy-four per cent of leaders expect AI to push up energy consumption by 2030, but only 52 per cent are confident today's infrastructure can handle the extra electricity. Grid modernisation and smart-grid technologies are the top investment priority for enabling AI expansion, named by 67 per cent, with energy storage second at 42 per cent. Confidence varies by market, with 74 per cent in Brazil and 70 per cent in India considering infrastructure adequate, against 40 per cent in the US and 38 per cent in the UK. The report says energy and digital infrastructure investment must move forward together, supported by cybersecurity, trusted AI-ready data, shared standards, sound governance and a skilled workforce.

Articles.Title: Energy Leaders Move AI From Pilots to Core Operations: ADNOC-Backed Report - News and Statistics

stories.Headline: Inductive Bio's Alex Taylor on AI in Drug Discovery
stories.Summary:
Alex Taylor is Vice President and Head of Medicinal Chemistry at Inductive Bio, a chemical intelligence and AI-driven drug discovery company. Inductive Bio was founded in 2022 and incorporated in 2021 by Josh Haimson, the CEO, and Ben Birnbaum, the President and CTO. It is headquartered in New York City and builds virtual chemistry labs and machine learning platforms to help biopharmaceutical teams design, evaluate and optimise small-molecule therapeutics. In July, the company placed first in OpenADMET's PXR Blind Challenge, beating more than 350 researchers across large pharma, biotech, academic and AI organisations. Taylor joined Inductive in mid 2025 after almost 20 years in the industry, always working in small molecules across all stages of discovery projects.

Taylor described two of the company's tools. Beacon-2 is a predictive dosing model that extends beyond ADMET and provides a unified system of models that predicts a molecule's efficacious human dose directly from its chemical structure. By combining Inductive's predictive ADME models with measured or predicted potency values, it lets teams visualise and reason about the pros and cons of individual compounds as they relate to the ultimate MPO. Indy is an LLM-based chemistry agent that harnesses cutting-edge LLMs for medchem-specific thinking and workflows. It can help with everything from enumerating compounds and getting their ADME predictions in Beacon-2 to QC'ing assay data to evaluating the characterisation data of a new set of compounds synthesised at a CRO.

Asked about critics who say AI models memorise patterns instead of physical laws, Taylor said his software engineering colleagues half-jokingly call LLMs very fancy auto-complete algorithms. He said LLMs on their own can only reliably generate output within the bounds of the data they have seen, but they become powerful when linked to tools as agents. He said AI is used daily with partners and that Indy recently generated a table of literature-reported VHL binders, calculated their TPSA and tabulated structure, reported potency and TPSA in a few minutes, work that would have taken hours. He said humans are best at leading iterative learning cycles and designing compounds to address specific hypotheses, because generative algorithms often make several changes at once, so unexpected results may not be traceable to a single change.

Taylor said the best way to think of scientific AI tools today is as early-career associates who are extremely well-read on theory, rarely forget past project work and have incredible attention to detail, though they make mistakes from time to time. He said collaboration is the way to go, with big firms like Anthropic and OpenAI refining LLMs and connecting them to tools while small groups focus on specific problems. He said completely de novo virtual prediction of small molecule binders to proteins remains almost intractable, with extremely few successful examples in the literature, so he is not optimistic that protein design advances will quickly translate to small molecules. He said his boldest prediction for the next five years is that advances in choosing efficacious drug targets and predicting toxicity would really move the needle, noting that 25 years ago the main reason drugs failed in clinical trials was insufficient exposure.

Articles.Title: Inductive Bio's Alex Taylor on AI in Drug Discovery

stories.Headline: Tyler Technologies Q3 2026 slides: record cash flow, AI momentum
stories.Summary:
Tyler Technologies reported its third quarter 2026 results on October 28, 2026, and presented the figures in an earnings slide deck. The company posted revenue of $647.6 million and non-GAAP earnings per share of $3.52, which slightly beat analyst profit expectations while missing revenue forecasts by less than 1%. Shares fell in pre-market trading but recovered to close at $394.30, up 4.14% from pre-earnings levels. Investors focused on expanding margins and a strengthening recurring revenue base.

Revenue grew 8.7% year-over-year, or 10.2% excluding the impact of a Texas payments contract. SaaS revenue rose 21.2% to $242.2 million, transaction revenue rose 9.5% to $220.4 million, or 14.2% excluding the Texas contract, and annualized recurring revenue grew 11% to $2.28 billion. Free cash flow rose 11.9% to $277.0 million with a 42.8% margin, and non-GAAP operating margin improved 150 basis points to 28.1%. Recurring revenue was 87.8% of the total at $568.8 million, up 11.0% overall or 12.8% excluding the Texas contract, while maintenance revenue fell 4.6% as expected amid cloud migrations.

The company said government budgets were healthy and volumes of requests for proposals and product demonstrations were high. About 300 deals containing AI components closed year-to-date, with 130 signed in the third quarter alone, SaaS bookings grew 14.0%, total bookings grew 7.3%, and new SaaS annual contract value surged 75%. Tyler cited wins including enterprise ERP deals with Gallup, New Mexico and Vero Beach, Florida, public safety systems for Baker County Sheriff in Florida and Azusa, California, and SaaS flips for Buffalo, New York and Honolulu, Hawaii. It also described its largest workforce management deal to date, with the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, plus contracts with the Department of Justice and the National Institutes of Health.

Tyler positioned AI as expanding its market beyond software into government labor augmentation, building on a $2.0 billion recurring software base. It cited more than 16,000 client relationships, a national sales force, procurement through contract amendments, and client trust as advantages for scaling AI. The company said it uses data from its clients and works with Microsoft, OpenAI, AWS, and Anthropic. It reported $2.33 billion in 2025 revenue, 87% recurring, 98% gross client retention, and an approximate 27% free cash flow margin, with revenue split across ERP and financial, state and federal, courts and justice, public safety, K-12, civic services, and appraisal and tax.

Articles.Title: Tyler Technologies Q3 2026 slides: record cash flow, AI momentum

stories.Headline: Patient AI in Primary Care: 114 Patients, 0 Stops [2026]
stories.Summary:
A chatbot interviewed 100 real patients about their symptoms before they saw a doctor, and supervising physicians stopped none of the chats. Researchers at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston and Google tested Google's conversational AI, called AMIE, in a live urgent care setting. The trial ran from April to November 2025 and enrolled 114 patients, with 98 followed through both the AI chat and the actual appointment. The study was reported on November 1, 2026 by Technology Org and published in The Lancet on October 8, 2026, according to Unite.ai.

Patients scheduled a new, non-emergency urgent care visit and chatted with AMIE from home up to five days before the appointment, with a median gap of one day. The design was a single-arm, single-center feasibility study with no control group, so it can show the approach is workable and safe under supervision but not that AMIE improves outcomes. The final diagnosis appeared in AMIE's top seven possibilities 90% of the time, in the top three 75% of the time, and ranked first in 56% of cases. Panels of three blinded evaluators found the quality of the differential diagnosis, the appropriateness of the plan and the safety of the plan statistically similar to clinicians' plans, though physicians won on practicality and cost-effectiveness.

A board-certified internal medicine physician supervised each conversation through live video with screen sharing, and four predefined triggers allowed the supervisor to halt a chat. Across the 98 analyzed encounters, none fired, though ASCO AI reports one hallucination, an incorrect surgery date, and five cases where the supervisor needed to clarify something. The paper's own conclusion, as relayed by ASCO AI, is that AMIE was conversationally safe within this physician-supervised, single-complaint, urgent care setting. Patient attitudes toward AI improved significantly after the chat and the improvement persisted after the visit, but patients voiced doubts about the confidentiality of what they shared and about the chatbot's honesty and trustworthiness.

The authors list several limitations, including no comparator group, a text-only interface with no images or multimodal input, and no access to patient records or ability to examine anyone. Participants skewed younger than the clinic's usual urgent care population, where more than half of the 1,452 visits involved patients over 60, per Unite.ai. Pregnancy and mental health complaints were excluded, and the live AI supervisor may have discouraged patients from testing the system's boundaries. Adam Rodman, a co-author, served as a visiting researcher at Google during the study, a conflict the paper discloses.

Articles.Title: Patient AI in Primary Care: 114 Patients, 0 Stops [2026]

stories.Headline: Accountable for AI the CIO Never Approved | Kovrr
stories.Summary:
When an AI system fails inside a large company, the question that follows is who was responsible for it. The answer usually falls on the CIO, even though the CIO often had no part in choosing, approving or deploying the system that failed. The article describes this as a structural problem rather than a governance problem, because the authority to introduce AI has spread across the business while answerability stayed in one office. Surveys cited in the article consistently show that IT is frequently not the source of approval.

Schellman's 2026 State of AI Governance report, which surveyed 525 professionals involved in evaluating, deploying or governing AI, found that 42% name the CIO or head of IT as primarily responsible for AI purchasing decisions. A Dataiku and Harris Poll survey of 685 CIOs across eight countries found that 84% say employees build AI agents and applications faster than IT can govern them, and 60% have no central governance layer spanning their enterprise applications and environments. The same Dataiku research found CIOs divided on who is primarily responsible when an agent causes harm, with no answer commanding more than a quarter of responses. Thoughtworks reached a similar reading in its 2026 global CIO survey, describing authority over AI as already divided across central IT, business units, executive leadership and dedicated AI roles, with accountability not always aligned to responsibility.

The article argues that an executive who is answerable for something they cannot authorize cannot resolve the position through diligence, so the work is to change what they can see and measure. It recommends a real inventory of every AI system touching corporate data, including ones inside software already licensed, with the surface that detected each one recorded alongside it. It calls for named ownership on both sides, a business owner and a technical owner per asset, so a question about any one of them has a destination. It also calls for exposure stated in financial terms the board can compare against other risks, and for evidence an auditor would ask for, collected continuously.

Schellman found only 54% of organizations report AI governance regularly to their board or executive leadership, and just 36% of boards regularly discuss third-party AI risk. The same research found 74% of organizations believe they could pass an AI compliance audit today while 27% describe their governance as fully mature, and 90% have already allocated funding. The article says money is not the constraint, and that the gap between what leaders believe and what an auditor would find closes through evidence rather than budget. It says Kovrr's AI Security and Governance Platform maintains that inventory continuously and quantifies what sits inside it, and it invites readers to book a demo with its AI risk experts.

Articles.Title: Accountable for AI the CIO Never Approved | Kovrr

stories.Headline: Sanford Health surgeon weighs in on AI in surgery
stories.Summary:
A Sanford Health surgeon discussed artificial intelligence in surgery in a report published by KFYR-TV on November 1, 2026. The report was updated about 11 hours after it first appeared. It asked whether people would trust artificial intelligence to perform their next surgery. The article notes that artificial intelligence is already being used to drive cars. The report does not give the surgeon's name or say what the surgeon requires or what would change.

stories.Headline: The AI-Native Job Interview Is Different. Here’s Why.
stories.Summary:
Doug Levin wrote in a Substack post dated November 1, 2026 that he had taken part in several interviews at AI-native companies and noticed the questions, expectations and substance differed from the traditional software and SaaS era. The old playbook stressed experience, functional expertise, leadership and a record of execution, and those still matter, but the companies want people who understand how AI works, where it creates value, where it fails and how it changes a business's economics and operations. He said a consistent theme was that practical experience matters more than theoretical knowledge, with interviewers seeking specific examples of tools used, projects undertaken, mistakes made and lessons learned. Candidates also need to explain how they would measure success rather than simply what they would build, and honest accounts of failures and changing assumptions often carry more weight than polished success stories.

Levin listed the areas the interviews cover, including AI fluency and tooling, where candidates are asked what tools they use and what they have built, automated or broken. Product and strategy questions ask how AI changes product development, competitive advantage and build-versus-buy decisions, and what happens when everyone has access to the same models. Unit economics and business models questions cover how inference costs, token consumption, gross margins and usage-based pricing change traditional SaaS economics, while organization and operations questions ask what an AI-native organization looks like and which roles evolve or disappear. He also listed judgment, risk and governance, learning and adaptability, leadership and collaboration, and behavioral and case questions involving AI failures, investment decisions, competitive threats, customer satisfaction and difficult trade-offs under uncertainty.

Levin wrote that these are not simply new technical interview questions but reflect a fundamental change in how companies create value, organize work, allocate capital and compete. He said that in the SaaS era, experience scaling established processes and organizations was often a strong predictor of success, while in the AI-native era the ability to rethink those processes and organizations may matter just as much. He said the emerging hiring question is no longer simply what someone has accomplished but increasingly what they can accomplish differently because AI exists. He added that perhaps the most revealing question of all is what a candidate has learned that caused them to change their mind.

Articles.Title: The AI-Native Job Interview Is Different. Here’s Why.

stories.Headline: Vercel Labs Open-Sources agent-desktop for Agent Computer Use
stories.Summary:
Vercel Labs released agent-desktop, an open-source command-line tool for AI agent computer use, on October 30, 2026. It works on macOS, Windows and Linux. The tool reads each app through the operating system's accessibility tree rather than through screenshots. An agent receives a JSON snapshot with a reference for every element it can act on. Version 1.0.2 shipped under the Apache-2.0 license.

The tool is a Rust CLI and a C library with 60 command names, 56 of them operational. It runs on macOS 13 and later, Windows 10 1809 or Server 2019 and later, and Ubuntu 24.04 and later, on x64 and ARM64 with a plain CPU and no GPU. Each command prints one JSON envelope and exits, and the observe, act and verify loop stays in the agent. A snapshot assigns qualified refs such as @s8f3k2p9:e8, and a bare @e8 is rejected with INVALID_ARGS. When the UI changes, an action returns STALE_REF or AMBIGUOUS_TARGET, and the agent takes a fresh snapshot.

The builder reported a 78% to 96% token cut versus full-tree dumps in Slack, VS Code and Notion. In Apple Maps, the builder reported 3,811 tokens per look falling to 273, and a simulated 52-step task dropped from 198k to 31k tokens. These figures are self-reported, and there is no independent computer-use benchmark yet. Ref actions go through the accessibility API without moving the pointer or taking focus, and every ref action auto-waits up to 5,000 ms for a visible, enabled, stable target. The global --headed flag allows physical input when needed.

The articles describe agent-desktop as model-agnostic and say it returns structure, not images. They compare it with pixel-based tools: Anthropic's docs say each screenshot costs roughly 1,000 to 1,800 input tokens, and its toolset definition adds about 4,500 input tokens per request. Microsoft's UFO² also uses UI Automation but ships as a full Windows agent. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: Vercel Labs Open-Sources agent-desktop for Agent Computer Use

stories.Headline: AI pioneer Martin Ester named Canada CIFAR AI Chair for advancing precision medicine - Simon Fraser University
stories.Summary:
Martin Ester, a Distinguished Professor in Simon Fraser University's School of Computing Science and a Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada, has been appointed as a Canada CIFAR AI Chair by the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research. The appointment was announced by SFU in an article dated October 20, 2026. Ester is described as a leading Canadian researcher in artificial intelligence. His work explores how AI systems can learn from one another to speed up scientific discovery and generate new chemical structures.

Ester's research aims to improve medical diagnoses and treatment based on a person's genomics and lifestyle. His 2025 study introduced CGFlow, an AI method that speeds up the design of complex molecular structures for treating disease. The method generates effective drug candidates and also shows researchers how to synthesize them. Ester is one of seven researchers in a cohort backed by nearly $4.5 million in federal funding under Canada's national AI strategy.

The strategy supports leading scholars in advancing foundational AI science and developing solutions to pressing challenges. Dugan O'Neil, vice-president, research and innovation, said Ester's work places SFU at the forefront of applying machine learning to medicine and fits the university's mission to advance AI for the benefit of society. He called the appointment fitting recognition for one of Canada's leading AI scientists. Ester said machine learning as an enabling technology for precision medicine is one way to use AI for the greater good.

He said it is wonderful to be recognized by CIFAR for work he hopes will ultimately improve the health of patients in Canada and beyond. CIFAR works closely with three national institutes, Amii in Edmonton, Mila in Montreal and the Vector Institute in Toronto, to advance fundamental research and ensure AI is developed safely, responsibly and for the benefit of all. Ester joins SFU's growing presence at the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute, which is now home to six Canada CIFAR AI Chairs. They are Martin Ester, Angel Chang, Mo Chen, Ke Li, Angelica Lim and Jason Peng.

Articles.Title: AI pioneer Martin Ester named Canada CIFAR AI Chair for advancing precision medicine - Simon Fraser University

stories.Headline: Business leaders are leaning into AI, but they can’t do it without hiring humans. Where are the profits?
stories.Summary:
Business leaders are leaning into artificial intelligence, but they say they cannot do it without hiring humans. The Inquirer spoke with five business leaders about how AI is reshaping their companies, in a piece published on November 1, 2026. Professionals who can help companies implement AI and cope with its complexity are in high demand. Some businesses have to hire, not cut, to make AI work.

Bridgenext is a multinational consulting firm based in Conshohocken that employs 1,850 engineers, architects, data scientists, and other professionals. EPAM Systems is a Newtown-based IT outsourcing company with 65,000 workers. Norm Ai builds agents to automate and govern legal work, and its law firm affiliate Norm Law has more than 50 lawyers. Norm Ai has raised more than $140 million in investment capital from financial institutions such as Blackstone, Vanguard, Citi, New York Life, and TIAA.

One leader said the top corporate hiring position as of 2026 is the forward deployed engineer, who understands AI agents and the business and has solid change-management and relationship skills. Another said the most ironic thing about dealing with AI is that it involves more philosophical and human-centered issues than technology problems. A third said that if a business has unresolved problems, adding AI is not likely to solve them and could make things worse. One leader said AI will not take jobs away, and that resistance to change, experimentation, learning, and adopting these new technical realities is the threat.

The leaders described AI as the most transformative factor in business they have seen, and said data is really where the action is. One said AI deployments have proven more efficient and cost effective, and that AI should be deployed in a governed way with industry rules and oversight built in. Another said the HR function is becoming more important, not less, given its role in understanding the new technology and using AI insights to justify staffing decisions. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: Business leaders are leaning into AI, but they can’t do it without hiring humans. Where are the profits?

stories.Headline: AI "pets" for China's lonely carve out market of their own - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
Chen Yuechong, a Chinese consumer, bought three palm-sized AI "pets" called Fuzozos, according to a Xinhua report dated Oct. 31, 2026. She picks out clothes and accessories for them and bought a tiny wooden bed to place beside her own. She built a small play scene out of modeling clay, with ducks and other props, so the toys can pretend to squirt them. Her wish began with wanting someone who would listen, because there are things she cannot tell her elders and does not want to burden friends with negative emotions. After trying various AI chatbots, she bought the three toys because she wanted a companion that responds to her feelings, remembers shared experiences and is physically present.

China's retail sales of trendy and collectible toys reached 67.69 billion yuan, about 10 billion U.S. dollars, in 2025, up 45.4 percent from a year earlier, per a white paper from the China Toy & Juvenile Products Association. Online sales of AI toys reached 850 million yuan in the first half of 2026, up 183.9 percent year on year, according to Moojing Market Intelligence. Fuzozo has secured sales of over 300,000 units, Ropet nearly 40,000 and Loona more than 100,000, based on figures from their developers. Loona is a mobile robotic pet priced at around 3,000 yuan that can move around the home, follow its owner and greet people when they return. Guangdong Province aims to have AI toys account for over 30 percent of its toy products by 2027.

Zhang Yi, CEO of the market research firm iiMedia Research, said AI toys combine companionship, collectible toys and emotional consumption, and that advances in AI are turning once-static products into interactive companions. He Jiabin, co-founder and CEO of Ropet's maker, said AI products for companionship can start with a narrower task scope than household robots facing an unpredictable home environment. He said Ropet, a fur-covered robot with a constant body temperature of 37 degrees Celsius, was deliberately designed to be less intelligent than an adult, and that a touch or a moment of eye contact can be enough when people come home exhausted. He explained that people only feel at ease around a creature that is endearingly goofy and knows less than they do. Xin Cheng, product manager at Alpha Group, said an upgraded AI Lazy Goat toy with educational content has generated more than 100,000 orders this year.

China is the world's largest toy producer and exporter, accounting for roughly 70 percent of global toy production, and established companies are entering the AI pet market. Alpha Group, which owns animation properties including Pleasant Goat and Super Wings, has launched AI-enabled toys featuring characters from its series. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology called AI toys a "new engine" for the toy industry and encouraged toy makers to team up with AI companies on hit products. Chen does not describe her Fuzozos as products or assistants but calls them equals that are almost like younger siblings, and what she pays for is the feeling that someone at home is waiting for her.
