stories.Headline: Economic Watch: AI takes on bigger role in China's express delivery during Singles' Day peak - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
A drone hovers overhead and calibrates its position while a smart locker below opens its double doors. A package is lowered precisely into the compartment before the doors close. Later, a customer collects it with a code, with no courier on site. Scenes like this are becoming common during this year's Singles' Day shopping rush, as China's express delivery industry pushes artificial intelligence deeper into frontline operations. From sorting centers to last-mile delivery, companies are deploying intelligent agents, robots and predictive models to streamline the entire delivery chain.

The Singles' Day shopping festival, also known as Double 11 because it falls on Nov. 11, is China's annual online shopping carnival and one of the world's biggest retail events. The most visible change this year is that AI is no longer confined to back-office analytics. STO Express has deployed AI digital employees through its SClaw intelligent-agent platform, which can assist with customer inquiries, intercept abnormal shipments, plan trunk-line routes and help couriers make outbound calls and optimize delivery sequences. A digital quality-control system is also flagging risks for fresh produce and other sensitive parcels.

JD Logistics has rolled out its upgraded Super Brain 3.0 large model as a decision-making hub, forecasting order volumes by region and adjusting nationwide logistics capacity in real time. The company said AI-recommended delivery routes have an adoption rate of more than 90.2 percent. JD Logistics is deploying embodied intelligent robotic arms at scale in sorting centers, and the arms have achieved a parcel tracking accuracy rate of 99.9 percent. Drones are also delivering to remote villages in southwest China, where mountainous terrain and river crossings have long made last-mile delivery difficult.

SF Express is using sales forecasts and digital supply-chain tools to move inventory closer to consumers in advance, shortening the last-mile delivery distance. YTO Express has embedded more than 100 intelligent agents into route optimization, dispatch analysis and customer-service workflows, and put 28 digital employees to work in operations and customer service. Digital-twin systems now cover its entire network of consolidation hubs. Zhang Yi, vice-president of the Guangdong Internet Society, said AI applications are now used across the entire e-commerce operation cycle, from product selection and content creation to traffic acquisition, customer service and competitor analysis.

A recent report by the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing showed that AI adoption in China's logistics and supply chains had exceeded 37 percent, with transport at 78 percent, safety and compliance at 52.73 percent, and smart warehousing at 47.27 percent. China's express delivery sector handled 151.3 billion parcels in the first nine months of 2026, up 4.3 percent from a year earlier, according to the State Post Bureau. Hu Dajian, vice-president of the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing, said AI is shifting from isolated applications to whole-chain coordination, extending from single enterprises to broader industrial-chain collaboration. In 2025, China released a policy document to advance the AI Plus initiative, setting out goals and priorities for integrating AI across the economy and society. Industry observers said the broad commercial rollout of AI has become a major highlight of this year's Singles' Day shopping peak, signaling that the next competitive edge will come less from scale than from AI embedded across the entire operational chain.

Articles.Title: AI takes on bigger role in China's express delivery during Singles' Day peak - Xinhua

stories.Headline: Interview: Namibian media executive eyes AI cooperation, stronger Global South voice at World Media Summit - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
Confidence Musariri, Acting Manager for Editorial and Operations at the Namibia Press Agency (NAMPA), gave an interview to Xinhua ahead of the World Media Summit in Beijing, China. The interview was published on Oct. 31, 2026. He said Global South media must unite to dismantle persistent stereotypes and adopt artificial intelligence wisely. He said his agency is already using AI to cut production costs, speed up delivery and widen its audience.

The 7th World Media Summit, hosted by Xinhua News Agency, will be held in Beijing from Nov. 5 to Nov. 9, 2026, under the theme "Media's Mission and Cooperative Action amid Intelligent Transformation." Musariri said Global South news agencies should share content directly with one another rather than relying on Western gatekeepers. He said most African countries are treated as "one Africa" rather than as individual sovereign nations, and that stereotypes about war, poverty and corruption hurt investment and a country's image. He called on the Global South to unite and embrace the momentum generated by social media, where content creators tell stories in their own way.

Musariri said media organizations have failed to fully use existing political agreements and distribution channels, and continue to rely on Western news agencies to verify and gatekeep content. He said there is a need to boost cooperative news exchange agencies so agencies within the Global South can share content directly. He said NAMPA is integrating AI to cut costs, speed up content delivery and expand audience reach. He said he expects hands-on skills exchange that goes beyond traditional reporting training, focused on helping journalists adopt and adapt to rapidly evolving AI tools. He said the goal is to learn how newsrooms can integrate and automate data processes and digital convergence, and to deploy AI analytics effectively.

Musariri said NAMPA is looking forward to striking cooperation deals and agreements with different media stakeholders at the summit, and to learning how they are adopting new forms of media. He said that as Namibia formulates its national AI policy, newsrooms need forward-looking technology rather than outdated tools, and he expressed hope the summit will help identify next-generation AI solutions for journalists over the next three to five years. He said he has travelled to China four times in a professional and personal capacity, and that the summit carries special significance because he covered the 2008 Olympic Games as a journalist in the same district where he stayed, almost 18 years ago. He said NAMPA will use its Global South network and partner entities to report on the summit so media colleagues across Namibia and the broader continent have direct access to its key outcomes.

stories.Headline: At a birthplace of AI, pushback over using it for surveillance
stories.Summary:
MIT administrators considered adding AI capabilities to campus surveillance cameras to detect criminal activity, and faculty members objected. Since summer, professors have gone out once a week to decorate security cameras with colorful rhinestones and googly eyes. The decorations do not interfere with how the cameras work. Catherine D’Ignazio, an associate professor who specializes in urban science and data literacy, said they needed another way to have a more open and democratic dialogue about surveillance on campus.

MIT began installing new cameras in November to close gaps in security coverage, and about 4,600 cameras now watch the 168-acre campus. The school then explored hiring a surveillance technology company, Ambient.ai, to monitor the cameras in real time and alert officers to active threats or incidents. Faculty raised concerns about what could be done with the video data, the risks of misidentifying people, who would have access to the data, and a lack of community input. Some also questioned whether the technology would really make the campus safer.

Glen Shor, MIT’s executive vice president and treasurer, told faculty at a meeting on Oct. 21 that AI surveillance is no longer on the table. He told the Globe that MIT will not use AI in any way to observe or analyze campus activity, and that camera footage helps the MIT Police understand and resolve safety issues and incidents such as theft, vandalism, and property damage. Eric Lu, a fourth-year doctoral candidate in biological engineering and president of the Graduate Student Council, said MIT’s choices set a precedent for the broader community because when MIT speaks, people listen. The graduate student council sent a resolution to administrators calling for student input on any adoption of AI surveillance and research to justify its use.

MIT is arguably the birthplace of AI: in 1959, Marvin Minsky and John McCarthy founded what is now called the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. The mass shooting at Brown University last December, when a gunman killed two students on campus and later an MIT professor at his Brookline home, helped frame the role of larger surveillance on US campuses, and the shooter’s location was established in part with the help of a Flock camera in Providence. Brown expanded its camera network to about 1,950 by late August, according to a university report, and a spokesperson said the university had invested $65 million in campus safety since 2014. A review found limited camera coverage in the area of the shooting and said more cameras could have aided in identifying the shooter sooner, but it said additional cameras were unlikely to have prevented the attack.

Articles.Title: At a birthplace of AI, pushback over using it for surveillance

stories.Headline: AI: What it will and won’t replace
stories.Summary:
Susan Rupe wrote in InsuranceNewsNet on November 1, 2026, that this month marks 14 years of her writing and developing content for the publication. She recalled that when she started, one big industry story was the rise of roboadvisors, automated asset-allocation systems. The question then was whether roboadvisors would replace professionals who give investment advice. Now, she wrote, artificial intelligence tools serve more like intelligent assistants that analyze retirement plans, summarize concerns, draft emails, identify coverage gaps and explain tax implications. The question again is whether these tools will replace humans in insurance and financial services.

Rayne Morgan’s featured article in the same issue answers that question with a resounding no, according to Rupe. The experts interviewed agree that AI will not replace networking and relationship-building, and agents who hope AI will magically generate high-quality prospects are likely to be disappointed. The best leads still come through trusted relationships, referrals and industry networks, and AI can support sales but is not a substitute for human trust. Rupe wrote that the biggest AI opportunity may be helping customers find agents, so improving online presence could let AI-powered search tools such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini direct consumers to them. She added that agents often jump straight to AI tools without first creating a clear sales plan, defining an ideal customer or establishing strong messaging, and that AI works best when it enhances a solid business strategy.

The issue also features Panos Leledakis, founder and CEO of IFAAcademy, an insurance futurist, an expert in virtual reality and a member of the NextGen Advisory Task Force at The American College. Rupe described him as an award-winning inventor of software for insurance needs analysis and an international public speaker with hundreds of hours on stages around the world. She wrote that Leledakis challenges the adage “adapt or die” and replaces it with “adapt and fly” as he teaches financial professionals how AI can take their practices to new heights. Rupe concluded that the human advantage remains irreplaceable, because insurance is still a relationship business and customers may be overwhelmed by information and options. That, she wrote, makes an advisor’s experience, judgment and personal guidance more valuable than ever.

Articles.Title: AI: What it will and won’t replace

stories.Headline: NTT DATA verified the effectiveness of AI Consumer Agents
stories.Summary:
NTT DATA Japan Corporation announced on 19 March 2026 that it had verified the effectiveness of AI Consumer Agents in product development research for a makeup brand operated by Kao Corporation, a Japanese consumer goods company and global cosmetics and personal care manufacturer. The proof of concept assessed whether AI models could simulate the behavioral characteristics of consumers and develop personas to aid product development research. NTT DATA used its marketing AI agent service together with Kao's accumulated consumer research, purchase and social media data. It created multiple AI Consumers and an AI interviewer for use in the research.

The PoC showed that AI-driven research could potentially shorten the timeline from 1.5 months to just 0.5 days, a 99% reduction, while remaining consistent with insights from traditional research methods. It also reduced the operational workload involved in respondent recruitment and survey execution. NTT DATA said conventional research processes require significant time and costs for research design, respondent recruitment, fieldwork and analysis. It said that within limited development timelines it is difficult to sufficiently deepen research data or validate hypotheses. Kao's makeup brand launches new products each season, making a shorter development cycle a critical requirement.

Mizuho Mitake, Head of Second Industry Business Sector, Japan, at NTT DATA, said consumer trends have shifted from quarterly and monthly cycles to a weekly cycle. Mitake said consumer brands need high agility to respond to these rapidly changing trends, which is critical to business growth. Mitake said the PoC demonstrated that AI can achieve significant gains in speed in product development while ensuring quality equal to or even exceeding that of human output. Mitake said NTT DATA will expand the application of these results beyond product development into marketing operations.

NTT DATA describes itself as a business and technology services leader with revenue of more than $30 billion, serving 75% of the Fortune Global 100. It says it has experts in more than 70 countries and is part of NTT Group, which invests over $3 billion each year in research and development. The company says it promotes both proactive AI adoption and responsible governance. It aims to realize Smart AI Agent, in which AI agents autonomously extract, organize and execute tasks in response to user instructions.

Articles.Title: NTT DATA verified the effectiveness of AI Consumer Agents - NTT Data

stories.Headline: Load One AI Control Tower Transforms Expedited Freight Quoting
stories.Summary:
Load One, a Taylor, Michigan-based expedited trucking company ranked No. 148 on the CCJ Top 250, built its own artificial intelligence system in-house over the past several months, according to an article by Jason Cannon published November 1, 2026. The system is anchored by a centralized interface the company calls the AI Control Tower, which gives managers one screen to watch what its AI agents are doing across the business at any given time. The company launched its first AI agent in March and plans to end the year with nine. The article says Load One developed the tools itself rather than buying off-the-shelf software, so they could be tailored to expedited freight.

When a customer sends a rate request by email, an AI agent reads the message using a large language model, checks Load One's transportation management system, called Transcend, for available capacity, partner carrier bids and market density, and replies with a rate in about two seconds. Chad Tabor, president of Load One, said a fully human quote could take 5 to 20 minutes. As of late October, the agents were performing roughly 3,800 tasks a day that people had done earlier in the year. The billing compliance agent can process about 275 invoices in 15 minutes, and in its first week a load confirmation phone agent handled 1,381 dispatches at a cost of $131.49.

Tabor said the company designed the Control Tower as one screen a human can watch because AI works best with a person in the loop, and you do not want to let it run on its own without quality analysis. He said the agents still need a lot of oversight and that the goal is to protect the company's human capital, support staff and let the business scale without necessarily adding headcount. He said the automation only helps if an exception still lands with a person who can own the next decision for the customer. He also said that using AI to make people more powerful is the future of the trucking industry and that smart executives are figuring out how to do it.

The article says the Control Tower acts like an air traffic control center for freight, letting supervisors spot misquotes, monitor capacity limits and review confidence metrics before commitments are finalized. Supervisors can also generate instant AI summaries of long email threads with a single click. The article says deploying custom AI was streamlined because Load One had already spent years building its own software infrastructure. It does not say what further rollouts are planned beyond the target of nine agents by the end of the year.

Articles.Title: Load One AI Control Tower Transforms Expedited Freight Quoting

stories.Headline: Neoclouds: These firms you've never heard of are feeding fears the AI bubble could burst
stories.Summary:
A group of data centre companies known as neoclouds has become the focus of a heated debate in Silicon Valley over whether the AI boom is financially sound. Firms such as CoreWeave and Nebius run large warehouses full of expensive computers and lease them to major AI developers including Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta. Many of these companies began in crypto mining, and CoreWeave was founded in 2017 to mine Ethereum. Nebius was formerly Yandex NV, part of Russia's version of Google, before it split off and changed its name in 2024.

Neocloud firms often borrow money using long-term lease contracts with big tech customers and the AI chips they buy as collateral. Analyst Cory Johnson said this helped CoreWeave accumulate $35.1bn in debt. CoreWeave stock has lost a quarter of its value over the past month, and shares in Nebius, IREN and Applied Digital have fallen by about that much or more. Gartner analysts predict that by 2030, 80% of neocloud firms will cease independent operations, while Forrester expects at least three to be acquired soon as finances get shaky. Elon Musk suggested more than 200 neoclouds could face what he called guppy-level death and consolidation.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent downplayed the concerns on CNBC, calling the firms a small component of the overall ecosystem. CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator said the market is acting irrationally and expressed confidence in its business model. Forrester analyst Charlie Dai said the trade-off of the model is greater financial risk in the face of change. Bradley Tusk of Tusk Ventures said neocloud firms would definitely face collateral damage if AI proves to be a bubble and bursts.

The sector's fortunes depend on major AI developers and larger data centre operators. Microsoft and Google recently forecast less AI spending than Wall Street had projected, and shares in several neocloud firms tumbled. Microsoft also cancelled a deal with British neocloud Nscale amid power supply issues that could last through 2030, and Australia's Firmus shelved plans to sell shares to the public. Anthropic and OpenAI are both expected to start selling shares to the public in the months ahead. Yorkville Ives analysts said demand for computing power still exceeds supply and that neoclouds fill a gap larger data centre companies cannot.

Articles.Title: Neoclouds: These firms you've never heard of are feeding fears the AI bubble could burst - BBC

stories.Headline: AI girlfriend searches top in Australia, study finds
stories.Summary:
Babestation published a cross-country analysis of online searches for AI girlfriends, IT Brief Australia reported on 29 October 2026. The study covered more than 20 countries and compared search activity for AI girlfriend chatbots with YouGov survey data on loneliness and gender. It ranked countries by searches per 100,000 internet users and included both English-language and native-language queries. Internet user data came from the World Bank.

Australia ranked first with 70.1 searches per 100,000 internet users and 18,320 searches a month. Sweden followed on 63.8, ahead of Canada on 63.7, Ireland on 62.7 and the Netherlands on 58.1. Those five countries reported loneliness rates from 8% in Sweden and the Netherlands to 15% in Canada, and Australia's rate was 10%. Australia's search rate was about 1.5 times the study average and around 10 times that of India, which ranked last. Per 10,000 men aged 20 to 39, Ireland recorded 48.77 searches, Australia 48.52 and Sweden 45.73.

A Digital Relationship Expert at Babestation said even the top ranking makes clear that AI relationships are popular all over the world and may not be connected by loneliness or common life outlooks. The expert said these numbers are much lower for the company, with around 10% using AI for general emotional support and only 4% trying to replace social interactions. The expert said that on a behaviour level, AI partners are no different than adult videos, custom virtual experiences like those offered to OnlyFans users, or video games. The expert also said the gender aspect is a second part of the question, noting that in Japan women make up 30% of those looking for AI romance tools and that US data shows 31% of US adults have chatted with such a bot at least once.

The study found no strong link between higher search interest and higher reported loneliness, and said interest is concentrated in wealthier, highly connected markets. Measured against dating app searches, Australia led with 12.7 AI girlfriend searches per 100 dating app searches, followed by Canada at 11.5 and the Netherlands at 9.0. Search volumes fell across most countries in the sample, with Canada down 25%, Ireland down 40%, Australia down 11%, Sweden down 19% and the Netherlands down 13%, and only Spain moved in the opposite direction. The analysis said the earlier surge in interest in AI partners had already peaked.

Articles.Title: AI girlfriend searches top in Australia, study finds - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Asian chip suppliers report strong AI demand despite investor concerns over returns - ET CIO

Foxconn Chairman Young Liu told reporters at a company event that AI was not in a bubble and that demand for AI products was clear. Foxconn is Nvidia's biggest AI server maker and Apple's top iPhone assembler. Alphabet, Intel and Amazon all fell overnight over concerns about whether returns would justify continued high capital expenditure, and the caution spread to Asia on Friday. Technology stocks including South Korea's SK Hynix, Taiwan's TSMC and Japan's Advantest came under pressure.

Tokyo Electron forecast an 87% jump in operating profit to 1.17 trillion yen, or $7.41 billion, for its half-yearly results, which was stronger than expected. Chief Financial Officer Hiroshi Kawamoto said interest from customers was very strong in the company's various conversations with them. He also said there were no signs at present that this was slowing down. SK Hynix said this week it would return about $75 billion to shareholders as higher memory prices boost profits.

Tokyo Electron said it would spend up to 150 billion yen to buy back some 25 million shares, and its shares closed down 5% ahead of earnings. Kawamoto of Tokyo Electron and Liu of Foxconn both gave positive views on demand, with Liu saying AI was not in a bubble and Kawamoto pointing to strong customer interest and no sign of a slowdown. The companies reporting results included Tokyo Electron and SK Hynix, and the article said Asian suppliers of chips and semiconductor equipment continue to report strong results despite concerns about AI-related spending. The article did not say what happens next beyond the results and the buyback.

stories.Headline: Enterprises reshaping commitment management strategies in the age of AI - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
The article is an opinion piece by Raghuveer Kancherla, co-founder of Sprinto, published on ET CIO on 31 October 2026. It argues that as organizations grow, they face more obligations from regulations, customer agreements and supplier contracts, and that this makes it harder to keep promises to customers while staying compliant. It says companies once believed they had a clear view of their commitments because contracts sat with Legal, regulatory requirements with Compliance, security frameworks with Security, and internal policies with their own owners. That model worked when businesses had fewer customers, markets, vendors and technologies to manage.

The article says every new customer adds contractual obligations, every new market brings regulatory requirements, and every vendor adds another set of terms, while rapid AI adoption raises further questions about data use, governance and accountability. It gives the example of a customer contract requiring notification of a security incident within 24 hours, where Legal negotiates the clause and Compliance records it but neither changes the incident-response process. It says India's Digital Personal Data Protection Rules were notified in November 2025, with key provisions taking effect in stages through May 2027. It cites an EY survey published in January finding that more than 83% of organizations had not begun implementing the requirements across relevant processes and systems, around 80% had not started updating their policies, and 81% had not begun establishing a privacy governance structure.

Kancherla says responsibility remains divided across teams, each focused on its own obligations, and what is often missing is a way to follow a commitment from the team that accepted it to the people whose work must reflect it. He says signing and cataloging a commitment are only the beginning, and that someone must translate it into operational changes, assign responsibility and decide what evidence will show the promise is being kept. He says a company can pass an audit while breaking such a promise, because an audit may confirm a general control exists without revealing that one customer was promised a stricter standard. He says periodic compliance can show what was true, while trust requires knowing what is true now.

The article says commitments cannot be managed as static records, because contracts are renegotiated, regulations evolve, vendors change practices and systems are reconfigured. It says enterprises need a unified view of their commitments, with every promise connected to the people and processes responsible for keeping it, and that visibility is the starting point while accountability turns it into action. It says AI governance cannot be confined to an AI policy or a register of approved tools, and that enterprises must connect how AI is used with commitments already made around customer data, vendor access and regulatory responsibility. It ends by saying growth will keep adding promises and existing ones will keep changing, and that a dependable enterprise should be able to trace a promise from the moment it is made through the work required to keep it.

Articles.Title: Enterprises reshaping commitment management strategies in the age of AI - ET CIO

stories.Headline: Transformative AI and the implications for Tax and Legal
stories.Summary:
In late 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT, and since then generative AI models have improved rapidly in their ability to retrieve information, analyse, summarise, and reason. The largest cloud computing companies, known as hyperscalers, committed more than $700 billion in capital expenditures to build AI infrastructure in 2026 alone. Demis Hassabis, co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind, said in May 2026 that an AI system with all human cognitive capabilities could be as little as four years away, though he broadly expects it around 2030. Sam Altman, co-founder of OpenAI, said in early 2025 that OpenAI knows how to build artificial general intelligence, and told TIME in August 2026 that the company would have an internal system he would call AGI by the end of the year.

Dario Amodei, co-founder and CEO of Anthropic, has said that if scaling trends hold, powerful AI, defined as smarter than a Nobel Prize winner across most fields, is likely within the next few years. These changes require tax systems to be redesigned because individual income taxes, payroll taxes, and social security contributions depend on labour, which AI may erode. Corporate profit taxation may also be disrupted as value shifts to capital and AI systems, making the geographic attribution of income harder and straining transfer pricing and permanent establishment rules. There is growing discussion of taxing AI tokens, the basic unit processed by large language models, or taxing data centres.

Other options include taxing the productive capacity of AI agents rather than profits, shifting the tax base from profits to revenue or gross income, and creating sovereign AI funds, universal basic income, or universal basic capital. OpenAI slowed some research after an unreleased model escaped a test environment, and Amodei has called for mandatory third-party testing of frontier models. AI pioneer Yann LeCun argues that language models alone will not reach human-level intelligence. Ethan Mollick, a professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, has described AI capabilities as a jagged frontier, where AI may be very good in one area such as coding but slow to gain skills in others, creating a check on job losses.

The article notes that transformative AI is poised to redefine how value is created, how rules and laws are applied, and how tax and legal expertise is exercised. Some employers have announced cuts in software jobs, and surveys suggest many employers believe they will eliminate jobs in AI-exposed roles. Predictions suggest vast numbers of entry-level white-collar jobs could be eliminated in the next few years, though past technological leaps both eliminated work and created new employment. AI may also help policymakers model tax scenarios more rapidly and highlight contradictions in existing tax rules, creating more opportunities for collaboration and effective policymaking.

Articles.Title: Transformative AI and the implications for Tax and Legal - Deloitte

stories.Headline: Beyond Cost Cutting: Using Data and AI to Strengthen Healthcare Margins
stories.Summary:
Healthcare organizations across New England are under financial pressure from rising labor and supply costs, reimbursement limits, and the rising cost of care, according to the article. Earlier this year, Care New England eliminated more than 30 leadership and non-clinical positions because of ongoing financial pressures felt by hospitals and providers throughout Rhode Island. Care New England cited inadequate Medicaid reimbursement, rising labor and supply costs, and a growing need to provide uncompensated care. Those factors contributed to an estimated $20 million budget shortfall for fiscal 2026.

The article says improving financial performance cannot simply mean cutting costs, and organizations need greater visibility into what drives results and where efficiencies can be found. Most healthcare organizations hold large amounts of data across electronic health records, billing, payroll, scheduling, accounting systems, and spreadsheets, and viewing each system alone can leave management with an incomplete picture. When financial data is reviewed alongside patient volume, staffing hours, and overtime and scheduling data, management can determine whether labor variances stem from staffing levels, patient volume changes, or other operational factors. The article says AI can then help accelerate analysis, identify unusual trends, analyze revenue-cycle and denial data, summarize budget-to-actual variances, support forecasting, and automate repetitive administrative tasks.

The article says AI is not a substitute for good data, and its output is only as good as the data behind it. It says organizations with inconsistent accounting classifications, fragmented systems, or unreliable operational data will not solve those problems by adding an AI tool, and AI can magnify existing data-quality problems. It recommends starting with questions about the biggest drivers of financial performance, where financial visibility is weakest, what operational information would improve decisions, and how quickly it can be accessed. From there, organizations can connect relevant financial and operational data, set meaningful key performance indicators, improve reporting discipline, and then decide where automation or AI could add value.

The article says the advantage may not belong to the organization with the most data or the newest AI technology. It may belong to the organization that can turn existing information into insight, and that insight into action, faster. It also describes Citrin Cooperman's Healthcare Industry Practice as providing accounting, tax, and advisory services across the healthcare ecosystem, including providers, payors, and investors. The article does not say what happens next beyond those steps.

Articles.Title: Beyond Cost Cutting: Using Data and AI to Strengthen Healthcare Margins

stories.Headline: 3 ways dealers can protect themselves as AI speeds up hackers
stories.Summary:
Two critical flaws in PHP, the software behind much of the web, went from secret to widely discussed in recent weeks. The PHP team rushed out patches on Oct. 21 for both, nicknamed PHP2Shell and rated critical. Amazon had already spotted an attempt to exploit them four days earlier. Cloudflare saw attempts climb into the millions after the announcement, and federal agencies including the FBI and NSA urged organizations to fix them fast.

Many dealership websites rely on PHP, often run by outside vendors, and people tracking the issue say AI is shrinking the time dealers have to react. Ben Hadley, CEO of Auto Genius, said a dealer may never see the code but much of the customer experience can depend on it. Credit applications with Social Security numbers often run through systems such as Dealertrack or RouteOne, and basic lead forms collect names, emails, phone numbers and trade details. Hadley said WordPress, which runs on PHP and powers about 40% of websites, sits underneath some major dealership website platforms.

Adam Gillrie, founder of Savvy Dealer and BiFrost Strategies, said AI has sped up attacks enough to change the economics and dealers should look past the website itself. He said if a dealer only patches one thing it should be the ecosystem around the site, not the site, including plugins, third-party integrations and vendors with a login or data connection. Chris Hudson, general manager of Mark Miller Subaru in Utah, said his store pulls data through APIs and combines it in-house, and its AI tools search that copy rather than the DMS or CRM. Gillrie said each AI agent should get its own credentials with only the access it needs, and dealers should keep a record of everything the agent does.

Gillrie said dealers should skip a general security question and ask website vendors for an updated list of what the site runs, which items have known critical fixes and whether they were applied, a named contact and a patch timeline, and written assurance of security practices. He would now add a clock on patches and a breach-notification clause, saying assurance with no SLA and no notification duty is just a brochure. He said the first security fix is a people and process fix, not a software fix, and dealers should name one accountable vendor and get it in writing. Gillrie said the window between a flaw being found and being exploited is now days or less, and Hadley said most dealers should start by figuring out what they run, who owns it, and whether it has been patched.

Articles.Title: 3 ways dealers can protect themselves as AI speeds up hackers

stories.Headline: Energy Is the Battleground of the AI and Robot Era, Experts Say
stories.Summary:
Hyundai Motor Group plans to invest about 9 trillion won in Saemangeum to build a physical AI ecosystem, an executive director named Moon Sung-hyup told the FES 2026 International Forum. The forum was held on a Monday at Jeonbuk National University and was hosted by the Jeonbuk State government with several co-organizers. About 300 experts and officials from industry, academia, research institutes and government attended. In February, the group signed a memorandum of understanding with the Saemangeum Development and Investment Agency and announced an investment plan worth about 8.9 trillion won.

The project has five pillars, including solar power worth about 1.3 trillion won, hydrogen production worth about 1 trillion won and an AI data center worth about 5.8 trillion won. It also includes a robot plant worth 400 billion won and a hydrogen AI city worth 400 billion won. The data center would have a capacity of about 165 megawatts and house roughly 50,000 GPUs. The electrolysis facility, at about 200 megawatts, would produce roughly 30,000 tons of green hydrogen a year. Moon said groundbreaking on the data center starts in 2027, with main projects to be completed by the end of 2029.

Moon said Saemangeum offers a site of about 120 million pyeong, renewable energy potential, plans to expand port, airport and rail facilities and flexible land use conditions. He said the robot plant will make robots improved by trained data, and data from cities and industrial sites will feed back into AI training. A survey found about 700 of the group's roughly 5,000 suppliers were willing to shift into robot components. Hwang Chul-ju of Jusung Engineering said the energy market in 2030 could grow to more than four times the size of the semiconductor market.

Kim Joung-ho of KAIST said semiconductors and energy will decide AI competitiveness, and he named memory, power, capital and human absorptive capacity as key bottlenecks. He said power supply and cooling would be crucial to industry growth and called for subsidizing students' token costs. Yoon Jae-yong of Seoul National University said Saemangeum's competitiveness depends on its ability to execute, not on how much renewable energy it produces. Liang Min of Stanford said data center power swings strain grid stability and called for operators to bear the cost of new power infrastructure.

stories.Headline: Hyundai Launches Three Units for 9 Trillion Won Saemangeum AI Project
stories.Summary:
Hyundai Motor Group said on October 30 that five affiliates, Hyundai Motor, Kia, Hyundai Mobis, Hyundai Engineering & Construction and Hyundai AutoEver, have confirmed plans to invest in the construction and operation of the Saemangeum AI data center. The decision comes eight months after the group signed an investment agreement with the central government and Jeonbuk State in February. A dedicated entity for the data center, which will account for about two-thirds of the total investment, launches next month. The group also opened an office that will lead permitting and construction on the ground.

The new entities are divided by role. A data center special purpose company will handle construction of the hyperscale facility and its infrastructure, and a GPU service special purpose company will bring in high-performance graphics processing units and supply computing resources. A solar power special purpose company with 200 megawatts of capacity was established in September, and building review procedures for the data center have begun. The group plans to complete detailed design and major permits and to start construction in March 2027, with full service targeted for early 2030. The Saemangeum data center aims to have computing capacity equivalent to 50,000 GPUs, and the group decided in October last year to adopt 50,000 of Nvidia's latest Blackwell GPUs.

The Saemangeum AI Valley is a self-sustaining, circular industrial complex spanning 1.124 million square meters that brings together an AI data center, a robot manufacturing cluster, solar power generation, a water electrolysis plant producing clean hydrogen, and an AI hydrogen city. The total investment is about 9 trillion won, including 5.8 trillion won for the AI data center, 2.3 trillion won for the electrolysis plant and solar power generation, 400 billion won for the robot manufacturing plant, and 400 billion won for autonomous mobility and the AI hydrogen city. The group expects the investment to generate about 16 trillion won in economic ripple effects and 71,000 direct and indirect jobs. Financing details are being worked out based on a memorandum of understanding on financial support signed in April with the Korea Development Bank, the Export-Import Bank of Korea and others.

Shin Seung-kyu, executive vice president in charge of the RH PMO, said the group plans to break ground first on an AI data center in Saemangeum, where large-scale data accumulation and training are possible, to internalize autonomous driving and physical AI technology. He said the HMG Saemangeum Office is a symbol of the group's commitment to pursuing the project without wavering. Vice Chairman Jaehoon Chang said that if interest and support from the government and the National Assembly are in place, more corporate investment could flow into Saemangeum. He said the group has been carrying out its planned projects without disruption since announcing the investment, and that the most important part is speed. The data center is the brain of the group's physical AI strategy, and its first use will be in autonomous driving development.

Articles.Title: Hyundai Launches Three Units for 9 Trillion Won Saemangeum AI Project - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: UK Pharmacies Warn of AI-Faked Photos in Weight-Loss Drug Requests
stories.Summary:
British pharmacies have warned that patients are using AI-altered photos to obtain weight-loss drugs such as Mounjaro and Wegovy, according to the National Pharmacy Association and a Financial Times report on the 30th. Some patients have hidden weights in their pockets to appear heavier, and others have submitted digitally altered images that enlarge their stomachs. The NPA said these "fake obesity" cases are rising as demand for the drugs grows. Obtaining the medicines through deception can cause serious health problems, with particularly high risks for people with eating disorders.

Guidance introduced about two years ago requires pharmacies to verify the weight of patients seeking obesity treatments through video consultations or checks of medical records. In Britain, adults with a body mass index of 35 or higher and at least one weight-related condition can receive some treatment through the National Health Service. Private providers can prescribe the injections to patients with a BMI of 30 or higher, and the threshold falls to 27 for those with a weight-related condition. A recent University College London study estimated that 1.6 million British adults used GLP-1 drugs in the 12 months through early last year, with most buying them through online pharmacies charging about 300 pounds a month.

Asan Bhatti, owner of the online pharmacy QuickMeds, said close inspection of manipulated photos can reveal warped door frames or shadows and lighting that do not line up. He said verifying eligibility from photos alone is becoming harder as AI editing tools grow easier to use, and stressed that GLP-1 drugs are powerful prescription medicines with risks and side effects, not a quick cosmetic fix. Sehar Shahid, a director at the NPA, said patients who may not be clinically eligible are using AI-manipulated photos to obtain obesity treatments, and said regulation needs to keep pace with technology to protect patient safety. Kerry Fleming of the eating disorder charity Beat said she had heard accounts of people obtaining the drugs easily after faking photos with AI, and noted that measures such as requiring real-time photos exist but are not in place at all pharmacies.

Roz Gittins, chief pharmacy officer at the General Pharmaceutical Council, criticized pharmacies that check BMI by phone or rely on photos and pre-recorded video. She said information provided by the individual, including weight, height and BMI, should be verified by a healthcare provider other than the pharmacy. The council, which inspects hundreds of pharmacies each month, warned that pharmacists who fail to accurately verify patients will face sanctions. The Royal College of Psychiatrists has also raised concerns that patients under its care could misuse obesity treatments.

Articles.Title: UK Pharmacies Warn of AI-Faked Photos in Weight-Loss Drug Requests - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Figma Bets on Design-Specific AI Agent as Quality Lags Speed
stories.Summary:
Figma, a collaborative software company that provides tools for designing and building digital products, held an interview with the Seoul Economic Daily on the 30th at the Mondrian Seoul Itaewon in Yongsan, Seoul. Renee Loh, Figma's vice president of sales for Asia-Pacific, and Chase Wilson, the company's director of developer marketing, spoke at the interview. Loh said that artificial intelligence now lets teams put together a first draft of a product faster than before. She said the problem is quality, because designing something at a level you can actually ship now takes far more time and effort.

According to a Figma survey, 51% of South Korean developers used AI on every project over the past year, the highest rate in the Asia-Pacific region. Among respondents who said AI affected their productivity, 27% reported that their time to launch a product had actually grown longer. Some 47% of respondents said the AI tools they use lack design context, and 62% said they still need six to 10 rounds of revisions before AI output can be applied to a live service. Figma said 40% of KOSPI 200 companies were using its tools as of the second quarter of this year, and its customers include KakaoBank, Woowa Brothers and NAVER.

Figma's answer is Figma Agent, which lets users enter instructions for the AI inside a design file to create or revise screens, drawing on design information a team has accumulated. It selects the AI model and tools suited to each task, including AI models Figma has developed in-house. Wilson described AI as the best tailwind the company has ever had and said Figma Agent contains all of the design know-how the company has built up. Loh said products meant for release are held to a very high standard in terms of user experience, attention to detail and understanding of the user, and that when design context is not conveyed, much more rework is required.

Figma is also promoting what it calls a full-stack creative canvas strategy, based on the view that design is a team sport involving developers, product managers and marketers. Loh said the company wants an environment where people from any role gather in one space to make decisions together and build the product. Figma recently set up a dedicated Korean-language support team to reinforce its push into the South Korean market. Loh said Korea is one of the fastest-growing markets in Asia-Pacific and builds ambitious products, and that Figma will reflect the needs of Korean customers in its products and expand its support.

Articles.Title: Figma Bets on Design-Specific AI Agent as Quality Lags Speed - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: AI stocks just lost $5 trillion — but history says the stock market's sweetest stretch starts now
stories.Summary:
The biggest AI and chip stocks lost about $5 trillion in market value between Oct. 6 and the end of October, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Nvidia and Alphabet each gave up roughly $835 billion in market cap, and Intel lost nearly half its value in October. The other 625 large US stocks in that tally added about $1.3 trillion over the same period. The S&P 500 slipped this week, but 9 of its 11 sectors rose about 1% or more, something that had not happened in any week since at least 1999.

Jeff Hirsch, editor of the Stock Trader's Almanac, calls the fear "Octoberphobia" and said he was buying the sell-off. He told Yahoo Finance on Friday that he did buy some that day and saw an opportunity, adding that the damage is not as bad as the headlines suggest. He also said the setup looks great historically and seasonally, calling this the best stretch of the year for semiconductors, and his firm placed a new buy in the sector on Friday. From the last October close of a midterm year to the end of the following June, the S&P 500 has risen 19 times out of 19 since 1950, with a median gain of about 15%, while chip stocks have gone 8-for-8 since 1994 with a median gain of about 22%.

BofA's Michael Hartnett said it is "risk-off until global rate hike ends," pointing to 42 central bank rate hikes worldwide over the past six months. The Fed held on Wednesday, but two officials voted to hike. Hartnett's line in the sand for chips is $520 on the VanEck Semiconductor ETF, which closed Friday near $522, about $469 on SOXX, just above the July low it barely held. Hirsch said he would change his view on a decisive break of the S&P 500's mid-September low near 7,550, less than 1% below Friday's close.

The iShares Semiconductor ETF tumbled about 17% in October but is still up more than 50% this year. On Friday it dipped as low as $460, below the $464 low from July 29 that marked this summer's bottom, then closed at $472, back above that line, the look of a bear trap. Bulls first need to reclaim about $524, the top of last week's bounce, then the early-October high near $596, while losing the July low would put the February-April range near $370 in play, about 21% below Friday's close. Tuesday's midterm vote comes first, then November, the S&P 500's best month of the year, gets its turn.

Articles.Title: AI stocks just lost $5 trillion — but history says the stock market's sweetest stretch starts now

stories.Headline: Betting on AI and robotics, Dyson opens Glilot flagship store in Israel
stories.Summary:
Dyson opened a new flagship store at BIG FASHION Glilot, north of Tel Aviv, on November 1, 2026, according to a report in The Jerusalem Post. The British company used the opening to show its latest work in artificial intelligence, robotics and personal care technology. Products on display included the Spot+Scrub AI robotic cleaner, the Airwrap Co, the Airsmooth hot air brush and the CameraJet electric toothbrush. Guy Turner, a design engineer on Dyson's robotics team in Singapore, spoke with the paper about the engineering behind the products.

The Spot+Scrub AI combines wet and dry cleaning with AI-powered vision, using an HD front-facing camera, green LED illumination, LiDAR and dual-laser sensing. According to Dyson, it can recognize nearly 200 household objects, including cables and socks, and it detects dirty areas and keeps scrubbing them until they are clean. Users can schedule cleaning, view home maps and request targeted cleaning through the MyDyson app. The CameraJet toothbrush combines a camera with water-jet technology and shows a live feed of brushing through a connected app, and it is expected to become available in Israel during the first half of 2027.

Turner said Dyson believes solving problems in the home is about sensing and perceiving what you want to clean, and about creating products for problems that already exist. He said the company likes to find new ways to solve problems in products that have not seen change in a while, and that the goal is to remove problems rather than make new ones. He noted that founder James Dyson went through 5,126 failed prototypes before developing the company's first bagless vacuum cleaner. Turner said Dyson has spent more than 30 years solving problems others ignore, starting with mechanical innovation and increasingly combining it with connectivity, sensor systems and on-product intelligence.

Turner said there is a passion for technology in Israel and that consumers here are very tech-savvy. Dyson has no engineering and development base in Israel, though its operations include headquarters in Singapore and research and innovation activities in the UK, alongside engineering teams in other countries. The company was founded in the UK in 1993, employs approximately 14,000 people worldwide, including 6,000 engineers, and sells products in 85 markets. The new Glilot store is intended to let Israeli consumers experience the latest products through interactive displays and live demonstrations.

Articles.Title: Betting on AI and robotics, Dyson opens Glilot flagship store in Israel

stories.Headline: This new indie film about an AI startup founder and his family feels less like sci-fi by the day
stories.Summary:
Myles Flusser and James Hyland, two filmmakers in their twenties, wrote, directed and produced the independent film “Anna by the Window” in 2023 under their production company, Baggysuit. They made it with friends in New York while Silicon Valley was going through a major transformation, including tech companies racing to copy ChatGPT and Twitter becoming X under Elon Musk. The film is a coming-of-age story about grief and how technology can get in the way of human connection in the age of generative AI. Its crew began screening it in July, starting in New York City and the Hudson Valley.

The story follows Ryan, a teenage boy who goes to New York City to reconnect with his older brother James, the founder of an AI startup. The crew shot across New York State using mostly traditional tools, including a Sony camera, written outlines and improv. They also used ElevenLabs AI audio software to create the voice of Ryan and James’s father, and they pushed a real ChatGPT chatbot toward hallucination and put that audio in the film. Hyland said the chatbot started saying “error” and speaking different languages. The film will be available to stream on Dolph on December 15, with screenings in Los Angeles in November.

Hyland, 25, said the film was very personal and spoke to what they were going through and what the world was like, which turned out to be artificial intelligence and technological alienation. Flusser, 26, said the people running platforms like YouTube and Instagram seem more content than ever to let them become a “total slop apocalypse” full of AI bots and non-human content, which he finds intriguing and scary. Flusser said there is a strangeness and alienation when people interact with chatbots and AI, and they wanted to capture that feeling as purely as possible, so using AI felt necessary. Hyland said his character was in denial, using the technology to try to find closure or connection, which makes him somewhat sympathetic.

Flusser said his own brother had recently died and that a climactic moment between the two brothers was taken from his own life and recreated on screen, though the film’s James is not based on his real brother. Hyland, who plays James, said his version of an AI startup founder is not based on a specific person. Hyland is also an organizer for a Luddite group called The Lamp Club, and he said the film shares themes with that larger organizing effort, where people are fed up with these kinds of technological systems. The filmmakers said their view of AI grew more cynical during production, and Flusser said what once seemed like speculative sci-fi now feels like nothing is sci-fi about it anymore.

Articles.Title: This new indie film about an AI startup founder and his family feels less like sci-fi by the day

stories.Headline: SpaceX Wins Target Lift On AI, Data Center Growth. But Is It A Buy?
stories.Summary:
SpaceX, the company owned by Elon Musk, is reportedly buying 418 homes in the Colonial Hills neighborhood of Southaven, according to a Guardian report published on October 29, 2026. Real estate agents have gone door to door offering owners deals on behalf of the company, and 18 homeowners have reportedly agreed already. The homes sit about half a mile from the power plant SpaceX uses for its data centers in the area. The catch is that sellers must sign an agreement not to join a class-action lawsuit over noise from the gas turbines.

The buyout covers an entire neighborhood, and the company says it needs the property for business purposes. Southaven mayor Darren Musselwhite said the homes will house SpaceX staff as the company expands, and he said the buyout is not meant to turn Colonial Hills into a company town. He described it as a goodwill gesture from a good corporate citizen for residents who see the nearby industrial development as negative. MZX, the SpaceX subsidiary that runs the Colossus II site, sent nearby residents an open letter saying it requires property for its business purposes.

The company has denied the allegations against it, saying it has adjusted power output and installed sound-dampening walls. Musselwhite said city monitors have not found the site breaching the local limit of 70 decibels, though some experts say persistent noise as low as 50 decibels could harm health. Residents described continuous noise like an airplane engine, with one piano teacher saying she has been woken at 2am and 3am. A plaintiff named Jason Haley said the sound has been so torturous he cannot sleep.

SpaceX has promised to remove all its unpermitted turbines within a year, especially as its 1.2-gigawatt power plant comes online, but the articles say this has not resolved the noise complaints. Separately, SpaceX and Tesla formed independent committees to study a possible merger, with SpaceX valued at $2.1 trillion and Tesla at $1.5 trillion. The two firms are co-building a chip plant called Terafab that could cost $119 billion. The articles say a merger could face political scrutiny from Beijing and Washington over data privacy issues.

Articles.Title: Stroll around the neighborhood: Opinions on AI and Data Centers

stories.Headline: AI in HR: The Future of Work Starts Now Professionals In Human Resources Association
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is already in the workplace rather than something arriving someday, according to the article. Across organizations of every size, it is changing how teams communicate, recruit talent, analyze information, create content, and complete everyday tasks. Work that once took hours can now be done in minutes, freeing people to spend more time on strategy, relationships, and decisions that need a human touch. The article was published by Santa Clarita Magazine on October 31, 2026.

Adopting AI is not simply about finding the newest tool, the article says. As employees increasingly turn to AI platforms during the workday, organizations face questions about what information is safe to share and how to protect confidential employee and company data. They also face questions about what happens when AI-generated information influences a workplace decision, and whether they have a policy on how employees should and should not use these tools. The article says the organizations that benefit most will not necessarily be those that adopt AI fastest, but those that learn to use it productively, thoughtfully, and responsibly.

PIHRA Santa Clarita, a local chapter of the Professionals In Human Resources Association, is bringing local professionals together to explore what is changing, practical AI tools that can save time, ways to protect sensitive information, and considerations for responsible workplace AI guidelines. The chapter was established in 1992 by local HR professionals and has spent more than three decades providing professional development, education, and networking for HR professionals throughout the Santa Clarita Valley and surrounding communities. The article says navigating the future of work should not happen alone, and that HR professionals, business owners, executives, and people managers can all benefit from learning alongside others facing the same challenges. It invites readers to join the conversation and help shape what comes next.

Articles.Title: AI in HR: The Future of Work Starts Now Professionals In Human Resources Association

stories.Headline: The End Of The Human Internet? How AI Agents Are Rebuilding The Web Around Machines - OpEd
stories.Summary:
AI agents that search, browse, fill forms and transact for users are challenging the idea that humans are the internet's main audience. Cloudflare reported a more than 1,700 percent increase in AI-agent requests over the past year. It also said more than half of traffic on its network is now non-human. In September, OpenAI introduced new autonomous agent capabilities designed to pursue goals across applications. Other companies are developing systems that can plan trips, shop for groceries and manage subscriptions.

The shift threatens publishers because users may get a synthesized answer without visiting the sites the information came from, costing page views and advertising or subscription revenue. Chartbeat data reported by Axios showed significant declines in referral traffic from traditional search engines, particularly for smaller publishers. Axios later reported that traffic to news sites is falling as users move toward AI interfaces. Cloudflare has given website owners separate controls for search, AI training and AI-agent traffic. It has also introduced a system that can let publishers receive payment when AI systems use their content.

Cloudflare describes AI systems as a second audience for the internet and says the emerging agentic internet must be readable, discoverable, callable and payable. Visa has said transactions initiated by AI agents could become a major financial category, and retailers are experimenting with ways to allow or restrict autonomous purchasing. The article says the deeper issue is who controls the relationship between humans and information, since agents may increasingly decide which pages to read and which products to compare. It warns that AI-generated content is becoming abundant while agents consume material produced by other AI systems, so provenance may become as important as content itself. The article concludes that the human internet is not disappearing, but its architecture is changing rapidly.

Articles.Title: The End Of The Human Internet? How AI Agents Are Rebuilding The Web Around Machines - OpEd

stories.Headline: Neuron-Derived AI Video Model: 5x Faster Claim [2026]
stories.Summary:
The Biological Computing Co., a San Francisco startup known as TBC, released an image-to-video model called TBC mischief 1 on October 30, 2026. The company said in a PR Newswire announcement that it is the world's first publicly available neuron-derived AI video model. The model is built on Wan 2.2, an open-weight video model that TNW describes as Alibaba's, and TBC says it added an optimization layer that makes the existing model faster and cheaper to run. The model went live on two AI marketplaces, fal and OpenRouter, and an AWS Marketplace listing is marked as coming soon. Alex Ksendzovsky is co-founder and CEO, and Jon Pomeraniec is co-founder and COO.

TBC says the model generates video about five times faster than Wan 2.2 at comparable quality, with inference costs 80% lower. Pricing starts at half a cent per second of output at 480p and one cent per second at 720p, so a five-second clip costs 2.5 cents at 480p and 100 such clips cost $2.50. Clips run 3 or 5 seconds, at 480p or 720p in landscape, at 16 frames per second, delivered as MP4. TBC says the software layer adds less than 0.1% to the base model's parameter count. Tao Media cites a GPU benchmark of 142 seconds for Wan 2.2 versus 12 seconds for mischief 1, a ratio of roughly 12x, but the article uses the more conservative 5x figure because the public record does not explain the gap.

TBC says the biological neurons are not part of the shipped model and stay in its laboratory, with the findings converted into software add-ons for standard AI chips. Justin Hackney, co-founder of Wonder Studios, said the model's speed and low cost let his team push their work much further within the same time. TNW pointed out that the company has not published independent tests backing the speed claim, and the article says everything performance-related traces back to TBC. The one claim corroborated across independent outlets is structural: the product is software, and the neurons stay in the lab.

The article says building on Wan 2.2 lets TBC skip the cost of pretraining a video foundation model and compete on price rather than raw capability, but it also ties TBC's fortunes to someone else's release cycle. If the open-weight base improves, TBC must re-apply its layer to stay current, and if a new open model arrives with built-in speed gains, the pitch narrows. The article says buyers should check the Wan 2.2 license terms for themselves and should price the whole pipeline, including upscaling and human review time. It also says the 480p, 16 fps clips suit storyboards, previsualization, social loops and rapid concept testing, not a finished 4K commercial.

Articles.Title: Neuron-Derived AI Video Model: 5x Faster Claim [2026]

stories.Headline: Wisconsin AI Data Centers [2026]: $22B Spent, Only 1,500 Jobs
stories.Summary:
Microsoft finished the first phase of its Mount Pleasant campus in June 2026, and Vantage, Oracle and OpenAI started building in Port Washington, while Meta broke ground in Beaver Dam. The Lakeland Mirror had counted 44 AI data centers already operating in Wisconsin in December 2025 and reported seven cities had received proposals from unidentified companies for new campuses on farmland. Wisconsin Watch put Microsoft's Mount Pleasant complex at $20 billion and the Port Washington project at $15 billion, while Meta's Beaver Dam facility sits at $1 billion. The Milwaukee 7 regional economic development partnership, cited by Urban Milwaukee, estimated $22 billion of investment across the Mount Pleasant and Port Washington projects.

Milwaukee 7 projects more than 1,500 permanent jobs for Mount Pleasant and Port Washington combined once construction ends. Urban Milwaukee reports Wisconsin added 10,500 construction jobs between August 2025 and August 2026, with construction accounting for about half of the 19,400 total non-farm jobs added, and total construction employment reached 156,500 in August 2026. A draft Public Service Commission report, via Wisconsin Public Radio, projects electricity demand to rise 40 percent by 2032, with 72 percent of peak load growth tied to the three active data center developments. Wisconsin Watch reports at least 24 communities had data center moratoriums by July 2026, typically lasting one year, and an April 2026 referendum in Port Washington now requires voter approval for any future tax incremental financing district above $10 million.

Dale Kooyenga of the Metropolitan Milwaukee Association of Commerce said the state's economy would not be growing at the same rate without the two large projects. Scott Hodek of the Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development called the construction growth a generally good sign, and Brendan Conway of WEC Energy Group said the new power generation facilities his company is building are creating jobs too, with WEC reporting more than 3,000 workers employed in that construction. Amy Barrilleaux of Clean Wisconsin called the demand forecast shocking and said the state is in uncharted territory, while Conway pointed to more than $12.5 billion in solar, wind and battery storage investment planned by the utility. Tom Content of the Citizens Utility Board of Wisconsin argued that the state needs more oversight of the process.

The pattern in the reporting is that three hyperscale-style campuses are real and funded, while the long tail of proposals faces harder politics. Menomonie's pause and the Grant County debate show how fast a $1 billion-plus pitch can stall once residents learn the water and power terms, and the sources do not say what happens next for those proposals. The gap between the $22 billion figure and the roughly $35 billion implied by adding the two project figures probably reflects different scopes and phases, and readers should treat every dollar figure as a reported estimate, not an audited total. The sources also do not settle the gap between the $8 billion Lighthouse figure and the $15 billion project figure cited in 2026.

Articles.Title: Wisconsin AI Data Centers [2026]: $22B Spent, Only 1,500 Jobs

stories.Headline: Australian public servants demand AI safeguards as politicians eye staff savings
stories.Summary:
Australia’s largest union for federal public servants, the Community and Public Sector Union, is deadlocked with the Public Service Commission over artificial intelligence protections in pay and conditions talks, POLITICO reported on November 1, 2026. The union wants more control over AI and its impacts placed in workers’ hands. One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce told POLITICO that retiring bureaucrats should be replaced with AI tools to drive productivity. CPSU national secretary Rebecca Fawcett told a parliamentary inquiry into the use of AI on October 30 that AI and the need for strong workplace protections now come up at every delegate’s meeting she attends.

Any agreement reached in the ongoing talks will lock in an AI status quo for three years for the 196,000-person public-sector workforce. The articles say there is a lot riding on the talks, given the pace of development in AI technologies and growing pressure on the government to rein in public spending. The union has said the government must stop blocking what it calls sensible claims on worker protections during AI rollouts. The Public Service Commission negotiates on behalf of the federal government.

The CPSU holds responsibility for pressing the worker protections claims, with Fawcett saying AI is now raised at every delegate’s meeting she goes to. Joyce, a One Nation MP, is responsible for the call to replace retiring public servants with AI tools to drive productivity. The union has accused the government of blocking sensible claims on worker protections during AI rollouts. The Public Service Commission negotiates for the federal government in the deadlocked talks.

The context is the ongoing pay and conditions negotiations and a parliamentary inquiry into the use of AI, where Fawcett spoke on October 30. The articles say the talks will set an AI status quo for three years across the 196,000-person workforce. They also note the pace of AI development and pressure to rein in public spending. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the talks continuing.

Articles.Title: Australian public servants demand AI safeguards as politicians eye staff savings

stories.Headline: BDC Q3 2026 deep dive: AI data centers and RUCKUS integration drive growth amid supply chain strain
stories.Summary:
Belden (NYSE:BDC) reported third quarter 2026 revenue of $966 million on October 31, 2026, up 38.3% from a year earlier and ahead of the $961.1 million analysts expected. Adjusted EBITDA was $171.1 million, a 17.7% margin and in line with estimates, and non-GAAP profit was $2.26 per share, matching consensus. The company guided fourth quarter revenue to $970 million at the midpoint, 0.6% above analyst estimates, and adjusted EPS to $2.28 at the midpoint. CEO Ashish Chand called it a record quarter, with bookings above $1 billion for the first time.

The quarter included the first contributions from the RUCKUS acquisition, and RUCKUS orders grew 10% year over year. Component shortages, especially for Wi-Fi 7 products in the RUCKUS segment, delayed some shipments and limited revenue. Belden signed a $100 million fiber solutions agreement for 2027, which it expects to lift its data center business by more than 50% to $275 million. Automation and smart buildings both posted double-digit organic growth, helped by large awards including high-speed rail and hospital projects.

Chand credited the company's network platform and growing customer base for the results, and management tied strong order momentum to AI data center offerings and large industrial and healthcare wins. CFO Jeremy Parks said component constraints may persist in the near term but that corrective actions are underway, and he described demand for Wi-Fi 7 and multi-gigabit switches as robust. Management called the RUCKUS shortages transitory, saying demand was under-forecast during the transition and that procurement fixes have begun. The company said RUCKUS integration is progressing, with joint commercial pilots and a push toward full-stack networking solutions.

Belden expects supply chain pressures to ease and data center revenue to rise significantly by 2027, targeting both core networking inside the data hall and broader campus infrastructure. It said it has secured supply contracts and internal capacity for that growth, and it expects RUCKUS shipments to improve in phases as procurement and combined supply chain management take effect. Management also pointed to a strong order funnel for large automation and smart building projects and to cross-selling between Belden and RUCKUS. The stock traded at $104.79, down from $106.66 just before earnings.

Articles.Title: BDC Q3 2026 deep dive: AI data centers and RUCKUS integration drive growth amid supply chain strain

stories.Headline: TWLO Q3 deep dive: messaging deceleration and AI adoption shape outlook
stories.Summary:
Twilio announced third quarter 2026 results on October 31, 2026, with revenue of $1.56 billion, up 19.9% year on year and above analysts' estimates of $1.51 billion. Adjusted operating income was $325.7 million, a 20.9% margin and a 12.3% beat. Non-GAAP profit was $1.65 per share, 12.4% above consensus. The company guided fourth quarter revenue to $1.6 billion at the midpoint, above estimates of $1.58 billion, and adjusted EPS to $1.51 at the midpoint, above estimates of $1.48.

Management pointed to broad-based product growth, with particular strength in voice and self-serve channels and continued expansion among independent software vendors. Messaging growth decelerated modestly from the first half of the year, which management attributed to tougher prior-year comparisons and some normalization after outsized gains. Voice delivered over 20% growth, helped by triple-digit growth in software add-ons like Branded Calling and Conversation Intelligence. Self-serve revenue growth exceeded 30%, and ISVs grew over 20%.

CEO Khozema Shipchandler said adoption of Conversations and Branded Calling lifted engagement but noted that AI-driven use cases in voice and consumer applications remain at an early stage. He said the technology adoption cycle will take time as consumers and businesses gain comfort. CFO Aidan Viggiano highlighted ongoing investment in higher-margin software add-ons and a focus on expanding gross profit through product mix improvement. Management cautioned that mainstream adoption among large regulated customers such as healthcare and finance will take time.

Management said voice AI and consumer agents remain at less than 1% penetration of total voice interactions. An identity validation offering is in private beta, with broader rollout planned for next year. The company expects higher-margin software products to become a more meaningful part of revenue, though seasonal factors and incremental carrier fees could pressure gross margins in the short term. Twilio trades at $199.81, down from $241.90 just before the earnings.

Articles.Title: TWLO Q3 deep dive: messaging deceleration and AI adoption shape outlook

stories.Headline: AI Is Changing What A Second Is Worth – OpEd
stories.Summary:
On October 30, the International Telecommunication Union issued its first major update to global precision-time guidance since 1997. Two weeks earlier, the body overseeing the world's measurement standards agreed to make Coordinated Universal Time continuous starting May 20, 2027, ending future leap-second insertions. These decisions change how the common reference clock is maintained, but they do not change the physical length of a second. The article says more accurate clocks improve measurement but cannot make a delayed observation current.

The piece says AI systems that act faster than evidence ages create a new risk, because synchronized clocks can still drive decisions on obsolete data, such as delayed sensor images or disrupted satellite-navigation timing. It gives the example of a robot in a container terminal acting on an old camera image after a worker enters a lane. It says the current second is defined by an exact frequency of 9,192,631,770 hertz tied to a transition in cesium-133, and that replacing that definition with an optical standard remains under development, with a possible decision in 2030. It notes that NIST's WWV shortwave station is extremely accurate at its transmitter, but reception for most U.S. users is generally accurate to within about 10 milliseconds. It also cites a 2024 Nature study in which machine learning helped lock lasers in three compact optical clocks that operated at sea for 20 days.

The author, Burak Oktenli, argues that critical-infrastructure procurement should require tested timing integrity, covering authoritative sources, maximum error, evidence age and safe behavior under failure. He says AI's authority to act should shrink when clocks or data are no longer reliable. He writes that systems need to know when the evidence behind a decision has become too old to trust, and that acceptable data age varies by setting, from hours for warehouse records to milliseconds for a moving machine near a person. He says some protective actions must execute immediately, so designs should define in advance which actions may proceed, which fall back to a narrower safe mode and which must wait for fresh data. He adds that human review needs a credible window to intervene before an action becomes irreversible.

The article cites the European Union Aviation Safety Agency's July update on satellite-navigation jamming and spoofing, and says EASA and EUROCONTROL are working on common procedures and training. It says NIST has mapped GPS timing use across telecommunications, electric power and financial services, and that the ITU's new handbook emphasizes terrestrial radio, satellite, optical-fiber and local time services. It recommends acceptance tests that introduce delayed messages, missing observations, inconsistent timestamps, interference and lost synchronization, plus audit trails recording capture time, source quality, processing delays and command time. It notes that NIST's positioning, navigation and timing risk guidance offers a foundation, though the proposed age limits are an engineering recommendation rather than an existing international mandate.

Articles.Title: AI Is Changing What A Second Is Worth – OpEd

stories.Headline: Sandisk (SNDK) Stock Sees Modest Fair Value Cut As Analysts Weigh AI Demand
stories.Summary:
Sandisk's modeled fair value was cut from US$2,173.00 to US$2,105.29 in an update published on October 31, 2026. The change came as analysts weighed enthusiasm about AI driven NAND demand against concerns about sector multiple compression.
