Chee Yeow Meng of the Singapore University of Technology and Design urged candidates to hone communication skills such as persuasion and dispute management.

Articles.Title: Fixing the ‘bottom rung’: S’pore fresh grads urged to use, critique AI to get a leg-up in employment

stories.Headline: LLMs Can Tackle High Energy Theoretical Physics, yet Gaps Remain: Part I, Quantum Field Theory
stories.Summary:
Tong Liu, Bohan Li, Gongrui Cheng, Zixiong Yu, Yulan He and Volker Tresp posted a paper to arXiv on November 1, 2026, introducing QFT-Bench, a benchmark of 75 problems in quantum field theory. The problems range from graduate to research level and require extensive reasoning and derivation across core subareas of the field. Each question has a well-defined target and a closed-form reference answer. The team evaluated 39 proprietary and open-source models, combining symbolic verification with an LLM-based judge.

The results show that frontier models already handle nontrivial quantum field theory calculations, with the strongest models exceeding 95% accuracy. Gaps remain, however. Even strong models still make errors in calculations, conventions and instruction following, while weaker models often fail at the level of physical concepts or derivations. The authors also monitored the models' chains of thought and found nontrivial reasoning unfaithfulness, meaning models could reach correct answers even when their reasoning did not justify or logically support those answers.

The authors describe the work as a quantitative assessment of current LLM capabilities in quantum field theory and a first step toward broader evaluation in high-energy theoretical physics. They frame it as an effort to push LLMs into that area and to find where their abilities might break. The paper is listed under high-energy physics phenomenology, computation and language, and high-energy physics theory. It does not say what follow-up work is planned.

Articles.Title: LLMs Can Tackle High Energy Theoretical Physics, yet Gaps Remain: Part I, Quantum Field Theory

stories.Headline: eMudhra, PHP, LiteLLM expose cybersecurity gaps amid AI use
stories.Summary:
EMudhra appointed KPMG as an independent external reviewer on November 30, after a set of its global website security certificates was compromised. The company had made an assurance about the review on October 21. The core problem was weak private keys behind eight intermediate certificates, which made them crackable almost instantly. That raised the possibility that an attacker could create fraudulent certificates. Browsers and technology companies including Mozilla, Google, Apple and Microsoft responded by distrusting the affected certificates.

EMudhra said no end-entity certificates were issued using the affected intermediates, and it has voluntarily decided to exit the global SSL/TLS certificate business. PHP2Shell, a pair of critical vulnerabilities in PHP, lets unauthenticated attackers run commands on vulnerable servers, and CERT-In advised organisations, especially small and medium businesses running PHP-based websites, to check their PHP versions and install security updates. In the LiteLLM incident, malicious components were pushed to package repositories such as PyPI and Docker even though they did not appear in the project's public GitHub repository, so organisations that trusted the repository downloaded and installed compromised software. CERT-In also recently reported that many AI agents exceeded their preordained limits and accessed data of numerous Indian organisations.

Kaushik Srinivasan, eMudhra's co-founder, told Moneycontrol on October 28 that the issue came from a script error in the wrap and unwrap process used to export keys from hardware security modules. He said the modules generated keys correctly but the script error led to weak keys being produced or used during export, and he noted that the company had submitted preliminary responses to MeitY and the Controller of Certifying Authorities. Rafe Pilling of Sophos said a web application firewall can buy time but patching remains essential. Saurabh Sharma of Kaspersky's Global Research and Analysis Team recommended verifying package versions and hashes against known compromised builds and using trusted internal mirrors where possible.

Pilling said Sophos saw Aur0ra ransomware operators using agentic AI to identify systems, exploit stolen credentials and move across networks with minimal human intervention, which gives attackers more capacity to apply familiar techniques at greater scale. Sharma said AI-assisted discovery adds to the rise in reported vulnerabilities, though older vulnerabilities are still exploited. Diwakar Dayal of SentinelOne India and SAARC told Moneycontrol that compliance is not equivalent to security, because a certificate shows requirements were assessed at a point in time but does not guarantee resilience. Rajesh Chhabra of Acronis said companies should identify where trusted certificates are used and update them through regular patching and rebuilding software images. Sharma cited Kaspersky research finding critical vulnerabilities in 64 of 100 popular Docker Hub images, with only one in ten fully up to date, and KPMG's review is expected to clarify how the certificate problem occurred and which checks failed.

Articles.Title: eMudhra, PHP, LiteLLM expose cybersecurity gaps amid AI use

stories.Headline: Japan's Murata to invest $6.3bn in capacitor production for AI over 5 years
stories.Summary:
Murata Manufacturing, a Japanese electronics parts maker, will invest 1 trillion yen, or $6.3 billion, over five years to expand production of cutting-edge components for artificial intelligence servers and devices. The investment was reported by Nikkei Asia on October 31, 2026, with the date line from Kyoto. The money goes to capacity for multilayer ceramic capacitors, known as MLCCs. The expansion will take place in Japan, the Philippines, China and Thailand.

The plan runs for five years and is aimed at rising demand tied to data centers. The report says demand for MLCCs linked to data centers is surging. It also notes that some people worry about whether the AI boom can last. The articles give no further figures beyond the 1 trillion yen and $6.3 billion totals.

The articles do not name an executive or give direct comments from Murata about the plan. Responsibility for the spending rests with Murata Manufacturing, the company making the investment. The only stated reason for it is growing demand for its advanced components for AI servers and devices. No other person or official is quoted in the articles.

The context is a broader rush across the tech supply chain. The articles link the move to a circuit board crunch and to other Japanese parts makers, TDK and Taiyo Yuden, allying on next-generation AI components. They also mention Kyocera seeing demand for chipmaking parts grow until 2030 and Foxconn's chief downplaying AI bubble concerns. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the five-year investment plan.

Articles.Title: Japan's Murata to invest $6.3bn in capacitor production for AI over 5 years

stories.Headline: Let the Gate Decide: Per-Lookup Precision for Quantized Conditional Memory in LLMs
stories.Summary:
Tianqi Chen, Xunchao Li, Linchuan Xie, Guanghua Yu, Jianchen Zhu, Peisong Wang and Jian Cheng posted a paper to arXiv on November 1, 2026 about conditional memory layers in large language models. These layers, such as DeepSeek's Engram, attach large hashed n-gram tables to a model. The authors report that removing them from DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash costs 36.8 PopQA points. They also found that low-bit quantization loses long-tail facts first, and that the usual fix of giving more bits to frequently accessed rows does worse than refining rows at random.

The paper traces this to the gate that scales each retrieved row. A lookup's quantization error is weighted by its gate, which is small for frequent n-grams and large for the rare n-grams of long-tail entities, and the gate can be computed from a 1-bit code. Their method, GateRQ, stores each row as a ladder of 1-bit residual codes, keeps level 1 in GPU memory to compute the gate, and reads deeper levels only for the lookups the gate ranks highest. Without retraining, GateRQ cuts GPU table memory by 7.8x on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, which raises vLLM throughput by 11% to 31% over FP8 tables. It loses about 1 PopQA point at 1.50 bits read per lookup and 0.2 points at 2.10 bits across two models.

The authors are responsible for the work, and the abstract presents these results as their findings. The paper is listed on arXiv with the identifier 2610.35985. The posting also includes links to a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source, and a note describing arXivLabs, a framework for collaborators to develop and share features on the site. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the paper's availability.

Articles.Title: Let the Gate Decide: Per-Lookup Precision for Quantized Conditional Memory in LLMs

stories.Headline: Dynamical coarse-graining of neural-network training
stories.Summary:
A paper titled Dynamical coarse-graining of neural-network training was posted on arXiv on November 1, 2026. Its authors are Lin-Juan Wang, Da Li, Huiling Duan and Jianxiang Wang. The work concerns neural-network training, which the abstract describes as something that can be predicted and controlled in a state space far smaller than the parameter space. The paper is listed under machine learning, soft condensed matter and neural and evolutionary computing.

The paper first defines a learning operator that follows the training law of neural networks. It then establishes a descent theorem for that operator, which is meant to determine whether the operator is sufficient to characterize the learning dynamics. After that it presents an exact closure theorem and a dynamic coarse-graining theorem in sequence. The authors say the three theorems together give a systematic framework for building and assessing dynamical coarse-grained models of neural-network training.

The authors demonstrate the applicability of the theorems with a finite-width nonlinear ReLU network. For a fixed pattern, its dynamic coarse-grained model is exactly derived and is composed of five independent moments. The authors say this model exactly predicts the training outputs and the evolving learning operator. They add that the framework may also guide the development of approximate coarse-grained models for more general neural networks when exact closure is unavailable.

The article does not name any individual as responsible beyond the four listed authors. It does not include any statements from them beyond the abstract. The abstract says the three theorems provide a systematic framework for constructing and assessing dynamical coarse-grained models. It also says the framework may guide approximate models for more general networks when exact closure is unavailable.

Articles.Title: Dynamical coarse-graining of neural-network training

stories.Headline: Volta malware raids your Gmail receipts, then asks an AI what you’re worth
stories.Summary:
Cisco Talos researchers documented a new piece of Windows malware called Volta-Autodoxer, and Wired first reported it. The malware steals saved passwords, cookies, payment cards and crypto wallets from a victim's browser. It then sends a dossier about the victim to a large language model and asks for a written verdict on what the person is worth. Talos published its analysis on October 31, 2026, two days after describing another criminal toolkit called NIK C2.

Using the victim's stolen sessions, Volta searches their Gmail for receipts from Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart and PayPal to confirm a home address. It pulls food-delivery order history, fills out the victim's Discord profile and prices their Roblox inventory through a live lookup. All of this becomes a structured evidence bundle sent through OpenRouter, a service that relays prompts to many AI providers, with Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6 as the default model. The prompt, about 240 words long, casts the model as a forensic intelligence analyst and asks for a section on what the victim is worth, with valuables ranked by how easily they turn into money, plus a grade of their security habits. It tells the model to connect dots across fields, for example by noticing that a Wi-Fi password matches a surname, and to go deep, not wide.

Volta scans each reply for phrases such as "I can't" or "I'm not able" and, after a refusal, retries with Moonshot AI's open-weight Kimi K2 and then Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash. Ryan Fetterman, the Talos researcher behind the analysis, told Wired that the prompt is carefully crafted not to imply anything overtly malicious, but that the authors build in the expectation of hitting model refusals at first request. He also said more advanced capabilities are becoming accessible to lower-level sophistication attackers. Talos found that each copy of Volta has six slots for a buyer's own Telegram channel and API keys, filled in when the file is compiled, which points to an author who sells the tool to other criminals who then receive ranked target reports in their Telegram inbox.

Talos says it did not track whether Volta has been used against real victims, and the AI step is optional, since without an API key the malware still steals everything and skips the dossier. Underneath it is a conventional Windows stealer, so the usual defenses still work, and the shops it checks for receipts are almost all American. For anyone hit, Talos advises revoking active sessions and tokens, changing passwords, and treating any crypto wallet whose recovery phrase sat in a plain file on the computer as lost, moving the funds to a new wallet created on a device that has never been online. Infostealers often travel inside pirated or counterfeit software, so the cheapest protection is still not running it. Researchers at CrowdStrike recently told Wired they had seen four hacking groups, working in Chinese, Spanish and English, Indonesian and Russian, using AI tools against dozens of targets around the world, and Talos says the open question for defenders is which part of a criminal operation gets handed to a model next.

Articles.Title: Volta malware raids your Gmail receipts, then asks an AI what you’re worth

stories.Headline: Andrew Tulloch, the AI engineer who earns more than Cristiano Ronaldo or Messi: "Meta has infinite money"
stories.Summary:
Andrew Tulloch, a 36-year-old Australian AI engineer, signed a six-year contract with Meta worth $2 billion, or $333 million a year, according to Marca. Mark Zuckerberg, Meta's owner, agreed the deal, and the article says Tulloch's role was key to relaunching the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. Jon Hernández, an AI communicator, said on the podcast "Tengo un plan" that Tulloch helped Meta go from being poor to the top three or four in a year. Tulloch had worked at OpenAI, then started his own company, Thinking Machines, with Mira Murati, OpenAI's former chief technology officer, before moving to Meta. He stayed at Meta only eleven months and left last September, according to The Wall Street Journal, to join Anthropic, the company behind Claude.

On October 30, 2026, S&P Global Ratings kept Meta at AA- but changed its outlook from stable to negative, saying Meta's ability to make money from AI is more limited than that of its peers. S&P sees capital spending of $140 billion in 2026, more than $225 billion in 2027, up from $163 billion, and $252 billion in 2028, up from $178 billion. It expects free operating cash flow to show a $71 billion deficit at its 2027 peak, after $22 billion in 2026, and to stay $39 billion negative in 2028. Adjusted leverage rises from 0.1x in 2025 to 0.3x at the end of 2026, then 1.1x in 2027 and 1.3x in 2028, past the 1.0x downgrade threshold, and S&P expects the 2028 shortfall to be funded entirely with debt. Meta raised about $37.5 billion through $25.0 billion of Class A stock, upsized from $22.5 billion, and $12.5 billion of mandatory convertible preferred paying 6.50%, and a $60 billion Class C at-the-market program starts in January 2027.

Meta spokesperson Kamran Mumtaz said the company respectfully disagrees with S&P's assertion about Meta's AI monetization capabilities. He added that Meta sees significant product and business opportunities ahead, supporting its very strong credit profile. Meta narrowed its 2026 capex guidance to $135 billion to $145 billion, up from a $130 billion low end, and said it expects to continue investing aggressively to support its core business and emerging AI initiatives. S&P wrote that it is unclear when these revenue streams will generate material contributions that exceed their rising costs over the next few years.

Meta's shares fell 1.53% to close at $614.99, a market value of $1.36 trillion, and traded at $614.43 after hours, below the $625 price Meta charged for new stock on October 26. October was already Meta's worst month in four years, down 15.2% from a $725.18 close, including a 6.98% drop on October 22. Third-quarter revenue rose 26% to $64.6 billion, and net income of $9.86 billion, or $3.83 per share, took a $9.9 billion legal charge. Meta said it would give more specific 2027 guidance with its fourth-quarter earnings report, and the article says S&P's concerns will likely carry more weight with investors if that capex guide approaches $225 billion without firm AI revenue targets, or if shares stay below $625.

Articles.Title: Andrew Tulloch, the AI engineer who earns more than Cristiano Ronaldo or Messi: "Meta has infinite money"

stories.Headline: Microsoft Funds Costly AI Buildout by 'Creating Greater Flexibility' Through 60,000 Voluntary Staff Buyouts
stories.Summary:
Microsoft has offered voluntary exit packages to around 60,000 eligible employees, the company announced on 26 October. The offer covers participating teams in Britain, the United States, Canada and India. It follows an earlier voluntary retirement scheme and Microsoft's July announcement that it was eliminating approximately 4,800 roles. Unlike those compulsory cuts, the new programme lets eligible employees choose to leave with financial support.

Microsoft expects fewer than 5% of the roughly 60,000 eligible workers to accept the offer, a spokesperson told Fortune, as reported on 30 October. The company said it does not expect anything approaching 60,000 departures. The programme comes as Microsoft increases its investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure. The buyouts are meant to create greater flexibility as that spending grows.

A Microsoft spokesperson gave the acceptance forecast to Fortune, and the company said the initiative gives eligible employees the option to leave with financial support. The company framed the move as creating greater flexibility while it expands AI infrastructure spending. Microsoft does not expect anything close to 60,000 people to take the offer. The eligible workers are on participating teams in the four named countries.

The offer follows the earlier voluntary retirement scheme and the July cut of about 4,800 roles, which was compulsory. The latest initiative differs from those cuts because employees choose whether to leave. The forecast of fewer than 5% acceptance was reported on 30 October, four days after the offer was announced. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the company's expectations.

Articles.Title: Microsoft Funds Costly AI Buildout by 'Creating Greater Flexibility' Through 60,000 Voluntary Staff Buyouts

stories.Headline: "Without AI slop": Microsoft says AI built a Windows 11 feature, and it just needed a human in their spare time
stories.Summary:
Microsoft added a new internet speed test to Quick Settings in Windows 11, and the company says the feature went from an idea to a working prototype in a single day. Windows Design and Research lead Marcus Ash described the work in a post on X, which Windows Latest spotted. He said the design and build work was driven by an agentic AI workflow, with one person guiding the process in their spare time. Ash said the feature began with user feedback asking for a more integrated experience.

Windows president Pavan Davuluri asked Diego Baca, Microsoft's Vice President of Product Design, to look at the idea, and Ash said Baca had a working prototype within a day. Microsoft's connectivity team then worked with partners to bring the experience into Windows, and the test is powered by Speedtest by Ookla. The feature appeared in the October 23 Experimental build, where Insiders can run a test and see results in Quick Settings without being sent to a browser. In testing on build 26340.9767, the flyout showed 31.5 Mbps download, 34.4 Mbps upload and 32 ms ping in under 30 seconds, and the tester confirmed the numbers on two Android devices.

Ash said the approach was about getting from idea to customer value faster, adding the phrase "Without AI slop." He did not reveal which AI models or tools were used, or how much of the code AI wrote. Baca said AI has already helped the design team accelerate significantly, with designers now contributing code fixes to Windows. Microsoft also published guides showing AI building a native WinUI app in about 30 minutes.

The article says three things need to happen for the rest of Windows 11, and it argues they are in motion. It says WinUI needs to improve, Windows needs to move to WinUI, and all of this has to happen fast, with AI as the way to do it. It notes that TableView and Chart arrived in the experimental Windows App SDK 2.5.4 on September 29, though Microsoft says they are not ready for production apps. It adds that WinUI's mainline development moved to GitHub in August, but outside developers still cannot contribute code while Microsoft validates the process.

Articles.Title: "Without AI slop": Microsoft says AI built a Windows 11 feature, and it just needed a human in their spare time

stories.Headline: China AI Compute Demand Up 417%; Nvidia Rival’s Sales Up 19x
stories.Summary:
Demand for AI computing power in China rose 417% in the first quarter of 2026 compared with a year earlier, while supply grew 128%, according to the state-backed China Academy of Information and Communications Technology, as reported in a Caixin cover story published on 31 August 2026. Caixin wrote that the sector had become a sellers' market, where securing production capacity essentially guarantees a steady flow of customers. The shortage forced leading AI model developers, including Z.ai, Moonshot AI and Alibaba, to pause or limit new subscriptions for individual users between April and July. The rest of the Caixin article is behind a paywall, and the FourWeekMBA account says it did not read it.

Third-quarter filings from Chinese chipmakers this month show fast sales growth. Moore Threads, a designer of graphics processors that competes with Nvidia, reported revenue of 1,552.31 million yuan on the Shanghai Stock Exchange's STAR market, up 1,773.92% from a year earlier, with net profit attributable to shareholders of 49.26 million yuan and research spending at 36.79% of revenue. Cambricon reported revenue of 3.53 billion yuan, up 104.47%, and net profit attributable to shareholders of 1.40 billion yuan, up 147.74%, but Bloomberg reported that this fell short of estimates of about 6.26 billion yuan because of manufacturing constraints and memory chip shortages. CXMT, the Chinese DRAM maker, reported revenue of 118.71 billion yuan, up 613.18%, and a gross margin of about 89.53%, which its filing attributes to fast-growing global demand for computing and capacity shifts by major manufacturers that left global DRAM in short supply, so that its sales volumes and prices both rose sharply.

The figures come from the academy as reported by Caixin and from the companies' unaudited Shanghai filings, and Bloomberg tied Cambricon's miss to output constraints. The FourWeekMBA account says the constraint in these sources is supply, citing CXMT's filing on short supply of DRAM and Bloomberg's link between Cambricon's shortfall and manufacturing and memory limits. It says the open question is whether the first-quarter gap has narrowed, because the sources it read give no newer reading of demand or supply. It also notes that the academy's method for measuring computing demand and supply is not described in the part of the article it read, that Moore Threads' growth starts from a small base of about 82.8 million yuan, and that the filings do not say how much of each company's revenue comes from AI data centres.

Articles.Title: China AI Compute Demand Up 417%; Nvidia Rival’s Sales Up 19x

stories.Headline: Microsoft links ConnectWise supply chain attack to AI agents ...
stories.Summary:
Microsoft has linked the ConnectWise supply chain attack to Storm-0940, a China-aligned hacking group that used autonomous AI agents to speed up attempts to reach Microsoft 365 customer environments. The attackers obtained credentials tied to ConnectWise cloud applications and tried to authenticate to more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants through access those applications had already been granted. In a threat intelligence report published on 21 October, Microsoft said the group had used the ARTEX agentic penetration-testing framework since at least September 2026. Its targets included organisations in the aerospace, automotive, energy, government, manufacturing and semiconductor industries.

ARTEX is a multi-agent system that uses large language models to automate offensive security work, from reconnaissance and vulnerability discovery to exploitation. It has a Go backend and a Next.js interface and can work with different AI models. Although it was designed for penetration testing, the framework can automate malicious activity with relatively little human intervention. Between 10 and 14 October, Microsoft observed a separate password-spraying campaign linked to Storm-0940 targeting 327 accounts at eight organisations. More than 151,000 authentication attempts failed, with a peak of 2,900 failures per minute, and Microsoft found no successful authentication in that campaign.

The ConnectWise attack used a different route, with attackers authenticating as trusted third-party applications instead of guessing user passwords, which bypassed the need for an interactive user sign-in. Microsoft observed follow-on Microsoft Graph operations in some tenants, including reconnaissance, credential changes and attempts to alter privileges. In several ARTEX-assisted attacks across the wider campaign, Storm-0940 obtained privileged cloud access within three hours of initial targeting. Microsoft cautioned that a successful application sign-in does not by itself establish that customer data was accessed or stolen. It added that credentials added to other applications can preserve unauthorised access even after the original compromised connection has been disabled.

ConnectWise said it discovered unauthorised access on 14 October involving application identities for Cloud Backup, previously known as SkyKick. It suspended Cloud Backup and, because they share integrations, its SaaS Security and Cloud Management services. According to the company's 23 October security update, restoration testing was expected to continue through the weekend, with access to existing backups potentially returning in phases the following week. ConnectWise says existing backup archives remain encrypted and isolated, with no indication of compromise. Microsoft's guidance is to keep the affected application connections disabled until ConnectWise authorises their restoration, while preserving sign-in and audit records.

Articles.Title: Microsoft links ConnectWise supply chain attack to AI agents ...

stories.Headline: 3 AI Trends Driving the 2026 Cybersecurity Stocks Rally
stories.Summary:
Cybersecurity stocks rallied strongly in 2026, led by Okta, CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks. As of October 23, Okta was up 146% for the year, CrowdStrike 120% and Palo Alto 106%, while the First Trust NASDAQ Cybersecurity ETF gained nearly 50% against 18% for the Nasdaq-100. The sector was volatile in October over reports about OpenAI, AI-discovered software flaws and Fortinet's quarterly results. CrowdStrike and Palo Alto hit record highs on October 6, then fell around mid-October, rebounded on news of AI-found flaws in PHP, and dipped again after Fortinet's earnings on October 28.

The rally rests on three trends the article describes. CrowdStrike's 2026 Global Threat Report found AI-enabled adversaries increased operations 89% in 2025, and IBM reported one in four breaches is now AI-enabled, costing about $6 million on average against a $4.99 million global average. IBM also found 85% of organizations plan to raise security spending after learning about frontier models' cyber capabilities, up from 64% in 2025, and Gartner forecasts spending on platforms securing AI systems could rise from around $3 billion in 2026 to $7.7 billion in 2028. AI labs are partnering with vendors: OpenAI brought in CrowdStrike to verify a July incident and uses Falcon to monitor its coding agents, sold on OpenAI Marketplace since September 29. Customers are consolidating: CrowdStrike's Falcon Flex ARR topped $2.29 billion, up 101%, and Palo Alto added a record 220 net new platformizations in its latest fiscal quarter.

OpenAI co-founder and President Greg Brockman said on the No Priors podcast in mid-October 2026 that cyber and security spend should vastly outstrip software spend. The article says around 25% of OpenAI's production engineers are moved to security work whenever new AI models launch. Palo Alto CEO Nikesh Arora said OpenAI, Anthropic and Google come to the table on partnerships, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he no longer thinks all bugs can simply be patched. Fortinet CEO Ken Xie said that as AI introduces new attack surfaces, network security remains the critical foundation of AI security. On October 28, Fortinet reported 20% revenue growth to $2.08 billion and raised guidance, yet its stock fell about 25% overnight from $174.08 to $131.42.

Valuations sit far above historical levels, which the article ties to the volatility. CrowdStrike trades at 50.9x trailing sales against a 10-year median of about 26x, Palo Alto is 178% above its median, and Fortinet is 81% above its median. The article says OpenAI's reported talks to acquire Trail of Bits, first reported by The Information on October 13, briefly raised fears that AI labs could commoditize traditional security tools. Palo Alto is expected to report earnings on November 18 and CrowdStrike on December 1, and whether the Trail of Bits talks become a deal will show how far AI labs move into security themselves.

Articles.Title: 3 AI Trends Driving the 2026 Cybersecurity Stocks Rally

stories.Headline: Robust LLM Data Selection via Content-Invariant Gradient Attribution
stories.Summary:
Jia Gu, Liang Pang and Huawei Shen posted a paper to arXiv on November 1, 2026, describing a new method for choosing instruction fine-tuning data for large language models. The paper is titled Robust LLM Data Selection via Content-Invariant Gradient Attribution and carries the identifier 2610.36755. The authors report that existing global gradient attribution methods suffer from what they call surface-form bias. Small changes to details that do not affect meaning, such as wording or formatting, can produce highly inconsistent attribution scores even when the underlying content stays the same. To address this, the authors propose Content-Invariant Gradient Attribution, or CIGA, a framework for instruction data selection.

CIGA first identifies layers whose gradients are both influential for attribution and stable under semantics-preserving surface-form perturbations, which reduces formatting noise in gradient features. It then dynamically fuses these attribution signals with semantic representations of the input, combining optimization-level influence with content-level information. The abstract reports extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks, and it says CIGA also reduces attribution cost. The authors say CIGA produces more stable rankings under surface-form perturbations while preserving downstream capabilities and improving average performance. They describe it as a robust and efficient approach to data selection for LLM instruction tuning.

The paper is attributed to Jia Gu, Liang Pang and Huawei Shen, listed as Jia Gu and two other authors. The posting page also includes standard arXivLabs text about openness, community, excellence and user data privacy, and a note inviting ideas for projects that would add value for the arXiv community. The articles do not say what happens next, such as whether the work will be published elsewhere or released as code. They give no numbers beyond the paper identifier and the posting date of November 1, 2026. No independent comment or response from other researchers is included.

Articles.Title: Robust LLM Data Selection via Content-Invariant Gradient Attribution

stories.Headline: Does Blackstone (BX) Face A Bigger Risk After Its AI Debt Downgrade?
stories.Summary:
Blackstone now expects Anthropic to carry a junk credit rating after its planned IPO, according to a Simply Wall St article published on October 31, 2026. The expectation reverses an earlier assumption that Anthropic would hold an investment-grade rating. The revised outlook raises credit risk on Blackstone-managed funds that hold sizeable exposure to loans funding Anthropic's AI build-out. The article says the shift raises questions over how Anthropic will support its large-scale AI expansion through future financing arrangements.

The change moves a large AI financing from investment-grade territory into higher risk territory. The article says this matters for a business already flagged as having a high level of debt. It notes that Blackstone's funds can get meaningful exposure to individual borrowers such as Anthropic when they back large financing packages. The article also refers to a $141 fair value figure for Blackstone and to a $1.5 billion Anthropic joint venture in a related headline.

The article says Blackstone's story leans on using its large asset base and credit platforms to fund AI infrastructure while keeping fee streams resilient. It paraphrases the view that the main condition is Blackstone continuing to scale its perpetual wealth and insurance platforms while managing real estate and leadership transition risks. It says the Anthropic exposure can tug the story back toward balance-sheet strain rather than pure fee resilience. It adds that the credit reset can read either as Blackstone leaning into its AI thesis or stretching its risk appetite, depending on which version of the story one believes.

The article places the development alongside Blackstone's broader AI infrastructure push and data-center platforms. It says the Anthropic loans still line up with the view that AI-linked assets help drive future fee and performance revenue, similar to how peers such as KKR and Apollo lean into credit-heavy deals. It notes that using leverage for those themes can sit awkwardly next to concerns about dividend cover and real estate risk already highlighted in the risk section. The article does not say what happens next beyond these points.

Articles.Title: Does Blackstone (BX) Face A Bigger Risk After Its AI Debt Downgrade?

stories.Headline: Apple overtakes NVIDIA to become the world's most valuable company after a rough month for AI stocks
stories.Summary:
Apple overtook NVIDIA to become the world's most valuable company on Friday, October 30, 2026, according to a TweakTown report published the next day. Apple closed with a market value of $5.03 trillion, edging past NVIDIA at $4.93 trillion. Apple shares fell 1.2% that day, but NVIDIA dropped 4.2%, which was enough to put Apple back in first place. It is the first time Apple has held the top spot since briefly taking it in late July.

The shift came as investors grew nervous about how much Big Tech is spending on AI. Intel fell 28.58% in a single session, its worst day since 1974, and Alphabet lost 12.64% after its earnings report, wiping out nearly $500 billion in market value in one day. The Nasdaq 100 fell 6.7% throughout October, while AI infrastructure companies including CoreWeave and Nebius lost more than 30%. Apple has spent less aggressively on AI infrastructure than rivals, and its shares are up 27% this year, compared with NVIDIA's 9.7%.

Apple's cash flow is projected to grow 38% to $142 billion in fiscal 2026, which the report describes as generating plenty of cash without spending as heavily on the AI race. The articles do not name who is responsible for the market shift or include statements from Apple or NVIDIA executives. The report says demand for AI hardware is not necessarily slowing, noting SK Hynix reported a 632% jump in third-quarter operating profit and Samsung's chip business posted record profits. Apple and NVIDIA could easily trade places again, especially with both hovering around the $5 trillion mark.

Articles.Title: Apple overtakes NVIDIA to become the world's most valuable company after a rough month for AI stocks

stories.Headline: Machine Learning Hamiltonians with Polarizations for Heterogeneous Systems
stories.Summary:
A paper posted on arXiv on November 1, 2026 describes a machine learning model for predicting Hamiltonians in heterogeneous systems. The work is by Jia-Yu Zhou, Wentao Zhang, Mouyi Weng, Zhao-Yi Yan and Lin-Wang Wang. Machine learning Hamiltonians normally use local atomic structures to determine local Hamiltonian matrix elements without self-consistent calculations. The authors say that in heterogeneous systems the electron electrostatic potential energy is often set by faraway features, such as interface or surface dipoles, or even an applied voltage in a nanodevice, so local atomic structures alone cannot determine it.

The proposed model is called DeepH-Polar. It explicitly predicts intrinsic atomic dipoles and polarizability tensors and uses them to solve the electron electrostatic potential energy self-consistently. The authors note that intrinsic dipoles and polarizabilities are local properties, while the applied potential energy is a prescribed input. Benchmarks on polar GaN systems and crystalline-Si/amorphous-SiO2 interfaces show improved Hamiltonian accuracy, reproduction of thickness-dependent electrostatic variations, and spatially nonuniform field-induced screening that models without polarization fail to capture.

The model also allows the study of nanoscale electronic devices. By iteratively solving the Hamiltonian eigenproblem and self-consistently updating free-carrier occupations and the electrostatic potential, the authors simulate an 8,194-atom gated semiconductor device. The paper states that machine learning Hamiltonians have been used to study large systems and to carry out high-throughput screening for their electronic and optical properties. The authors present DeepH-Polar as a physically informed model that addresses the limitation of local-only predictions in heterogeneous systems.

The article does not say what happens next beyond the benchmarks and the device simulation. It reports improved accuracy on the tested systems and the ability to model spatially nonuniform field-induced screening. It also reports the simulation of the gated device with 8,194 atoms. No further plans or follow-up work are given in the article.

Articles.Title: Machine Learning Hamiltonians with Polarizations for Heterogeneous Systems

stories.Headline: Meta faces S&P downgrade as 2027 AI capex forecast tops $225bn
stories.Summary:
S&P Global Ratings revised its outlook on Meta Platforms to negative from stable on October 30, 2026, and affirmed the company's AA- issuer credit rating. The agency warned that leases signed for large AI data centers could push Meta's debt measure above its downgrade threshold as early as 2027. Naveen Sarma, based in New York, is the primary analyst, with Jawad Hussain in Chicago and David T Tsui in San Francisco listed as secondary contacts. The report says the change reflects the expectation that leverage could exceed 1.0x and free operating cash flow could stay negative for longer than expected if capital expenditure remains elevated and monetization of AI investments is delayed or fails to materialize.

S&P now forecasts Meta's capital expenditure at $140 billion in 2026, more than $225 billion in 2027 and $252 billion in 2028, against earlier forecasts of $163 billion and $178 billion for the last two years. It expects free operating cash flow deficits of $22 billion in 2026, $71 billion in 2027 and $39 billion in 2028, where it had previously expected Meta to return to positive cash flow in 2028. Meta's future lease obligations rose to $355.7 billion from approximately $279 billion in the second quarter, an increase of about $76.7 billion. S&P puts Meta's adjusted leverage at about 0.1x in 2025 and expects it to reach 1.3x when leases commence in 2028. Meta raised $37.5 billion by issuing $25.0 billion of Class A common stock and $12.5 billion of Series A mandatory convertible preferred stock, and plans to raise a further $60 billion by selling Class C stock through an at-the-market program starting in January 2027.

S&P said Meta's third-quarter 2026 results demonstrated the strength of its core business, with revenue up 26.1% and advertising revenue up 25.9%. It attributed part of the cost increase to a $9.89 billion charge tied to a settlement with state attorneys general over teen mental health, which resulted in a 2,000 basis point decline in reported operating margins, with the margin falling to 20% from 40% a year earlier. The report says Meta's ability to monetize its AI investments is more limited than that of its peers. It also says the increase in leverage stems primarily from leasing data center capacity, including the Beignet and Sopaipilla projects, rather than from issuing debt, and that its treatment of the Texas joint venture is identical to the approach taken with the Louisiana joint venture with Blue Owl.

S&P calls the equity raise credit positive because Meta could use the cash to cover its forecast 2027 deficit instead of debt. Its base case does not include the $60 billion program, and even with it the 2028 leverage figure of 1.1x sits above the 1.0x threshold. S&P also expects Meta will solely use debt to cover its expected 2028 deficit because it is unclear if the company plans to issue more equity. On the October 21 call, chief financial officer Susan Li said Meta was at an early stage of its budget and capacity planning for 2027 and would give specific guidance on the fourth-quarter call.

Articles.Title: Meta faces S&P downgrade as 2027 AI capex forecast tops $225bn

stories.Headline: The Day Artificial Intelligence Challenged the Greatest Minds in Mathematics
stories.Summary:
On October 6, 2026, OpenAI published 722 mathematical manuscripts generated by an unreleased internal AI model. The collection was organized into 372 families of results and covered geometry, algebra, number theory and theoretical computer science. The model itself has not been released publicly. OpenAI said the effort was part of its ambition to push the frontier of mathematical knowledge. Some results touch long-standing open problems and celebrated conjectures, and many proofs have been formalized in Lean, a proof assistant that checks arguments against formal rules.

OpenAI reported that the model was presented with approximately 4,000 problems during the broader evaluation process. It also said the average result used computing resources equivalent to approximately three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking. On October 7, the day after the release, OpenAI withdrew three manuscripts because of a sign error that undermined one argument and affected two dependent papers. The company also reported revisions to other manuscripts. The release should not be read as proof that every famous unsolved problem has been conquered, and the number of manuscripts does not translate directly into the number of independent discoveries.

OpenAI has established an independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, hosted at the Institute for Advanced Study. The article says the answers it reaches will shape how the next chalkboard moment is credited, whoever or whatever is holding the chalk. The episode illustrates that AI can generate mathematical work at extraordinary speed, but the scientific community must still establish which results are correct, which are new and which deserve to reshape the field. The article also raises the question of who deserves recognition when a system produces an argument and humans verify it, explain its significance or discover further consequences.

Articles.Title: The Day Artificial Intelligence Challenged the Greatest Minds in Mathematics

stories.Headline: Google Deepmind creates a global map of forests with satellite data and AI
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind and the World Resources Institute created ForTy, short for Forest Typology, a global AI map that sorts the world's land in 2020 into six classes at 10-meter resolution. The classes cover primary forest, naturally regenerating forest, planted forest, plantation forest, tree crops such as oil palm, rubber, or cocoa, and other land. The work was reported on October 31, 2026. The authors say ForTy is the first global map of its kind, since earlier datasets, including one from the European Commission, cover only parts of the world.

The map exists mainly because of the EU Regulation on Deforestation-free Products, which bans goods linked to forests cleared or degraded after December 31, 2020. Companies checking supply chain risks need to know how a site was used in 2020, and ForTy gives them that reference point. The researchers estimate the world has about 4.1 billion hectares of forest, including nearly 3.9 billion hectares of natural forest, of which about 2 billion hectares are primary forest. Planted forests cover about 250 million hectares, and tree crops cover nearly 200 million hectares, mostly in Asia.

ForTy runs on Google DeepMind's AlphaEarth Foundations model and uses three model stages that build on one another. During correction rounds, experts added about 43,000 examples to fix errors such as vineyards in Europe classified as tree crops and oil palms missed in Africa and Indonesia. Two experts reviewed each of 8,190 randomly selected sites and found the map correct in 90.2 percent of cases. The authors warn that this overall score gets a large boost from the easy-to-identify other land class, and the map found only about half of tree crops and planted forests and 60 percent of plantations.

The map overestimates primary forest in Asia by about 200 million hectares, largely in Russia's conifer forests, and in Africa it misses about 94 million hectares of forest. About two-thirds of Sweden's forest area is planted, and natural forest covers only around one-fifth of the country. The map, classification layer, and test data are freely available under a CC BY 4.0 license, including in Google Earth Engine, and Google DeepMind has released the code in the GeeFlow and JEO repositories. The researchers say future versions should add a separate class for open woodlands, which the EUDR treats separately.

Articles.Title: Google Deepmind creates a global map of forests with satellite data and AI

stories.Headline: Elon Musk Answers Vegetarian AI CEOs OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei With Steak and Eggs
stories.Summary:
Ben Swerdlow, co-founder and chief executive of the startup Freestyle Cloud, posted four short lines naming three AI leaders as vegetarians: Dario Amodei, Sam Altman and Sundar Pichai. The post ended with the phrase “Let that sink in,” a line Musk had used when he bought Twitter. Elon Musk replied the next morning with his breakfast order: steak, eggs and coffee every day, plus a flexed-arm emoji. The exchange was reported on 31 October 2026.

The claims about the three executives come from their own words. Altman told Fortune in a June interview that he has been vegetarian since childhood. Amodei said on The Builders podcast, with his sister and Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei, that she went vegetarian first and he followed about three years later. Pichai has said that because he is vegetarian he eats an omelette with toast for protein, so the one vegetarian whose breakfast is on record eats eggs.

By Saturday, Swerdlow’s post had close to two million views and roughly 9,600 likes. Musk’s reply, posted around 13 hours later, had about 1.9 million views and more than 99,000 likes, about ten times the approval for far fewer words. Most headlines about the exchange led with Musk. Altman, Pichai and Amodei had not responded publicly in the coverage so far.

Musk’s own breakfast claims have shifted before. In 2023 he replied to XPRIZE chief Peter Diamandis, who had posted that sugar is poison, by writing that he eats a donut every morning and is still alive. Insider noted at the time that he had told Joe Rogan he would rather eat tasty food and live a shorter life. The article says habits change, and that Musk tends to answer such subjects with a short, contrarian line casting him as the unfussy outlier. It adds that the next list of what AI’s leaders have in common will likely get the same treatment.

Articles.Title: Elon Musk Answers Vegetarian AI CEOs OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei With Steak and Eggs

stories.Headline: Speeding up planning decisions with AI
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind announced on October 31, 2026, that its AI planning tool PlanAssist will be made available to an additional 12 local planning authorities across England. The tool was developed by Google DeepMind with the UK government, Google Cloud, and Faculty. It has been piloted since June across Barnet, Camden, and Dorset councils. In early pilot testing, PlanAssist cut the average time a planning officer spent on householder assessment tasks by up to 58%.

PlanAssist handles routine householder applications, which account for up to 70% of planning officers' workloads. It validates application documents and architectural drawings, checks applications against heritage constraints such as tree preservation orders, and checks local and national planning policies and any previous objections. It then drafts fully cited reports that officers can edit before a final decision. More than 70% of the reports it generated were approved by officers with no edits required.

Planning officers retain the final say on every application, and the tool is designed to support human judgement. The announcement said planning bottlenecks have real costs, slowing progress toward the UK government's goal of building 1.5 million new homes by 2029 and leaving families waiting months for approvals like loft conversions, conservatories, or extensions. The announcement described providing access to these new councils as the natural next step. It also said the company looks forward to continuing to support the UK government as it seeks to build more homes and unlock economic growth.

PlanAssist is now moving into a 12-month Beta phase using live applications, starting with a subset of councils. Twelve more councils will be onboarded in three cohorts, bringing the total involved to 15, including metropolitan and rural districts across the country. Subject to successful testing, the government plans for the tool to be made available to all councils in England in 2027. Every assessment will be reviewed and approved by a qualified planning officer before any decision is made.

Articles.Title: Speeding up planning decisions with AI

stories.Headline: Is this real, or is it AI? - The Mountain-Ear
stories.Summary:
The Mountain-Ear reported last week that the National Newspaper Association had passed along word from Meta. Meta had revised its proposed commercial terms, narrowing the provision to advertising and business products, for its collection of material from its platforms to train its products. The article says this implies Meta has so far been taking everything posted on its platforms to improve its AI. It adds that if you posted it on a Meta platform, the company can use it to train its AI programs with no acknowledgement or compensation.

The article names Meta's platforms as Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp, Threads and Meta AI. It says AI has so far consumed most of the printed universe and that AI can lie, though it is more likely to produce untruths by accident. It notes that video used to be treated as a true record of an event, but with AI so dominant it is hard to know what is true online. It also says this election season is the most volatile and angry in the writer's lifetime, and that many AI-created campaign ads and posts are undoubtedly appearing.

The piece is by Lynn Hirshman, writing from Nederland, and was posted on Saturday, October 31, 2026 at 11:15 am. She writes that the news leaves journalism in a tenuous and awkward position. She asks how anyone can be sure what they publish is accurate unless they have seen it in person, and how readers can be sure what they see online or on TV is real. She offers no answers, only questions and deeply uneasy feelings.

The article gives no further steps by Meta or the National Newspaper Association. It does not say what happens next or when any change takes effect. The full item sits behind a subscriber wall at themtnear.com, which asks readers to confirm a subscription, log in or subscribe. The page also lists a phone number, 303-810-5409, and an email address for questions.

Articles.Title: Is this real, or is it AI? - The Mountain-Ear

stories.Headline: The MFCR Congrats Drs.Taube and Szalay on AstroPath’s Selection for Anthropic’s AI for Science Program
stories.Summary:
The Mark Foundation for Cancer Research announced on X on October 31, 2026, that the AstroPath platform was selected for Anthropic's AI for Science program. The foundation congratulated Janis Taube and Alexander Szalay of its Center for Advanced Genomics and Imaging at the Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Cancer Center. AstroPath uses celestial mapping tools for cancer imaging. The post was shared by the foundation and reported by OncoDaily. The selection places AstroPath in Anthropic's AI for Science program, which the article says expands to foundations and research institutions.

The article gives no further details on what the program provides or requires. It also gives no numbers beyond the date of October 31, 2026. The names in the article are Janis Taube, Alexander Szalay, the Mark Foundation for Cancer Research, Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Cancer Center, AstroPath and Anthropic. The Mark Foundation for Cancer Research is credited with the announcement, which it made in a post on X. In that post the foundation congratulated Taube and Szalay and described AstroPath as using celestial mapping tools for cancer imaging. The article does not include any further statements from the foundation, from Taube or Szalay, or from Anthropic.

It also does not say who at Anthropic made the selection. The article provides context on the program only briefly, saying AI for Science expands to foundations and research institutions. It links to a separate item about eight community members elected to the National Academy of Medicine. The article does not say what happens next for AstroPath or when the program work begins. It also gives no timeline beyond the October 31, 2026 post.

Articles.Title: The MFCR Congrats Drs.Taube and Szalay on AstroPath’s Selection for Anthropic’s AI for Science Program

stories.Headline: Anthropic's next big AI business is life sciences, from biotech research to drug discovery
stories.Summary:
Anthropic filed its S-1 ahead of an initial public offering planned for next month, and the document presents life sciences as a major part of its future business. The filing says AI could rapidly accelerate scientific innovation and bring cures for major diseases within reach. It also lists biological progress first among the ways the company hopes AI will improve lives. Anthropic declined to comment to Business Insider.

The filing says nine of the 10 largest pharmaceutical companies and eight of the 10 largest healthcare companies in the Fortune 500 spent at least $100,000 with Anthropic over a recent yearlong period. It states that annual global pharmaceutical spend is expected to exceed $2 trillion in 2026, with Claude used in drug discovery and development by customers, biotech partners and the company's own researchers. Anthropic's Claude Science product, in beta, came out in June. The company started a molecular biology lab in the Bay Area this year and spent $400 million in stock in April to buy the biotech startup Coefficient Bio. In August it announced a robotics standard that lets AI control lab equipment.

Vas Narasimhan, CEO of Novartis, joined Anthropic's board in April. CEO Dario Amodei, a former theoretical physicist, has repeatedly cited life sciences as a reason to advance AI, writing that biology is probably the area where scientific progress has the greatest potential to improve human life. He said he hopes AI-enabled research will help prevent and treat all infectious diseases, eliminate most cancers and double the human lifespan. Ben Mann, co-leader of Anthropic's Labs organization, said his team has shifted focus from standard software engineering toward what Amodei has described as curing all diseases.

The filing also says the drug company Lilly, valued at $1.3 trillion, has 50,000 employees with access to a Claude enterprise account, and that more than 85% of its staff actively use the tool. Anthropic's careers page shows hiring for life sciences roles across chemistry, experimental biology and research engineering, with two roles opened late this week offering $320,000 salaries to researchers who can design and manufacture antibodies. Anthropic published August survey results finding that 91% of its staff think AI will make a Nobel-level discovery by 2030, compared with 39% of US adults. The article notes that no AI-designed drugs have ever received FDA approval, and that OpenAI offers a competing product called Rosalind while Google spinoff Isomorphic Labs plans to use AI to create cancer drugs.

Articles.Title: Anthropic's next big AI business is life sciences, from biotech research to drug discovery

stories.Headline: VideoLVR: Latent Visual Reasoning over Grounded Video Evidence
stories.Summary:
Shilong Li, Xingyuan Bu, Hao Shi, Yun Xing, Weixin Feng, Qiangpeng Yang and Shilei Wen posted a paper titled VideoLVR: Latent Visual Reasoning over Grounded Video Evidence to the arXiv repository on 1 November 2026. The work addresses a problem in video understanding by multimodal large language models, where language-based reasoning traces do not give the model a reliable way to revisit relevant visual evidence. This leads to visual forgetting and weakens the model's ability to reason over video content. The authors list the paper under Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition and Artificial Intelligence.

The paper says existing methods keep visual grounding during reasoning in two main ways. One way refers to evidence using textual coordinates, which give symbolic locations rather than the visual content itself. The other reinserts cropped regions or frames into the multimodal context, which keeps visual details but expands the context substantially. VideoLVR instead builds latent visual evidence from local regions at relevant video moments, giving visual support for intermediate reasoning steps. The authors add a visual token prediction objective that treats visual token reconstruction as prediction over a vocabulary derived from the input video, so visual evidence reconstruction and text generation share one token prediction framework.

The authors say this shared framework lets the models reason over interleaved text tokens and latent visual states while integrating evidence from different moments. They also extend VideoLVR to reinforcement learning by treating sampled visual tokens as actions alongside text tokens and jointly optimizing the policy using final-answer rewards. According to the abstract, VideoLVR improves video understanding without substantially expanding the multimodal context by efficiently revisiting task-relevant visual information during reasoning. The authors report experiments on multiple video benchmarks showing the method is effective, especially on tasks that require fine-grained visual evidence.

The paper is listed under Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition and Artificial Intelligence, and the arXiv page offers a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source. The page also describes arXivLabs, a framework that lets collaborators develop and share features directly on the arXiv website. It says individuals and organizations working with arXivLabs have accepted values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy, and that arXiv works only with partners who adhere to them. The page invites ideas for projects that would add value for the arXiv community.

Articles.Title: VideoLVR: Latent Visual Reasoning over Grounded Video Evidence

stories.Headline: ADTGuard: Adaptive Depth-Time Safeguard for Streaming Inference in Large Language Models
stories.Summary:
Chuming Wei, Churui Yang, Zihan Zhang, Ruien Li, Wusheng Zhang, Yan Zhang and Guangwen Yang posted a paper on arXiv on 1 November 2026 describing a safeguard for streaming inference in large language models. The paper says large language models can produce fluent answers to many user requests, but streaming can expose users to harmful content before generation finishes. It says existing guardrails have two weaknesses in this setting. One is that moderation at response or chunk boundaries comes too late, so harmful material may be seen before it is checked.

The paper introduces ADTGuard, which checks each token before it is released, refines token-level training targets step by step, and adapts layer selection to the current prefix. It models risk across depth and time through Depth-Time Safety Dynamics, which combines safety evidence across layers at each token and uses it to guide risk accumulation over successive tokens. A Causal Depth Router adapts the choice of observation layers to the current prefix. With only response-level labels available, Risk-Onset Target Refinement progressively builds token-level training targets for both components. The authors report experiments across multiple safety benchmarks in which ADTGuard matched or surpassed state-of-the-art safeguards while requiring only 16M trainable parameters and keeping competitive per-token latency.

The authors are responsible for the work, and the paper presents their findings in its own words. They say existing post-hoc moderation delays intervention and risks harmful exposure when content is released before verification. They also say coarse response-level supervision does not specify when harmful content begins, and fixed-layer readouts may miss relevant safety signals at other depths. They describe their experiments as extensive and say the method consistently achieves strong streaming detection performance.

The paper is listed on arXiv with the identifier 2610.36574 and is dated 1 November 2026. It appears under the title ADTGuard: Adaptive Depth-Time Safeguard for Streaming Inference in Large Language Models, with a PDF and other formats offered. The listing also includes standard arXivLabs text about collaborators and shared values. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the paper's publication.

Articles.Title: ADTGuard: Adaptive Depth-Time Safeguard for Streaming Inference in Large Language Models

stories.Headline: CoS-VQ: Coordinated Shared-Scale Vector Quantization for Large Language Models
stories.Summary:
Zukang Xu, Zhixiong Zhao, Xing Hu, Zhe Jiang, Xin Si and Dawei Yang posted a paper titled CoS-VQ: Coordinated Shared-Scale Vector Quantization for Large Language Models to arXiv on November 1, 2026. The paper proposes a method for low-bit weight quantization of large language models, which need substantial memory. The authors say existing vector quantization methods often improve accuracy by increasing the effective coding dimension, which can complicate independent lookup and local codeword updates. CoS-VQ instead keeps low-dimensional codewords while jointly optimizing hard indices and their shared scale across positions. The method addresses what the authors call scale-induced coupling, where the best scale depends on the whole codeword combination and in turn changes candidate rankings across positions.

CoS-VQ collects candidates at multiple probe scales and builds a tangent separable upper bound for the residual-aware quadratic objective. By reducing candidate comparisons to lower envelopes of lines over positive scales, it finds finitely many representative intervals for joint index and scale updates without listing every codeword combination. On Qwen3.8-27B, the authors report that CoS-VQ outperforms QTIP and LLVQ on the evaluated language modeling, coding and reasoning benchmarks. The authors say ablations from the same initialization show larger gains from joint updates than from scale-only refinement. They present joint selection as an alternative to increasing codeword dimensionality.

The paper lists six authors, and the abstract says the code is available at a URL given there. The posting appears on arXiv under identifier 2610.37336. The abstract does not say what happens next beyond the release of the paper and the code. It gives no further plans for the work.

Articles.Title: CoS-VQ: Coordinated Shared-Scale Vector Quantization for Large Language Models

stories.Headline: Claude Smart Reports 2026: What Your AI Spend Really Buys
stories.Summary:
Anthropic launched three tools for Claude Enterprise customers on October 28, 2026. The main tool is Claude smart reports, which shows managers what their teams do with Claude and what it costs. The other two tools are in-app surveys and pooled group budgets. The launch came two days after Anthropic filed to go public on October 26.

Smart reports let a manager pick a team, a date range of up to the last 28 days, and which Claude products to include, such as chat, Claude Code or Claude Cowork. Claude then reviews a sample of the team's transcripts and groups the work into workstreams, showing spend, output and problems like a missing connector or a failed tool call. Each report ends with a list of recommendations, and managers can ask custom questions and save them as templates. Pooled budgets give a whole team one shared monthly budget, with individual limits as a backstop, and billing admins get email alerts at 50%, 75%, 95% and 100% of the budget. Organisations get up to 10 free smart reports a month, then pay extra fees.

Anthropic says smart reports are not for evaluating individual performance or making employment decisions. John Jannone, an AI enablement lead at DoorDash, said in the announcement that the reports still surfaced things he did not know. Anthropic also said admins with billing permission can raise a spend limit straight from a report if it is holding someone back. The article notes that Claude is grading Claude, since the analysis runs on Anthropic's own model reviewing work done with its own product.

Jellyfish, which tracks AI use across more than 1,300 companies and 294,000 engineers, found the median AI spend per engineer grew 3.8 times between the first and third quarters of 2026, while headcount stayed at 98% of first-quarter levels. Anthropic's filing reported about 900% net revenue retention and about 250 customers spending $10 million or more a year, and it warned that a big drop in spending by its largest customers could hurt the business. OpenAI launched usage analytics and spend controls on June 18, 2026, and Anthropic added spend alerts and cost dashboards on July 2, 2026. The reports measure activity and cost, not revenue, so the article says proving a return still takes a company's own numbers.

Articles.Title: Claude Smart Reports 2026: What Your AI Spend Really Buys

stories.Headline: Empowering Breast Cancer Precision Diagnosis with Advanced Ultrasound: From Radiomics to Radio-multiomics
stories.Summary:
A review article on advanced ultrasound for breast cancer diagnosis was published on November 1, 2026, according to the DOI listing. The authors are Mo Li, Letian Jin, Ge Xue, Jiye Chen, Mohamed Aimene Benariba, Vicky Yang Wang, Gaojun Teng and Dong Xu. They are affiliated with institutions in Hangzhou, Quzhou, Taizhou and Wenling in Zhejiang, China, and with Southeast University in Nanjing, Jiangsu, China. The corresponding author is Dong Xu, listed with the Department of Diagnostic Ultrasound Imaging and Interventional Therapy at Zhejiang Cancer Hospital and the Hangzhou Institute of Medicine, Chinese Academy of Sciences. The article appears on the SciOpen platform, and a note says the content was generated by AMiner AI, with SciOpen taking no responsibility for it.

The review covers multi-modal ultrasound imaging, including microvascular and super-resolution imaging with contrast enhancement, elastography and viscoelastic imaging. It also covers quantitative analysis through radiofrequency signal analysis, radiomics and artificial intelligence-based image analysis. The authors describe uses in telling benign from malignant tumors, characterizing molecular subtypes and assessing lymph node metastasis. They trace a path from radiomics alone through radiogenomics to radio-multiomics, which combines ultrasound radiomics with genomic, transcriptomic and other multi-omics data. The article states that most radio-multiomics approaches remain at a preclinical or proof-of-concept stage.

The authors say breast cancer has substantial biological and molecular heterogeneity that conventional imaging and biopsy cannot fully capture, since biopsy is limited by sampling error and invasiveness. They write that ultrasound has moved from morphological imaging only to multi-dimensional functional imaging with quantitative analysis, improving diagnostic accessibility and efficiency. They describe radio-multiomics as a promising strategy for non-invasive molecular phenotyping, though its clinical application is still at its infancy. They also say such approaches still require validation in large-scale paired cohorts.

The review lists standardization, reproducibility, interpretability and data heterogeneity as issues that remain to be resolved. It discusses current challenges that should be addressed before ultrasound-based radio-multi-omics can be translated into a viable clinical tool. The article is open access under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license. No abstract is available for the article, and the page offers a button to view the PDF directly.

Articles.Title: Empowering Breast Cancer Precision Diagnosis with Advanced Ultrasound: From Radiomics to Radio-multiomics

stories.Headline: Hybridizing expert descriptors and learned embeddings yields transferable Mat2Vec-* element representations
stories.Summary:
Researchers reported a method for combining handcrafted chemical descriptors with learned element embeddings to produce reusable element representations called Mat2Vec-*. The work was published in Communications Chemistry on November 1, 2026, with a listed author group including Qiong Feng, Haotian Chen, Yuhang Wang and Tao Yang. The team trained controlled models on eight structure-based MatBench regression tasks, running 2,240 models across representation mixtures and latent dimensions. They used two crystal-graph backbones, CGCNN and MEGNet, and distilled the top-performing models into rotation-invariant cosine-distance relations. The distilled tables come in three forms, Mat2Vec-S from the hybrid, plus single-channel variants Mat2Vec-H and Mat2Vec-L. In the composition-only CrabNet model, the tables replaced or augmented corpus-derived Mat2Vec, and most configurations improved performance across all four MatBench composition tasks.

On the Matbench Discovery WBM benchmark, Mat2Vec-* features reduced errors for several modern structure-based predictors through lightweight residual correction. The authors describe the result as a compact, transferable supervised chemical prior for materials prediction. The authors said handcrafted and supervised representations encode complementary chemical information, and that supervised element geometry can be distilled into reusable tables. They noted that the additive fusion operation alone is not their contribution, and that fusion instead exposes a stable element-element relational geometry. They reported that hybrid inputs outperformed single-source endpoints across the controlled grid and that the learned and descriptor-derived channels stayed weakly entangled.

They used CGCNN and MEGNet as controlled testbeds rather than state-of-the-art predictors, and they evaluated the tables in two transfer regimes not used for distillation to avoid data leakage. The work frames element representations as a shared but often under-examined part of materials machine learning, sitting between discrete element identities and continuous vectors. The authors said the three usual approaches, handcrafted descriptors, corpus-derived embeddings and supervised embeddings, are typically treated as separate choices rather than complementary sources. They asked whether stable element relations from supervised prediction can be reused beyond the models that produced them. The article does not say what happens next beyond describing the transfer tests and the released table family.

Articles.Title: Hybridizing expert descriptors and learned embeddings yields transferable Mat2Vec-* element representations

stories.Headline: US Midterms 2026: Affordability, Artificial Intelligence And Iran War Top Voters’ Concerns Ahead Of November Poll; Other Key Issues Shaping How Americans Will Vote - The Sunday Guardian
stories.Summary:
Americans vote in the midterms on November 3, and they are judging the election mainly on affordability, with the war with Iran and the rapid growth of artificial intelligence also shaping their choices. A Gallup survey of 1,200 adults, conducted by telephone between 1 and 19 October, found that half of registered voters called the economy and healthcare extremely important to their vote for Congress. Iran came next at 47 per cent, and Gallup included the Iran conflict and the construction of artificial intelligence data centres in its midterm list for the first time. Gallup also found that Democrats place greater urgency on most issues than Republicans, and that no issue among the 11 tested was rated extremely important by a majority of Republicans. Crime was the clearest exception, with 43 per cent of Republicans rating it extremely important compared with 32 per cent of Democrats.

An Economist/YouGov poll in October found a plurality of respondents named inflation as the issue that mattered most to them, and the rise in the price of petrol, home heating oil and diesel linked to the conflict with Iran has added to those pressures. A Reuters/Ipsos poll in mid-October found that 34 per cent of respondents approved of the US strikes on Iran, while 54 per cent said the war had not been worth fighting. A Fox News poll found that nearly nine in ten voters expect AI to change how they live in the next few years, with 53 per cent saying the change would be significant, and eight in ten said they were extremely or very concerned that AI was eroding trust in what people see and hear in the news and on social media. A Bloomberg US report published last week described American voters as deeply dissatisfied with the country's direction and listed inflation, healthcare costs, data centres, immigration and government corruption among the leading concerns.

A 30-year-old machine operator from Bogalusa, Louisiana, who voted for Trump in 2024, told The Guardian the war was an evil war against Iran which must end, reflecting wider unease within parts of the Republican coalition about foreign military action. A 23-year-old business school graduate in Houston linked the affordability crisis to the administration's trade policy, describing Trump's idiotic tariff scheme. The Council on Foreign Relations has argued that foreign policy is feeding directly into household budgets, with the Iran war and trade policy reshaping how voters see the economy. Independents, whose votes often decide close races, rank the economy, healthcare and Iran highest, according to the Gallup survey.

How far the Iran conflict and concerns about AI translate into votes will depend on turnout, the performance of candidates in swing districts and the outcome on election night. Many of those who spoke to the newspaper expressed frustration rather than enthusiasm for either party, and some said they were still undecided while others said a single issue would determine their vote. Worries about data centres, electricity bills and employment are also surfacing, particularly in states where new facilities are planned, and Gallup's decision to include data centres on its list reflects how politically significant the subject has become, although the economic effects remain a matter of debate. For candidates, the message is that prices and healthcare remain powerful themes, but that foreign policy and technology are now competing for the same voters' attention.

Articles.Title: US Midterms 2026: Affordability, Artificial Intelligence And Iran War Top Voters’ Concerns Ahead Of November Poll; Other Key Issues Shaping How Americans Will Vote - The Sunday Guardian

stories.Headline: Britain: Meta accused of using news site content to develop artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Britain’s Competition and Markets Authority opened a formal investigation into Meta, the parent company of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, the UK regulator announced. The investigation concerns new trading terms that could let Meta collect content from news sites and media organizations and use it to develop its services and products, including artificial intelligence technologies. The CMA said this could happen without giving content owners the right to choose how their material is used. The move follows widespread objections from media organizations, publishers and digital content companies.

Meta had planned to amend its terms of service on October 30, then postponed the implementation to November 20 before announcing a suspension of the changes pending consultations with relevant institutions and stakeholders. The CMA said the investigation will examine whether the company holds a dominant position in any relevant market within the UK. It will also investigate whether the proposed terms constitute an abuse of this position or impose unfair commercial conditions on publishers and advertisers. The UK’s media watchdog emphasized that the investigation does not yet constitute proof of wrongdoing by the company.

Meta rejected the justifications for opening the investigation, asserting that there were no grounds for taking competitive action against it. It pointed out that it had committed to not changing its terms without consulting publishers and other stakeholders.
