stories.Headline: Researchers are paid $5K for reporting a bug to OpenAI that would let attackers run code in logged-in sessions of all who opened the hacker's ChatGPT share link (Swati Khandelwal/The Hacker News)
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the security firm Parameter showed that a malicious ChatGPT share link could run an attacker's code in the logged-in session of anyone who opened it, letting them read private conversations. The researchers reported the flaw through OpenAI's bug bounty program on October 18, and OpenAI fixed it eight days later and rated it P1, its most serious category. The trap was an ordinary ChatGPT conversation shared through its public link, which could be sent by email, chat message, support ticket, or social post. The victim did not have to install anything, join a workspace, or sign in through the attacker. In the most reliable version, they opened the link and clicked ChatGPT's Preview button once, and in a later version the page opened Preview on its own.

Once the link opened, the attacker's code ran inside the victim's signed-in session with the same access as the real ChatGPT site. It listed the victim's recent conversations, opened a private chat that had never been shared with the attacker, and sent a small portion of it to a server the researchers controlled. The code called ChatGPT's own signed-in APIs directly rather than copying what was on the screen, and because it ran with the victim's full web access, its reach was not limited to those chats. The researchers wrote that they could essentially perform any action on behalf of the victim's ChatGPT account. The work was a controlled test, Parameter reported no real-world use of the flaw, and it ran its private-chat proof between separate accounts rather than against real users.

According to Parameter, the chain began with ChatGPT's Preview feature, which turns a block of HTML in a chat into a small web page. That page ran in a locked-down frame on a separate web address, and that sandbox held. The way in came from a second feature in the same conversation: an interactive graph that loaded a math library called MathLive into the main ChatGPT page, leaving a listener that accepted messages about its on-screen keyboard. Parameter found that this listener accepted a keyboard message from any sender and that the message could carry raw HTML, so the Preview could reach across the boundary and hand attacker HTML to the trusted main page. That HTML built a new frame the browser treated as part of chatgpt.com, and a script loaded from YouTube then supplied the code that ran inside it, because ChatGPT's content security policy blocked inline code but allowed scripts from YouTube.

Parameter said OpenAI reproduced both the code execution and the private-chat proof, raised the severity from P2 to P1, and rolled a fix across two versions of ChatGPT's web frontend. By October 26, both versions rejected the messages the attack relied on. Parameter published its writeup on October 28, after the fix, and OpenAI paid a total of $5,000 for the report. ChatGPT users do not need to do anything, because the fix is on OpenAI's side with nothing to install or reset.

Articles.Title: Researchers are paid $5K for reporting a bug to OpenAI that would let attackers run code in logged-in sessions of all who opened the hacker's ChatGPT share link (Swati Khandelwal/The Hacker News)

stories.Headline: Quad Pledges $85M for AI but Calls It ‘Super Intelligence’
stories.Summary:
The foreign ministers of the United States, Australia, India and Japan met in Atlanta on 31 October and said they intend to provide over $85 million of technical and financial assistance to support access to trusted Super Intelligence across the Indo-Pacific, according to a joint press release the State Department published after the meeting. The release uses the term SI eight times, including once in a subheading, and does not use AI at all. A footnote says that in Australia, India and Japan, Super Intelligence refers to artificial intelligence. President Donald Trump had signed Executive Order 14434 on 29 September, telling agencies to use Super Intelligence and SI in place of Artificial Intelligence and AI, and the SEC switched its examination priorities to SI on 23 October.

The release says the money is to flow in part through the Quad SI Accelerator, but it does not say how the $85 million is split among the four governments, which countries receive it, or over what period it is spent. The ministers said they will launch a new effort to identify semiconductor and SI supply chain chokepoints before they cause disruptions, with no money attached to that effort. They also committed to identifying priority countries for trusted 5G, 6G and Open RAN projects and to exploring future cooperation on SI RAN. The release welcomed a US commitment of $10 million to promote infrastructure and facilities in India and ASEAN countries that recover critical minerals from waste, and it announced the first-ever Quad Business Leaders' Forum, with Quad export credit agencies to convene in Tokyo on 18 November. It also restated concern about economic coercion, including through arbitrary export restrictions.

The pledge was issued in the names of all four ministers, 32 days after the executive order by the outlet's arithmetic, and the outlet describes it as the first document it has seen in which allied governments adopt the term, with the footnote translating it back for three of them. The release does not break the $85 million down by country, recipient or year, does not say what the Quad SI Accelerator funds, and does not name the chokepoints to be reviewed. By the outlet's arithmetic, the $85 million is 8.5 times the $10 million critical-minerals commitment in the same release and about 3% of the $2.6 billion in cash Aramco is contributing to the Saudi AI company HUMAIN in 2026. The outlet says it did not contact the four governments.

Articles.Title: Quad Pledges $85M for AI but Calls It ‘Super Intelligence’ - FourWeekMBA

stories.Headline: US or China? Why Kazakhstan refuses to pick sides as it eyes AI revolution
stories.Summary:
Kazakhstan is refusing to choose between the United States and China as it builds an artificial intelligence economy, according to the South China Morning Post. The report was published on 1 November 2026 and was written by Ben Jiang in Astana, the Kazakh capital. Jiang described driving along the city's wide boulevards and seeing signs of China's growing commercial footprint everywhere. He noted that Chinese cars from brands such as BYD and Changan were becoming a common sight, in a market once dominated by South Korea's Hyundai and Kia. His driver picked him up from the airport in a Changan electric vehicle.

The article says Kazakhstan is like other middle powers striving to build a new AI economy. It describes the Central Asian nation as trying to bridge a widening technology divide between the US and China. The report says the trip to the energy-rich region was prompted not by Chinese tech but by an American giant. The article does not name that company or give further details on the AI plans. It also gives no figures for investment or timelines.

The article attributes the observations about Chinese cars to the driver who collected Jiang from the airport. It does not record any statement from a Kazakh government official or from either of the two countries. No named person is quoted on the policy of not picking sides. Responsibility for the AI push is not assigned to a specific agency or minister in the text. The piece presents the balancing act as the country's approach rather than as a decision by an identified individual.

The context given is that Kazakhstan sits between the US and China as their technology competition widens. The article frames the country as one of several middle powers seeking a new AI economy while staying on good terms with both sides. It does not say what agreements, funding or projects are involved. The report also does not set out what happens next or any scheduled talks. It ends without stating future steps.

Articles.Title: US or China? Why Kazakhstan refuses to pick sides as it eyes AI revolution

stories.Headline: Editor’s Note | AI Is No Savior
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the company behind the Claude large-language model, filed its S-1 form this week, the first step toward becoming a public company. The filing lays out what the company is, the current state of its finances, and the risk factors investors should weigh before funding it. The Mississippi Free Press published an editor’s note about the filing on Oct. 30, 2026. The piece was written by an editor who describes Metallica’s “Spit Out the Bone” as a favorite song and says the track now lands differently.

The filing lists risk factors that come from people in the industry itself, including the potential for AI to destroy humanity. It states that concerns have been raised within the organization and by other researchers, regulators, policymakers, and industry participants. Those concerns hold that sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity. That could happen, the filing says, if such systems are not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures.

The editor is responsible for the note and frames the filing as a warning rather than a routine business step. The editor writes that the industry’s pioneers want to make AI integral to all of our lives quickly. The note compares the scenario to Skynet from “The Terminator” franchise and Ultron from Marvel Comics. The editor concludes that giving the industry carte blanche to integrate into our lives might not be the wisest move.

The article ties the filing to a New York City Council hearing on artificial-intelligence safety held on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. A photographer at the hearing stood next to a display listing AI security incidents, according to the caption. The note also mentions Metallica’s 10th album, “Hardwired…to Self-Destruct,” released 10 years ago. The articles do not say what happens next with the S-1 filing or the hearing.

Articles.Title: Editor’s Note | AI Is No Savior - Mississippi Free Press

stories.Headline: UMSL program helps St. Louis-area educators prepare students for AI-driven future
stories.Summary:
The University of Missouri, St. Louis has launched a program to help K-12 educators in the St. Louis region use artificial intelligence effectively and prepare students for a rapidly changing world. The effort is called Fundamentals of AI for Educators, a 12-hour course offered at no cost through UMSL's Advanced Workforce Center. It is available nationwide, and the Fox 2 story about it was posted on October 30, 2026. The course is aimed at teachers who need to guide students on using AI appropriately.

The program carries no fee and takes 12 hours to complete, and it is open to educators across the country, not just in St. Louis. Megan Valles, a library media specialist for the Lindbergh School District, said she had just finished the course. She said teachers have to stay on top of what is happening, how it is changing and how to support students in the right way, calling it an ongoing marathon. Colin Davitt, Lindbergh's Director of AI and Blended Learning, said AI is here forever and the question is how to work with it.

Davitt said the goal is to teach students what to do and what not to do and how to use the tool effectively. AJ Segel with Scale AI said the program was developed by educators who understand what actually happens in the classroom. St. Louis-area Congressman Wesley Bell said the future is right now, not tomorrow. He said young people must be prepared for the jobs and technology of the future because it will either happen with us or happen to us.

Organizers and educators at the event believe the program can make a major impact in classrooms in St. Louis and across the country. Lindbergh educators involved say AI is already part of students' lives, and society cannot afford to ignore it. The articles do not say how many educators have enrolled or when the course next runs. For more information, the Fox 2 story directs readers to UMSL's program.

Articles.Title: UMSL program helps St. Louis-area educators prepare students for AI-driven future - FOX 2

stories.Headline: Weekly Take: AI is exposing copyright’s limits, but games companies can fight back - Managing Intellectual Property
stories.Summary:
Simon Hembt of Bird & Bird said in a Managing IP weekly take published on 30 October 2026 that AI can exploit longstanding gaps in copyright protection at remarkable speed. The article states that EU law still provides tools for games companies to fight back. The piece is exclusive to subscribers, so the full argument is not available in the supplied text. The article appears under the headline about AI exposing copyright's limits.

The article gives no further numbers, dates or names beyond the author, his firm, the publication date and the reference to EU law. It says AI can exploit gaps in copyright protection quickly, and that EU law offers tools in response. It does not set out what those tools require or what changes they would bring. The rest of the page is a list of other items, including Masimo's judgment past $818 million, IP Service World 2026 in Munich from 23 to 25 November with 1,400-plus attendees from 55-plus nations, 100-plus speakers and 100-plus exhibitors, and other firm news.

The article attributes the view to Simon Hembt at Bird & Bird, who says AI can exploit copyright's gaps at speed while EU law still gives games companies ways to respond. No other responsible parties or statements are given in the supplied text. The page does not paraphrase further comments from him. It also does not say what action he recommends.

The context the article offers is that copyright protection has longstanding gaps that AI can now exploit quickly. It says EU law remains a source of tools for games companies. The supplied text does not say what happens next. More to follow.

stories.Headline: AI is stealing Indigenous Australian art and churning out ‘Temu slop’, artist says
stories.Summary:
Pitjantjatjara artist Sally Scales said AI is taking First Nations art and turning it into what she called cheap, low-quality goods, in comments reported on 1 November 2026. Scales chairs the National Gallery of Australia's First Nations advisory group. She said the technology undermines the agency of First Nations artists and the authenticity of their work, and amounts to a theft of cultural knowledge. She said AI has altered work, removed names and then sold it, which the peak body for Australian visual artists said causes cultural and economic harm. Searches on sites including Temu, Shein and Amazon show countless works described as Aboriginal paintings, plus items such as coasters and stubby holders with Aboriginal-style designs, mostly without attribution to any artist.

The articles say AI has already been trained without compensation on works by well known Australian artists including Kylie Minogue and Nick Cave. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has vowed to protect Australian creatives from copyright theft, and Attorney General Michelle Rowland has said there are no plans to weaken copyright protections. Prof Kathy Bowrey, an intellectual property specialist from UNSW Law, said one in five creators already had problems with copyright infringement without AI, and that the issues become more complex when the creators are First Nations people. She described an organisation paying to use artwork or images of Aboriginal people and later using AI to update or repurpose those images without permission. The National Association for the Visual Arts pointed to work by the Wuthathi and Meriam lawyer Terri Janke, who has documented AI scraping Indigenous art centre websites, removing artists' names and altering their work.

Scales said the name says it all, that it is artificial, and that she has seen works where she wonders whether a First Nations community or person was involved or whether it was something generic whipped up. She said it is a theft of the agency of the artist and rips out the authenticity, because the artist's family lineage and lived experience are not there. Bowrey said a corporate client can pay an artist once and then make unauthorised Aboriginal derivative work and use the faces of the artists without consent, so artists lose repeat business and then compete against an AI when making new work. Nava said Indigenous data sovereignty recognises the right of First Nations peoples to exercise authority over their data, cultural material and knowledge. A spokesperson for the attorney general said Australian creatives are world class and the government is committed to supporting them, and that it is continuing to consult with creators, media organisations and AI companies on options to ensure any future copyright changes deliver meaningful control and fair compensation.

Bowrey and a colleague, creative technologies expert associate professor Oliver Bown, have proposed a Copyright Plus framework. It would force AI companies to disclose their data sources and give artists the right to say no to having their work scraped or mimicked. They also proposed a levy on AI companies to pay creative professionals and establish a cultural fund, and the use of takedown notices for fake content. Bowrey said they wrote the draft policy based on the parameters of what the government has said so far. Nava's submission to the joint select committee inquiry on artificial intelligence said AI-generated Aboriginal-style images can be sold as Indigenous or Indigenous-inspired work, spreading misinformation, causing cultural and economic harm and competing with work by First Nations artists.

Articles.Title: AI is stealing Indigenous Australian art and churning out ‘Temu slop’, artist says - The Guardian

stories.Headline: Everything changed for the oil, AI and bond trades over the past month
stories.Summary:
Over the past month, oil futures rose while treasury yields fell, breaking an 80% correlation between the two that had held through 2026, according to Jeffrey Rosenberg, senior portfolio manager of the Systematic Alternatives ETF at BlackRock. Rosenberg said the change came as the leading artificial intelligence stocks, the Mag 7, declined in October. He pointed to Friday's Nasdaq market wipeout and, earlier in the week, Google's biggest single-day decline in its history, which wiped out half a trillion dollars in value. Rosenberg said the market now treats geopolitical risk as secondary to AI risk.

Rosenberg said bond yields fell because the market reads weakness in the AI trade as weakness in the U.S. economy. He said last week's GDP report backed that view, with business investment up 12.7% in the third quarter, the biggest increase outside the pandemic since 2011, led by a 37% rise in information processing equipment and a nearly 25% rise in industrial equipment investment. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, at Wednesday's FOMC press conference, noted that oil futures have continued to rise, a factor the central bank must weigh in fighting inflation. Warsh disagreed that the economy's strength is only in narrow pockets, saying the capex story is broadening. Rosenberg said any wobble in the AI trade will be seen as a growth wobble and as disinflationary, and that in such an environment only the long end of the treasury curve hedges.

Rosenberg cautioned that this is not a return to normal, where bonds hedged stocks, because oil price increases and inflation above target still challenge fixed income. He said the AI trade is a big piece of the bond market, and Microsoft returned to the public bond market after close to a decade away, a surprise to markets, with its deal oversubscribed. He said hyperscalers are reaching the limits of bank loan and private credit financing, and while a $40 trillion to $60 trillion global bond market can absorb an expected $4 trillion in AI debt over the next four years, its capacity is not unlimited. He said Microsoft credit default swaps trade near a five-year high of roughly 55, compared with Oracle spreads closer to 300, and that public credit markets let investors short the debt, unlike bank loans and private credit.

Articles.Title: Everything changed for the oil, AI and bond trades over the past month - CNBC

stories.Headline: Time to put AI cameras to better use on highways
stories.Summary:
Malaysia has invested in automated traffic enforcement, particularly through cameras that detect speeding and red-light violations, according to a letter published by The Star on Saturday, 31 Oct 2026. The writer, Alex Lee of Seremban, said this is a good start but asked whether the technology is being fully used. He pointed to motorists abusing emergency lanes to beat traffic jams, heavy vehicle drivers ignoring travel restrictions, and groups of irresponsible drivers turning public highways into racing circuits. He said these are not just traffic offences but dangerous behaviours that put innocent lives at risk.

The letter said heavy vehicle restrictions exist to manage traffic flow and improve road safety, particularly during peak hours and festive seasons, yet some drivers and logistics operators take their chances when enforcement officers are not around. It proposed AI-powered CCTV cameras with Automatic Number Plate Recognition at designated heavy vehicle restriction zones, which could identify vehicle types, capture registration numbers and flag violations based on the applicable restriction hours. It said the same approach should apply to emergency lane misuse, provided the system can distinguish genuine emergencies and officially activated SmartLane operations. For illegal racing, it said AI video analytics supported by ANPR and coordinated camera monitoring could help identify suspected racing activities and provide evidence for further investigation, while speeding alone should not be treated as proof of racing.

The letter said AI is not infallible and that there must be proper verification, reliable evidence, privacy safeguards and a fair appeals process before enforcement action is taken. It said roadside enforcement operations, while necessary, can sometimes contribute to congestion when vehicles are stopped along busy roads and highways, and technology could reduce dependence on continuous roadside operations without compromising enforcement. Lee said traffic cameras should not be thought of merely as speed traps and red-light detectors, and asked why Malaysia, which already has an extensive CCTV network and Traffic Management Centres, does not explore upgrading selected infrastructure and integrating it with JPJ, the police and highway concessionaires. He said technology should not just help catch offenders but also help prevent dangerous behaviour in the first place.

Articles.Title: Time to put AI cameras to better use on highways - The Star

stories.Headline: If Democrats Take Both Houses: What It Would Mean for Silicon Valley and the AI Money Loop
stories.Summary:
A scenario analysis published on November 1, 2026, looks at what would happen if Democrats win both chambers of Congress in the election on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. Forecasters and prediction markets lean Democratic in the House and more narrowly in the Senate, with markets putting House control at about 92 to 93 percent and Senate control at about 68 percent. Decision Desk HQ put the figures at 80 percent for the House and 60 percent for the Senate, projecting 52 Democratic Senate seats. Democrats need a net gain of four Senate seats to reach 51, since a 50 to 50 Senate would be broken by a Republican vice president.

A Democratic Congress would still face a Republican president until January 2029, so new legislation would need President Donald Trump's signature unless Congress overrides his veto. It could block Republican legislation, use appropriations, oversight, subpoenas and hearings, set the agenda for 2028, and pass bills that force vetoes, but it could not on its own raise the corporate tax rate, impose a new AI tax, break up a company, or repeal the 2025 tax law. Most major bills would also need 60 Senate votes to clear a filibuster unless Democrats changed Senate rules, a step with no agreed Democratic consensus in the material reviewed. The article describes the realistic outcome as Congress becoming a source of political, regulatory and financing risk for an industry that is already financially stretched.

The article says the AI buildout is no longer funded mainly from cash flow, noting that Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle sold roughly $274 billion of investment-grade bonds in 2026 through late September, versus an average of about $30 billion a year in 2020 to 2024. It describes a loop in which Nvidia invests in frontier AI labs, those labs sign multi-year compute contracts with cloud providers, and those providers buy Nvidia chips and in several cases also hold equity in the same labs. Nvidia alone has invested around $50 billion in frontier labs, and its letter of intent to invest up to $100 billion in OpenAI became a $30 billion equity investment. Remaining performance obligations at Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Oracle reached approximately $2.3 trillion at the end of the second quarter of 2026, up 186 percent in a year, with roughly half owed by OpenAI and Anthropic.

The article lists five ways a Democratic Congress would hit the sector, starting with oversight and investigations before legislation, which it says would change the cost of capital even without changing a contract. It cites the Artificial Intelligence Risk Management and Security Act of 2026 from Senators Mark Warner, Brian Schatz and Andy Kim, a separate framework from Senator Maria Cantwell charging NIST with developing standards, and House Democrats led by Rep. Sam Liccardo urging transparency and evaluation requirements. It also covers more antitrust scrutiny of the loop, the GRID Savings Act from Sen. Martin Heinrich on data-center grid costs, and tax proposals including a stock-buyback excise tax rise from 1 percent to 4 percent, an AI excise tax from Rep. Greg Casar, a 50 percent equity tax from Sen. Bernie Sanders, and a data-center excise tax from Sen. Ron Wyden. The article says Democrats themselves are divided on these ideas and that no comprehensive AI tax had advanced by late September 2026.

The article argues the loop's fate will be decided by revenue rather than by Congress, since Congress cannot directly unwind a $300 billion Oracle, OpenAI contract or a multi-year CoreWeave lease. It says stress is already visible at the weaker links, with Oracle's five-year credit-default-swap spread hitting a record 288 basis points on October 15, 2026, CoreWeave's 2032 bonds trading near 77 cents on the dollar, and Korea's KOSPI falling 8 percent into a bear market. It describes a base case of friction rather than fracture, and says that if OpenAI and Anthropic grow into their commitments the loop deleverages itself and political risk fades. If they do not, the article says a Democratic Congress would be an accelerant to a repricing that was already coming, not its cause.

Articles.Title: If Democrats Take Both Houses: What It Would Mean for Silicon Valley and the AI Money Loop - Social News XYZ

stories.Headline: Companies and organizations are taking notice of Gen-Z frustrations with artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Spotify announced on Oct. 20 that it had removed tens of millions of AI-made "slop and spam tracks" from its recommendations this year, according to Yahoo Entertainment. The company said it aims to put human artistry first and to strengthen AI protections. Spotify also rolled out features on the beta and mobile versions of its app that let users and publishers disclose when parts of a track, or a whole artist profile, are made with artificial intelligence, as noted on its support page. The San Diego Comic-Con, held in July, banned all artwork created by artificial intelligence from its 2026 art show, according to CNET.

In early October 2026, a Cedar Rapids, Iowa, theatre company ended its use of artificial intelligence, as reported by local outlet KCRG. Executive director Matt Ford said the company had used AI in the past for graphic design because of financial limits. He said he began questioning what those savings meant for artists whose work helps bring audiences to a production, and he spoke with the company's graphic designer, Jay Diers, about returning to art made without generative AI and paying him as much as the small company could afford. Ford pledged continued support for playwrights, performers, directors, designers, photographers, musicians, technicians and visual artists.

Dove Beauty states on its website that it is renewing its vow to champion real beauty, with a commitment never to use AI to create or distort images of women. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced a ban on artificial intelligence in New York City schools in kindergarten through eighth grade classrooms, as per Chalkbeat. The city will ban student-facing generative AI tools, like chatbots and tutors that respond to prompts. Chalkbeat explained that the policy could change and is currently only set to run for at least the current academic year, as city officials admitted they have little hard data on how much AI is currently in use across city schools. Mamdani and other city officials have shown commitment to creating a coalition of educators, students, parents, union officials and experts to help assess the policy and how, and whether, it should change.

Boston 25 News reported on Oct. 20, 2026, that many Boston students in college towns have taken part in walkout demonstrations as part of a nationwide protest against the use of AI. Students at LaGuardia High School in Manhattan adopted a similar anti-AI walkout protest in October 2026, as reported by Govtech.com. ScienceDirect has published information that some top AI tools received nearly 3 billion monthly visits in March 2024 alone. The Lamron reports that there may be a new trend of brands and organizations making a commitment against artificial intelligence, and that the demand for this commitment from consumers and young people is noticeable.

Articles.Title: Companies and organizations are taking notice of Gen-Z frustrations with artificial intelligence - The Lamron

stories.Headline: How AI Startups Are Stretching Their Runway With Free Cloud and GPU Credits in 2026
stories.Summary:
AI startups in 2026 are using free cloud and GPU credits from major providers to stretch their runway, according to a TechBullion article published on November 1, 2026. The article describes how almost every major cloud and AI provider now runs some form of startup program. These programs hand out credits worth anywhere from a few hundred dollars to several hundred thousand. Founders who stack them carefully can run for a year or more with close to zero infrastructure spend.

The programs include AWS Activate, which offers up to $100,000 in credits for startups that come through an approved accelerator, incubator or venture partner, with smaller self-serve packages for bootstrapped teams. Google for Startups Cloud Program packages reach up to $350,000 for qualifying AI-first startups, covering Google Cloud, Vertex AI and GPU and TPU instances. Microsoft for Startups offers up to $150,000 in Azure credits for eligible startups, along with access to Azure OpenAI Service. Smaller offers include Oracle's always-free tier, free starting credits from Deepgram for speech-to-text and voice agent APIs, a startup grants program from ElevenLabs, and GitHub programs that include free access to tools like Copilot.

The article says the biggest practical problem with startup credits is discovery, because offers launch, change terms and expire constantly. It recommends curated directories that track AI startup credits, cloud grants and developer perks in one place, and says founders should always confirm final terms on the provider's official page. It lists common mistakes, including letting credits expire, since most come with an expiry window of often 12 or 24 months, building lock-in around free compute, ignoring billing alerts, using unofficial shortcuts, and applying with an incomplete profile. For an early team, it suggests claiming free tiers and small credits first, then applying for the entry tier of one hyperscaler program, then upgrading after joining an accelerator or raising a round.

The article's context is that building an AI product in 2026 is cheaper than three years ago but still far from cheap, and compute can easily become the single largest line item after salaries for a pre-seed team. It says credits act as a buffer while a team is still figuring out pricing, caching and model choice, and that they are not a business model but one of the most effective ways for an AI startup to buy time. It advises reviewing the credit balance monthly and planning for the point where credits run out. The founders who benefit most, it says, treat credits as a planned resource, claimed deliberately, tracked carefully and replaced with sustainable unit economics before they run out.

Articles.Title: How AI Startups Are Stretching Their Runway With Free Cloud and GPU Credits in 2026 - TechBullion

stories.Headline: Fujitsu launches service combining rapid AI-driven incident investigation with expert response support
stories.Summary:
Fujitsu Limited announced on November 1, 2026, the launch in Japan of a new incident response service. The service combines AI-driven rapid threat investigation with support from security experts. It uses a threat analysis AI system powered by frontier AI to run 24/7 forensic investigations. The system traces signs of compromise, assesses damage, and performs threat analysis for malware and suspicious URLs.

The service is a retainer-based offering, and support from Fujitsu's experts for up to a certain number of hours is included in the base fee. Customers can upload suspicious files and device data to a dedicated portal for rapid analysis. Fujitsu can provide investigation reports in as little as one business day for threat analysis and two business days for forensic investigations. If the AI analysis shows widespread impact or the need for emergency intervention, Fujitsu's incident response team steps in to perform triage and log analysis and to propose and implement containment and recovery measures.

Fujitsu said the system performs investigations and analyses traditionally conducted by security experts in a significantly shorter period of time. It said results are verified and complemented by Fujitsu's security experts. The company said this helps ensure investigation reports with findings on signs of compromise, suspicious activities, and recommended countermeasures. Fujitsu said this facilitates rapid decision-making to support business continuity and strengthen overall cybersecurity.

Fujitsu said the rapid evolution of AI has increased the speed of cyberattacks and shrunk the time between an initial breach and significant damage. It said enterprises face pressure not only to prevent attacks but also to respond and recover swiftly. It said forensic investigations and malware analysis often require specialized expertise and can be time-consuming, potentially delaying decision-making. It also said securing cybersecurity professionals and maintaining round-the-clock incident response can be challenging for many organizations.

Fujitsu said it will continue to evolve the service under its Cyber Security Nerve Center framework, integrating AI with cybersecurity expertise. The company said it remains committed to supporting the cyber resilience of its customers. Fujitsu reported consolidated revenues of 3.5 trillion yen, or US$23 billion, for the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026. It has 100,000 employees and remains the top digital services company in Japan by market share.

Articles.Title: Fujitsu launches service combining rapid AI-driven incident investigation with expert response support

stories.Headline: Hitachi unveils a new global digital services company turning cloud, data, and AI into measurable business outcomes: Hitachi Digital
stories.Summary:
Hitachi, Ltd. announced on November 1, 2026 that it plans to launch Hitachi Digital Inc. on April 1, 2027, following an integration plan announced in January 2026. The new company will unite Hitachi's U.S. subsidiaries GlobalLogic Inc. and Hitachi Digital Services LLC under a single company using the Hitachi brand. A brand campaign launched the same day. Hitachi Digital will guide enterprise digital transformation at the convergence of cloud, data, and AI toward concrete business results.

The new company will have approximately 35,000 professionals in 27 countries and more than 880 active clients. It combines product and software engineering with enterprise systems and operational expertise, backed by more than 100 years of Hitachi experience in mission-critical infrastructure. Hitachi Digital will serve key industries with service lines including Physical AI, Data and Intelligence, Cloud and Site Reliability Engineering, and Enterprise Applications. Its work will also fuel IP such as HMAX by Hitachi, a suite of solutions bringing AI to social infrastructure. Hitachi Digital's synergy revenue with the Hitachi Group grew 46 percent year-on-year in the first half.

Anand Birje, CEO and Chairman of Hitachi Digital, said clients need one partner that understands how an industry works, keeps deep technology ecosystem relationships, and engineers what is new while modernizing and running what is underneath. He said Hitachi Digital brings digital engineering and operations together as one company at global scale, with Hitachi's industrial depth behind it. Jun Abe, Executive Vice President and Head of the Digital Systems & Services Sector at Hitachi, said the launch will help Hitachi evolve into a global digital services company providing end-to-end solutions from enterprise AI to physical AI. He said uniting GlobalLogic's digital engineering with Hitachi Digital Services' enterprise and operational expertise, with the Forward Deployed Engineer teams as a driving force, will support clients through business transformation.

ISG Research ranked the two companies as a Leader in Intelligent Robotics and Physical AI Services, Digital Engineering Services, and Generative AI Services. Gowtham Sampath, Assistant Director and Principal Analyst at ISG Research, said the outcomes result from what is now Hitachi Digital's differentiation, a fusion of deep industrial heritage with enterprise grade AI orchestration. Hitachi Digital will accelerate enterprise AI and Physical AI in industries including manufacturing, mobility and energy, and across the Hitachi Group through customer zero initiatives. The company said it will continue to scale through investment in AI, data and cloud talent, including Forward Deployed Engineers, along with expanded alliances and acquisitions.

Articles.Title: Hitachi unveils a new global digital services company turning cloud, data, and AI into measurable business outcomes: Hitachi Digital

stories.Headline: Can enterprise AI pay for the boom?
stories.Summary:
The artificial intelligence buildout is a large bet on what businesses will pay for intelligence, and research this summer argued that productive use by enterprise customers is a key indicator to watch. The research said the risk of a bubble popping rises if infrastructure supply catches up before productive monetization appears. It forecast that supply constraints and healthy funding appetites could allow a soft landing, and it named 2029 as the highest-risk year. The discussion also drew on Michael Burry’s analysis of Anthropic PBC, Apollo research by Torsten Slok, and the history of the personal computer and internet eras.

As of the recording, the Nasdaq was down 937 points after earnings from the big hyperscalers were not well received, with Google’s advertising disappointment and AWS capex spend and negative cash flow named as culprits. Anthropic’s S-1 showed revenue growth of 14x in the first half of 2026 to $16 billion, and the company reported $132 billion in liquid assets, with only Alphabet and Berkshire holding more cash among U.S. nonbanks. Anthropic had raised about $140 billion and burned $10 billion to reach a $32 billion revenue run rate. Burry’s diagram from the S-1 showed $537 billion of multiyear compute commitments across take-or-pay deals, minimum purchase agreements, lease deals and capacity conditioned on delivery.

Crawford Del Prete, former president of IDC and now senior adviser at PSG Equity, said early signs of productivity gains are appearing but not yet in the numbers. He said companies are automating workflows, starting with coding and customer service and moving into other tasks, and that this makes the impact uneven because work is not rewired. He described circular financing as a way to rebuild the stack around the world at the same time, and said demand depends on the customer. He said one customer would take all the capacity it could get from Lenovo, HPE and Dell, while others are matching models to workloads to manage token spend, and he said he is not seeing many customers pull back because competitiveness drives the spending.

Del Prete said there is no software company today that is not investing for AI, and that they must do it to make their product sets competitive. He said everybody is willing to spend and it comes down to the resources they have. He also raised whether a large adjacent platform using AI could absorb a company’s area, and whether customers can vibe code and create software instead of licensing it. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the discussion of these questions.

Articles.Title: Can enterprise AI pay for the boom?

stories.Headline: Texas A&M to open fully automated metallurgy lab, using AI and robotic workers to develop metal alloys
stories.Summary:
Texas A&M University announced a new Aggie AI Foundry, a laboratory created by A&M professors Raymundo Arróyave and Ibrahim Karaman. The College Station-based university said the lab will include a fully automated system to develop metal alloys using artificial intelligence and robotic workers. The announcement was reported on October 31, 2026. The university said this would increase the rate at which metal alloys are developed from months to just days.

According to the university, robots will mix, melt, and test materials using computer-controlled arms along an assembly line. AI could ultimately test as many as a trillion different combinations of periodic elements. The Aggie AI Foundry is supported by the WoodNext Foundation, a philanthropic organization founded by Roku CEO Anthony Wood and his wife Rusan, both of whom are university alumni. The WoodNext Foundation did not return a request for comment.

Arróyave said the move has not been without pushback, and that students, researchers, and others have raised concerns with him that a laboratory relying on artificial intelligence and robots rather than humans would dilute the profession of metallurgy. He said he may sound like one of those tech bros who minimize the impact of their frontier models on the workplace, and he gave his personal experience of learning to polish samples as a grad student at MIT, when his fingertips ended up bloody because his fingers were catching the polishing wheel. He said it was not that fun and he did not learn that much, and that he wished they had an automated polisher back then. He said there are parts that are not that romantic to the work of a researcher, and that an automated system can make it easier.

Arróyave argued that an AI-powered laboratory is like a skip-the-line fast pass at a theme park or getting to the Grand Canyon without having to drive there. He said what they are trying to do is get to the cool, fun part faster, but that is not going to negate the careful, detail-oriented process of investigation that happens once you find a really cool material. Though the lab is automated, students and humans in general will still play a role in the laboratory, and part of the creative vision is to enable students to focus on higher-level research instead of laboratory work. Arróyave called humans fundamental to the process and said they are going to train a new kind of scientist, who has to learn many more things than what they learned when they were students themselves.

Articles.Title: Texas A&M to open fully automated metallurgy lab, using AI and robotic workers to develop metal alloys

stories.Headline: Avenged Sevenfold’s Zacky Vengeance Defends AI Art, Calls Majority of Designers He’s Worked With "Lazy"
stories.Summary:
Avenged Sevenfold guitarist and vocalist Zacky Vengeance defended the band's use of artwork that some fans believe was AI-generated, according to Metal Injection. The dispute arose from the band's annual Misfits tribute, for which they recorded a cover of "Horror Business" for their Deathbats fan club. The artwork chosen to accompany that release drew criticism, and Vengeance responded on social media rather than backing down. The article was published on October 31, 2026, and his comments were posted on October 29, 2026.

Vengeance wrote that he fully embraces AI and that he loves physical art and the talented people who create it, calling himself one of them. He said the majority of designers he has worked with over the past 20 years are lazy and allowed themselves to be replaced through complacency and greed. He said he prefers his prompts and the collective hive mind and efficiency of the future, and added that AI will absolutely kill us all. He also likened the debate to arguments about tools, saying the problem is not the technology but how people choose to use it.

In replies to fans, Vengeance said AI cannot replace artists such as Wes, Cam and Micah, whom he said he deeply values and has long friendships with, but it can replace anyone replaceable. He said he has purchased artwork by someone named Eddie and praises him constantly, so he has put his money where his mouth is in support of real artists. He also criticized people who scream against AI while consenting to terms of service that give away their personal data. The articles do not say what response the band or anyone else gave, or what happens next.

Articles.Title: Avenged Sevenfold’s Zacky Vengeance Defends AI Art, Calls Majority of Designers He’s Worked With "Lazy"

stories.Headline: Azeem Azhar on the Explosion of Hacking and Other AI Issues
stories.Summary:
Azeem Azhar, a writer, researcher and investor with Exponential View, spoke with Paul Krugman about a PHP hack and the wider spread of AI-driven hacking. Azhar said AI models have become good enough to be used in code and directed to find vulnerabilities and bugs in software. Because AI systems are tireless and can be spun up in large numbers, they can find many vulnerabilities quickly and chain them together. He called the PHP hack a "Wuhan moment," comparing it to an infectious disease that has a much bigger impact than others circulating.

PHP is a programming language that 70% of websites run on, Azhar said. It was easy to use and cheap, and it got extended and extended, and Facebook used it a lot, so it became part of the internet's architecture. He said AI models crossed a threshold at the start of this year when Anthropic had a model called Claude Mythos, which he called the best cybersecurity model in the world. It was not made widely available, and only a small number of organizations got access to it. Over the summer, open-weight models started to approach Mythos's capabilities, and there has been a rapid increase in the number of vulnerabilities being discovered.

Azhar said the bad guys move more quickly in general, because they only have to find one vulnerability at one place, while the good guys have to defend every vulnerability all the time. He said the Deputy Chief Information Security Officer at Anthropic said it is going to be quite a rough 18 months. He said there are billions of computers connected to the internet and trillions of lines of code and systems that have not been updated for years. He said things can spread faster than we can figure out what to do about them, as happened with the virus first called 2019-nCoV before it was called SARS-CoV-2.

Azhar said many people already spend a lot of time in walled gardens, and he expects the number of AI agents to rapidly exceed the number of humans. He said the amount of browsing done by bots is now higher than by humans, and that will tilt enormously toward machines over the coming few years. He likened the change to Fifth Avenue in 1895, when more people strolled in the middle of the street than there were automobiles, but by 1920 people did not stroll down the middle of the street. He said the internet would need to start to filter out what AI systems need, because they move in milliseconds and have completely different technical requirements. He said people who want to be really secure might choose to stay in a safe enclave, and he gave Apple's App Store as an example.

Articles.Title: Azeem Azhar on the Explosion of Hacking and Other AI Issues

stories.Headline: Appraisal by AI: Model-driven victim prioritization in the VOLTA infostealer
stories.Summary:
A new Windows infostealer called VOLTA-AUTODOXER was surfaced through the CAIRN research effort, according to a Cisco Talos blog published on October 31, 2026. The malware is self-deleting and has no attacker-owned infrastructure, with all observed endpoints controlled by third parties. After stealing data, it sends a structured evidence bundle to a large language model to rank the victim's assets by monetization value. If a model refuses, it fails over to a chain of up to three models.

The stealer harvests browser passwords, cookies, payment cards, cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases, Discord, Telegram, Steam and Roblox sessions, Microsoft OAuth tokens, SSH and cloud-provider keys, Wi-Fi profiles and screenshots. It builds a bundle containing geolocation, home address, employer, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata and a live Roblox account valuation. It then uses stolen sessions to search Gmail for purchase receipts, pull UberEats and DoorDash order history, and enrich Discord accounts. The bundle is POSTed to OpenRouter under a system prompt asking the model to act as a forensic intelligence analyst, with output sections titled "WHAT THEY'RE WORTH" and "THEIR OPSEC."

The prompt tells the model to go deep, not wide, and to be blunt, specific and accurate. A hardcoded temperature of 0.2 suggests the attacker is emphasizing accuracy and consistency, and the fallback chain runs from Claude to kimi-k2 and then gemini-2.5-flash. The blog says the multi-model design suggests the operator anticipates refusals and pivots to smaller, more permissive models. The system prompt asks for a concise assessment of the victim's suitability as a target, backed by an auditable trail of citations, and encourages connections between sparse data such as names, addresses or universities and patterns in passwords.

Collected data is assembled locally in a file called Identity_Report.txt, serialized as JSON and sent to OpenRouter, with the reply received as AI_Analysis.txt. Both files exfiltrate together in volta_dox.zip, and exfiltration can happen in three stages: volta_log.zip after the stealer runs, volta_dox.zip after the AI call, and volta_doxnet.zip if network enrichment produces anything. The inference round-trip happens through the victim's own network connection on their own machine before the result is exfiltrated. VOLTA uses a template with six swappable slots filled in at build time, which the blog says suggests a builder model where the author sells access and compiles a custom binary for each customer.

Much of the token-stealing relies on bypassing App-Bound Encryption in Chrome, and an application control policy restricting which processes may launch Chrome with --headless would block that decryption path. Users should try to preserve the APPDATA%\volta_debug.txt file, a timestamped harvest log recording what was collected and whether the LLM call succeeded. Compromised tokens should be revoked and passwords changed, and a wallet whose seed phrase was in plaintext on disk should be treated as fully compromised, with funds moved to a new wallet generated on an air-gapped device. The blog says the question for defenders is not whether this pattern will appear elsewhere but which phase it touches next, and that refusal resilience may become a standard design requirement as AI integration in malware matures.

Articles.Title: Appraisal by AI: Model-driven victim prioritization in the VOLTA infostealer

stories.Headline: The AI boom's political reckoning
stories.Summary:
Opposition to AI data centers became a defining issue in the 2026 midterm elections, with data centers serving as a target for public anger. Voters in 10 states will decide on 41 data center ballot measures on Election Day, ranging from new requirements for developers to outright bans on construction. All six data center measures already decided this year, in New Hampshire, Wisconsin, Michigan and California, went against development, according to Ballotpedia. In Texas, incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott reversed course after years of courting the industry, halting new approvals pending an audit of projects after a backlash in rural communities. Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa supports a moratorium on new data centers until tougher rules are established.

In Utah, a coalition of state leaders, local residents and environmental groups opposed a data center project backed by Kevin O'Leary. In Ohio, incumbent Sen. Jon Husted is on the defensive over past support for data centers in a race that could help decide Senate control, and the state has 21 data center-related measures on the ballot Tuesday. Local activists galvanized by data center fights are running for office across the country. President Trump declared at a rally in Ohio that "we want them," forcing the Husted campaign to distance itself from his remarks. Trump said data centers were designed in a "very beautiful way" and called them a "Golden Goose" for the U.S. economy.

Tatishe Nteta, a political science professor at UMass Amherst and director of the UMass Poll, said the backlash reflects tech giants and AI becoming an easy target, and that the country is close to the largest wealth gap in its history. He called it a failure of marketing on the part of the AI companies themselves and said they need to make a clearer, stronger case for why there are benefits for communities. Trump has praised Mark Zuckerberg for Meta's financial contributions to local communities, including $50,000 bonuses for teachers in Louisiana. Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy has called on companies to provide free electricity to residents living near data centers.

Many communities are skeptical of promises of economic revitalization after watching factories open and later abandon their towns and jobs materialize and then disappear, and residents face nondisclosure agreements that limit transparency around new projects. Some companies such as Microsoft have decided to end data center NDAs with local governments, but these efforts could be viewed as the result of public pressure and may be coming a little too late. Candidates caught flat-footed may survive the 2026 midterms with the right talking points, but as the AI industry's infrastructure demands soar and the economic stakes grow with record-breaking IPOs, messaging alone won't cut it. Politicians will increasingly be forced to stake out concrete policy positions and decide whose interests come first.

Articles.Title: The AI boom's political reckoning

stories.Headline: Why unions are split over AI as data centers take off
stories.Summary:
Unions are divided over artificial intelligence and data centers, according to an Axios report published on October 31, 2026 by Nathan Bomey. Trade unions like the electrical workers and plumbers like the construction work that data centers bring. Other groups, including the Teamsters, want policies that restrict AI because it might replace jobs. The split has complicated labor's political alliances as both parties court union voters.

Trade unions have formed a new partnership with OpenAI and the real estate and financial firm Blackstone to fight moratoriums on data center construction. The AFL-CIO is pushing state legislatures to adopt restrictions on AI, including rules to prevent it from surveilling workers and making health care decisions without human oversight. Teamsters president Sean O'Brien is leading a charge to keep robotaxis and autonomous trucks off the streets unless they have a safety operator. The report gives no specific dates, vote counts or other numbers beyond the October 31, 2026 publication date.

Arthur Wheaton, director of labor studies at the Cornell ILR Buffalo Co-Lab, said it has always been a misnomer that labor must agree on everything, and that when one union loses another might gain. He said many unions will support technology if there is training for it and it does not replace jobs, but they want nothing to do with it if it replaces people. UAW president Shawn Fain criticized what he called a corporate narrative that technology should reduce jobs and make more profits, saying it does not have to be that way. Teamsters vice president at-large Peter Finn said labor has a duty to shape how AI is rolled out so it puts people first, and he criticized robotaxis as designed to get rid of the driver. Aurora CEO Chris Urmson told Axios that trucking is a very dangerous job with many health issues and that the Teamsters' effort to thwart self-driving vehicles is misguided.

The report says the advent of self-driving vehicles is a major flashpoint, pitting the Teamsters against Tesla, Waymo, Zoox and the self-driving truck startup Aurora. Autonomous-driving companies argue that too many people die or are injured in vehicle accidents to justify keeping human drivers once the technology is safer. Wheaton said labor is not one identifiable thing and has no single voice. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: Why unions are split over AI as data centers take off

stories.Headline: Spooky New Infostealer Malware Uses AI to ‘Autodox’ Victims
stories.Summary:
Cisco Talos researchers have found a new strain of infostealer malware that adds AI analysis to its theft, according to research shared exclusively with WIRED's Kernel Panic newsletter. The malware calls itself Volta-Autodoxer internally, and the researchers flagged it using their new CAIRN framework, which is built to identify hacking tools that use AI. Talos did not track whether Volta has been used in the wild. The finding shows how commercial LLMs are being used to enhance established types of malware.

Infostealers hide in counterfeit software and grab usernames, passwords, authentication tokens, cookies, credit card data and more from infected machines. Volta sweeps for passwords stored in browsers, Microsoft OAuth tokens, cookies, payment cards and crypto wallet seed phrases, and also for active Discord, Telegram, Steam and Roblox sessions. It then does a deeper second sweep, using a target's Gmail or another central account to build a picture of the victim, their location and habits, including receipts and order history from services such as UberEats and DoorDash. It feeds the results to AI tools through OpenRouter, defaulting to Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6, with fallbacks to Moonshot AI's Kimi K2 and then Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash in case guardrails block the requests. Its creators included a 240-word prompt telling the model to act as a forensic intelligence analyst and produce a structured, citation-backed assessment of the victim, covering an executive summary, what the person does, what they are worth and their opsec.

Ryan Fetterman, a security researcher at Cisco Talos, said Volta is mature as a stealer and casts a wide net for what it collects, compiling everything into a serialized dossier for the models. He said the prompt is carefully crafted not to imply anything overtly malicious, and that the creators built in the expectation of model refusals, planning failover to more permissible models down the chain. He added that the implant still works without the AI, and that the AI calls are above and beyond. He also said Volta contains clues it may have been built to sell to a range of attackers rather than for one actor's campaigns.

Fetterman said that identifying high-value targets faster probably gives attackers a better chance of using stolen credentials or tokens before they expire or passwords are changed. He said more advanced capabilities are becoming accessible to lower-level attackers, which he called interesting and disturbing. Researchers at Crowdstrike recently told WIRED they had seen four distinct hacking groups, operating in Chinese, Spanish and English, Indonesian, and Russian, use AI tools to compromise dozens of targets around the world, including government entities and businesses in health care, retail and travel. The article says the AI expansion foreshadows more invasive and sinister activity in the future.

Articles.Title: Spooky New Infostealer Malware Uses AI to ‘Autodox’ Victims

stories.Headline: Atlassian launches AI-native SDLC features for Japanese market
stories.Summary:
Atlassian announced on October 29, 2026, that it is launching a set of new features for the Japanese market to make the software development lifecycle AI-native. The company said the features were first outlined at its annual Team '26 Europe conference in October 2026. They cover seven areas: context, planning, design, development, review, maintenance and measurement. Atlassian's own engineers estimate that the AI-native process has raised development speed by more than seven times on feature work in existing codebases.

The features include Teamwork Graph, which combines code, documents, decisions, standards and more than 80 third-party sources into one permission-aware layer. Atlassian says internal testing showed answer quality improved by up to 44 percent and token use fell by up to 48 percent. Code Context indexes repositories in Bitbucket and GitHub and links code to Jira work items, Confluence pages, Loom videos, Slack and Google Drive. Planner turns rough ideas into Confluence plans and then into Jira work items, and Record for Agent converts Loom recordings into structured prompts.

Jira now supports third-party coding agents including Cognition's Devin, Factory and Warp through the Atlassian Marketplace, with OpenAI Codex due soon. Loom generates interactive pull request walkthroughs on Bitbucket, and Agent Sessions records AI agent work in Jira. DX AI Measurement is generally available, Code Context and Record for Agent are in open beta, and Planner, Agent Loops and AI Review are in private early access. Agent Sessions and interactive PR reviews are in a closed early access program.

Atlassian cited its 2026 AI SDLC survey, which found that 94 percent of engineering leaders already use AI in their teams, while only 6 percent have scaled and governed it effectively across the organization. The company argues that partial coding assistance does not fix bottlenecks across planning, design, review, maintenance and return on investment. It proposes a model in which humans set direction and judgment while AI agents carry out the work. Atlassian Japan was founded in 2013 and is based in Yokohama, with Stuart Harrington as representative director.

Articles.Title: Atlassian launches new features for the Japanese market that realize an AI-native software development lifecycle (SDLC)
