stories.Headline: Who pays for the AI power boom?
stories.Summary:
Data centers are currently paying for the electricity they consume and generally must cover the costs of connecting to the grid, according to Axios. The rules get murkier when it comes to building new power plants and upgrading the broader electric system. Those costs can be spread among customers, potentially raising household electricity bills. Under longstanding federal rules, data centers and other large power users generally do not have to pay both for their share of the existing grid and the new transmission infrastructure built to serve them.

More than half of states have taken or considered steps to protect residential customers, including special electricity rates and requirements that data centers pay for infrastructure built on their behalf. The issue is surfacing in key midterm races, with candidates in both parties calling for stronger protections against higher power bills. Congress is considering bipartisan legislation that would require large data centers to cover more infrastructure costs, even if projects are canceled. Who ultimately pays depends on where a data center is built, how its utility charges customers and whether new protections take effect.

Policymakers increasingly want technology companies, not everyday electricity customers, to shoulder more of the costs of the AI-driven buildout of electricity infrastructure, Axios reports. Decisions being made now about who pays for new power infrastructure could affect Americans' electricity bills for years to come. Data centers are becoming a major political issue as costs climb and communities push back against paying for the industry's expansion. The article does not say what happens next beyond the pending legislation and the state actions already taken or considered.

Articles.Title: Who pays for the AI power boom?

stories.Headline: Microsoft’s big buyout, Amazon’s trillion-dollar future, and an AI wearable reviews our show
stories.Summary:
Microsoft is offering buyouts to about 60,000 employees, about a quarter of its workforce, including some executives. The offer was reported by GeekWire in an episode published on October 31, 2026. Unlike the retirement program Microsoft offered in the spring, this one has no age or tenure requirement. Business leaders decide whether their groups take part. The buyout comes as Microsoft reports a blockbuster quarter, including $10 billion in revenue from OpenAI, more than the company made from Xbox or Bing.

Amazon CEO Andy Jassy predicts that AWS and Amazon’s stores business could each reach $1 trillion in annual revenue in the next five to 10 years. AWS grew 39% in the third quarter, its fastest pace in nearly five years. Amazon’s profit fell short of expectations as the cost of its AI buildout and growing debt cut into earnings. On the GeekWire Podcast, Todd Bishop and John Cook discuss what is behind the offer and why buyout stories draw so much interest from readers. Todd also tests Amazon’s new Bee AI wearable, which listens to the first part of the show, summarizes the conversation and offers a critique of its own.

The hosts talk about what it is like to wear a device that records the people around you, a concern raised by a former AWS security engineer. John starts to come around on the device, with reservations about its shopping features. The episode also includes the hosts’ Halloween costumes and a Trivia Challenge inspired by T-Mobile’s new T-Mix plans. The show was edited by Curt Milton, with music by Daniel L.K. Caldwell. Listeners are directed to listen above and subscribe in Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever they listen.

Articles.Title: Microsoft’s big buyout, Amazon’s trillion-dollar future, and an AI wearable reviews our show

stories.Headline: The $10 trillion AI buildout so far isn't stopping
stories.Summary:
A powerful backlash against AI and data centers has been building for months, and it has fueled local moratoriums and political opposition. The pushback has also raised fears that the $10 trillion infrastructure buildout could hit a wall. Despite more than 300 local moratoriums, U.S. data center development is moving at a blistering pace. The industry may add more than 50 gigawatts of capacity in 2027, according to research firm SemiAnalysis.

Construction on nearly half of that capacity is already at an advanced stage, and developers have signed $1 trillion in leases to support the expansion, SemiAnalysis says. The buildout is far from friction-free, and political, regulatory, supply and environmental hurdles are delaying some major projects. In New Mexico, Oracle took steps to protect itself from steep costs tied to delays of the $165 billion Project Jupiter stemming from local opposition, permitting roadblocks and power supply challenges. In Texas, an audit ordered by Gov. Greg Abbott is adding months of delays for projects seeking to connect to the state's electric grid. In New York, an executive order pausing environmental permits for larger facilities has delayed nearly 1 gigawatt of capacity, according to SemiAnalysis.

Local opposition and mounting regulatory scrutiny are creating isolated bottlenecks, but they have yet to derail the broader infrastructure boom. The stakes extend far beyond the U.S., and any backlash that slows the AI boom could have global consequences. The futures of politicians, economies and nations are increasingly tied to the race for technological supremacy. The midterm elections will offer an early test of whether growing voter resistance could become a more formidable obstacle.

Articles.Title: The $10 trillion AI buildout so far isn't stopping

stories.Headline: The AI trade's trick-or-treat earnings season
stories.Summary:
The latest earnings reports from big tech companies unsettled Wall Street, as the results offered conflicting signals about the AI boom. The tech-heavy Nasdaq briefly fell into correction territory, dropping 10% from its prior peak and losing $1.2 trillion in value during October. The declines followed a series of earnings reports that highlighted major risks in the AI trade. Investors found evidence in the same reports to support both optimistic and pessimistic views.

Google lost more than $500 billion in market value after its earnings, as AI overviews eat into ad revenue from search. Search queries are up, but results in AI mode carry lower margins. On the other hand, Google Cloud is closing in on Microsoft's Azure cloud revenue, a striking change for a company that was an also-ran in cloud a few years ago. Much of that success is tied to demand for Google's TPU chips, which analysts expect to grow sharply in coming quarters.

Microsoft and Amazon both posted explosive cloud growth, though the market was disappointed Amazon's was not higher. Amazon's net income fell even as operating profits soared, because it did not repeat the pretax gain from its Anthropic investment that had boosted earnings a year earlier. Microsoft's OpenAI investment lifted its net income slightly and raised its profit growth. Some asset-light tech companies have turned free cash flow negative to fund AI ambitions, saying demand is outstripping supply.

Jeetu Patel, President and Chief Product Officer at Cisco, told Axios he is bullish but said a major cyber event hitting the core of AI demand could be a downside risk. DeepWater partner Gene Munster said the street is waking up to the risks of an agentic world, asking how Google makes money without ad search revenue and how Amazon makes money if shoppers use bots. Tech stocks are broadly under pressure following these results. Those existential questions are not stopping the AI capex spending spree, for now.

Articles.Title: The AI trade's trick-or-treat earnings season

stories.Headline: Our AI agent experience: we scrapped $60,000 marketing jobs and hired one person for far more
stories.Summary:
In July, Accenture published guidance for companies worried about their AI bills, advising them not to cut usage across the board and to route work to the cheapest model that does the job. It said that in nearly every deployment it had examined, including its own, fewer than 10% of users and workflows drove the vast majority of the bill. On Oct. 1, according to an internal announcement obtained by 404 Media, Accenture began centrally funding $29 a month per person toward Claude, with anything above that charged to a project. Internal messages seen by the publication showed employees who had been spending $500 to $1,000 a month, and one who said their access was revoked entirely, while Accenture says reporting that it put a firm limit on access is incorrect.

The article's authors describe one of their portfolio companies, which needed a new website and faced an agency quote of $60,000. Instead, three people from the business team, none of whom had ever built a website, did it in three days, and the result worked on Windows and Mac computers, iPhones, Android handsets and Chinese phones running HarmonyOS. The agents also produced high-resolution logos, made marketing material consistent for the first time, and found customer testimonials and awards nobody knew existed, with tokens costing a few hundred dollars. The authors say they were about to hire several entry-level marketing people at around $60,000 each, but hired one instead at considerably more, and that one non-technical person does work the whole group could not have done.

The authors write that AI is sold by the token, roughly three-quarters of a word, and that a million tokens, about 750,000 words or eight or nine novels, costs between $2 and $8. They say a typical office worker asking 30 questions a day uses about 1.3 million tokens a month, roughly $6 of usage, while one agent task can consume 50,000 to 500,000 tokens, or about $12,000 a year for the most intensive person. They cite a Jellyfish study of 12,000 developers at 200 companies this year, where one finished job cost 28 cents in tokens among the lightest users and $89 among the heaviest. They also say one of them modeled deployments in four industries and found the token bill was about a quarter of the total cost.

Pope Leo XIV warned Friday against giving AI agents legal personhood or rights, telling AI experts at the Vatican that machines are tools, not persons and that responsibility should lie with their human creators. He said such systems do not undergo experiences, do not feel joy or pain and do not know from within what love, work, friendship or responsibility mean, and that granting them rights risks obscuring human responsibility. Leo, 71, whose first encyclical in May called for putting technology at the service of human dignity, said AI's future is not pre-determined and that humans must guide, change and, when necessary, reject its applications. He said decisions affecting human life, freedom and the use of force must remain under human oversight, repeated his call for a ban on lethal autonomous weapons, and urged shared standards, independent oversight and clear accountability.

Articles.Title: Our AI agent experience: we scrapped $60,000 marketing jobs and hired one person for far more

stories.Headline: Agentic AI for Immune-Related Adverse Event Detection in Cancer Immunotherapy
stories.Summary:
A study published in Nature Cancer on October 31, 2026, led by Jack Gallifant and colleagues, developed an agentic artificial intelligence system to detect immune-related adverse events in cancer immunotherapy. The system used large language models to extract from clinical notes whether an irAE was documented, whether it was current or historical, its severity grade, its attribution to checkpoint inhibitor therapy, and the clinician's certainty about that attribution. It was tested in three phases: retrospective testing on 289 expert-annotated notes, prospective silent deployment, and a randomized study of AI-assisted human review. The best performance came from GPT-4.1-mini within the agentic architecture.

The retrospective test set had 263 held-out notes after 26 were used for development. The system reached a temporality-agnostic macro-averaged F1 of 0.93 for note-level detection, with 0.92 for current events and 0.91 for past events. Exact multiclass CTCAE grading was harder, with an overall macro F1 of 0.66 for current events, highest for dermatitis at 0.73 and thyroiditis at 0.72, and lowest for colitis at 0.51. Removing the three-run self-consistency step dropped detection F1 from 0.92 to 0.78, while cost rose from about US$0.011 to US$0.021 per note. A rule-based system with 779 terms performed reasonably for simple binary detection but could not extract severity, attribution, certainty, or supporting evidence.

In the prospective phase, the system ran silently for three months between May and July 2025, evaluating 884 clinical notes and generating 31,824 label adjudications. Performance fell: binary F1 was 0.72 for current events and 0.79 for past events, and note-level predictions matched human review in 62% of cases for grade, 87% for attribution, and 83% for certainty. The authors attributed the decline to a broader case mix and evolving EHR templates, terminology, and documentation practices, and argued that clinical AI systems need continuous monitoring and periodic recalibration rather than one-time validation. The randomized 2 × 2 crossover study compared manual annotation with AI-assisted review, with 17 participants, 16 clinical research coordinators and one clinical research nurse, producing 316 evaluable timing observations.

The authors note that irAEs affect up to 40% of patients receiving checkpoint inhibitors and can involve almost any organ system, with myocarditis and pneumonitis among the potentially life-threatening events. Much of the evidence needed to identify these toxicities sits in free-text notes rather than structured EHR fields, and even ICD codes have limited sensitivity for hospitalization-associated events. The system covered six toxicities: pneumonitis, hepatitis, colitis, myocarditis, thyroiditis, and dermatitis. The study raises the question of whether AI can improve immune-toxicity surveillance without replacing the clinical judgment needed to interpret complex adverse events.

Articles.Title: Agentic AI for Immune-Related Adverse Event Detection in Cancer Immunotherapy

stories.Headline: DARPA Backs Project to Measure AI Energy Use at Every Stage of the Workflow
stories.Summary:
DARPA will put $1.83 million over two years into a project called E-CALC, which stands for Energy Calculus for ML Lifecycle Optimization. The work is led by Michigan Engineering, working with the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and the defense contractor BAE Systems. The goal is to estimate how much energy artificial intelligence uses at every stage of a workflow, from data processing and model training to real-world deployment. Michigan Engineering says misalignments between software and hardware can waste up to 30% of the electricity used in AI model training alone. The project is funded by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency.

The backdrop is that researchers still cannot say precisely how much energy AI uses today. The International Energy Agency forecasts that data center power use will more than double by 2030 from its 2024 level, which was about 420 terawatt-hours. The new system is meant to let developers estimate energy usage without relying on expensive, time-consuming trial-and-error testing across thousands of hardware and software configurations. Michigan Engineering says more energy-efficient AI would bring down electricity demand, cut the cost of AI and extend battery life for AI-enabled devices. The technology could matter especially in military and defense settings, where field equipment and remote computing systems must run complex AI algorithms under strict battery and power limits.

Mosharaf Chowdhury, a University of Michigan associate professor of computer science and engineering and the principal investigator for E-CALC, said AI is becoming part of everyday life, business, science and national security but requires enormous and rapidly growing amounts of electricity. He said that if that energy use continues to rise unchecked, it could increase costs, strain power infrastructure and make advanced AI harder to deploy. He described the project as tackling a practical question, which is how to get widespread benefits of AI with minimum energy. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the two years of DARPA funding.

Articles.Title: DARPA Backs Project to Measure AI Energy Use at Every Stage of the Workflow

stories.Headline: Google's AI satellite sends a very expensive haiku to Earth
stories.Summary:
Google on Friday celebrated receiving a poem from its first experimental orbital AI datacenter satellite. The company's Suncatcher satellite was launched at the start of the month and put into low Earth orbit. It responded to a ground station prompt asking for a haiku from the perspective of a TPU orbiting Earth, with the world spinning beneath it. Travis Beals, senior director of Google's interdisciplinary Paradigms of Intelligence research team, said the onboard Gemma 4 model achieved its "Hello World" milestone by sending an inference response from orbit. The satellite sent its reply as it passed over Svalbard, Norway, and the roughly 20 tokens would cost about $0.000012 through the Google Cloud API, based on Gemma 4 26B's pricing of $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output tokens, excluding input costs.

Google's calculations suggest that if launch costs fall to $200/kg, the amortized launch cost of about $810 to $7,500/kW/year could be comparable to current US terrestrial datacenter electricity spending of about $570 to $3,000/kW/year. Google predicts SpaceX could reach that by 2035, more or less, and considers it strategically beneficial to prototype well in advance. Laboratory testing of the Trillium Cloud TPU and AMD host server showed high-bandwidth memory is the most sensitive part, showing irregularities after a cumulative dose of 2 krad(Si), about 3× Google's minimum requirement of 750 rad(Si). Beals said that after the haiku, the team tested space-themed limericks and telemetry prompts reporting the technical status of the payload systems. Google researchers said that for typical transformer workloads, the observed silent data corruption rate of about one event per 17 rad, at an estimated orbital dose of 150 rad(Si)/year, translates to a very low failure probability on the order of one per 3 million inferences, assuming one inference per second.

They added that while this error rate is likely acceptable for inference, the impact of single event effects on training jobs and the efficacy of system-level mitigations requires further study. Next up are tests for evaluating how TPUs perform under thermal stress and radiation. Next year, the plan is to test a pair of interconnected satellites. Rather than lofting large satellites into orbit, Google anticipates sending a constellation of many smaller satellites that communicate with one another.

Articles.Title: Google's AI satellite sends a very expensive haiku to Earth

stories.Headline: A Look at AI, a Lens on Aging
stories.Summary:
Belfast Senior College will hold two free public events on Nov. 9 and Nov. 10, pairing a technology talk with the world premiere of a locally made film. The first event, “First Look at AI,” will be presented by Doug Chamberlin on Monday, Nov. 9, from 4 to 5:30 p.m. in the Abbott Room at the Belfast Free Library. The talk is co-sponsored by the library and will examine artificial intelligence from the average person’s perspective. It will address what AI is, how people can use it and how they can protect themselves from its risks.

Chamberlin will also consider whether AI is as dangerous as some suggest, drawing on four decades of technology experience. During his career as a software developer, systems analyst and database designer, he saw technology deployed both appropriately and in ways that missed the mark. He now assists Belfast Senior College with technical challenges and teaches technology courses. Registration for the library presentation is encouraged but not required at belfastseniorcollege.org/events.

The following day, “Growing Old Together in Belfast” will have its world premiere at noon Tuesday, Nov. 10, at the Colonial Theatre. The film was written and directed by Jeff Edwards and grew out of his Belfast Senior College class, “An Experiment in Creating a Movie,” with technical support from Belfast Community Media. It follows eight characters coming to terms with aging, told as a whimsical tale with a hopeful view of transformation and connection in later life. The cast includes Jeff Edwards, Sarah Edwards, George Frangoulis, Kristin Frangoulis, Lisa Kushner, Ned Lightner, Tycelia Santoro, Linda Garson Smith and Joanna Young.

Ned Lightner, Alex Chaplin and Anne Sezak provided technical support, and Andrew Elijah Edwards edited the film. Music by Belfast-based artists Elsie Gawler and Ethan Stokes Tischler is featured throughout the production. The film runs one hour and 19 minutes, and admission is free, but seating is limited to 120. Reservations are optional and may be made at colonialtheatre.com. Together the events reflect Belfast Senior College’s emphasis on practical learning, creativity and community, and both November events are open to the public at no charge.

Articles.Title: A Look at AI, a Lens on Aging

stories.Headline: A profile of White House OSTP Director Michael Kratsios, an ex-Peter Thiel aide who is among a handful of players steering the Trump administration's AI policy (Harry Lambert/Colossus)
stories.Summary:
Michael Kratsios is the director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy and Trump’s chief scientific advisor. He has worked for Trump every day in office since January 20, 2017, and watched Trump’s 2016 victory speech from the trading floor at Thiel Capital in San Francisco a day after turning 30. He had worked for Peter Thiel for six years by then, and he flew with Thiel to Trump Tower the Monday after the election. He stayed in Washington when Thiel flew back, and began to research the offices and agencies of the federal government. Kratsios has spent six years turning the traditionally irrelevant OSTP into what the article calls a consequential engine room of government.

The office has historically been maligned for producing little more than congressionally mandated reports, but he now uses it to set tech policy across much of the U.S. government. He sits between the President and Silicon Valley and effectively serves as the White House coordinator for critical emerging technologies, including science, space, nuclear, and quantum. He is one of a handful of players steering AI policy for Trump, insofar as anyone has latitude to act on an issue the President has commandeered. At the medal ceremony, Kratsios showed a video celebrating the lifetime achievements of Trump’s uncle, John G. Trump, a 1983 national medal of science recipient and an MIT professor for almost 40 years. He had reached out to Brett Ratner, who has become Trumpworld’s in-house director since making Melania earlier this year, to help make the video.

After it played, Kratsios brought out John G. Trump’s medal in a frame and presented it to Trump, who paraded it to the audience. Kratsios later said Trump loved it and asked him to get five more names for another ceremony. The article describes Kratsios as little known in the first Trump term who has now become one of the few White House aides entrusted with making presidential caprice a reality. As an 18-year-old in 2005, he had worked as an intern in Lindsey Graham’s office during the summer of John Roberts’ Supreme Court confirmation. He briefly began his career in investment banking before landing with Thiel, but he had always wanted to return to D.C. He helped organize the first meeting between Trump and the tech leaders of the day, and he thought this underutilized office could become the most important office for science and technology in America.

Articles.Title: A profile of White House OSTP Director Michael Kratsios, an ex-Peter Thiel aide who is among a handful of players steering the Trump administration's AI policy (Harry Lambert/Colossus)

stories.Headline: Investors trim growth bets over fears of US economy’s AI exposure
stories.Summary:
Investors reduced their bets on growth because of concerns about the US economy's exposure to artificial intelligence, according to the Financial Times on 31 October 2026. The article appeared under a headline saying investors were trimming growth bets over fears about that exposure. The Financial Times page did not provide the body of the report to readers without a subscription. The available text shows only the headline, the date and subscription offers.

The article as published gives no figures, no named investors and no specific dates beyond 31 October 2026. It does not set out what the shift requires or what it changes. The page offers trial and subscription plans, including a trial at one dollar for four weeks and then 75 dollars per month. It also lists Standard Digital at 45 dollars per month and Premium Digital at 75 dollars per month, with annual payment saving 20 percent. The FT Digital Edition is listed at 16.99 dollars per month.

The available text names no person who is responsible and carries no comments from investors or officials. It does not say who made the decisions or what they said about them. The only named company is the Financial Times, which publishes the article and sets the subscription terms. The page notes that markets data is delayed by at least 15 minutes and that the Financial Times and its journalism are subject to a self-regulation regime under the FT Editorial Code of Practice.

The context beyond the headline is not given in the available text, and the article does not say what happens next. The page does not explain the scale of the trimmed bets or which parts of the US economy are considered exposed to AI. It gives no indication of future reporting or follow-up coverage. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Investors trim growth bets over fears of US economy’s AI exposure

stories.Headline: Chinese archaeologists prepare for hi-tech excavations with AI and deep-sea robots
stories.Summary:
Chinese archaeologists are preparing to use AI and deep-sea robots in future excavations under a new five-year plan, the South China Morning Post reported on 31 October 2026. The 15th five-year work plan for archaeology sets out a hi-tech turn for the field. Scientists will be tasked with deploying big data technology and underwater drones to unearth centuries of lost history. The plan also aims to trace Chinese history, decipher the origins of East Asian humans and expand the country's cultural soft power.

Under the plan, scientists will develop technologies including remote sensing, ancient DNA analysis, underwater archaeology robots and AI models for virtual restoration of excavated artefacts. They will also expand international partnerships to conduct fieldwork across Asia. Joint research will be launched in the Austronesian-speaking regions, the Himalayan area and along the Silk Road and Maritime Silk Road. The article gives no further dates or figures beyond the 31 October 2026 publication date and the 15th five-year plan.

The article does not name individual officials or scientists and carries no direct comments from those responsible. It attributes the details to the 15th five-year work plan for archaeology. The scientists will be tasked with deploying the big data technology and underwater drones, according to the report. No specific person is quoted saying anything about the plan.

The context given is that the plan aims to trace Chinese history, decipher the origins of East Asian humans and expand the country's cultural soft power. The article does not say what happens next beyond the work set out in the plan. It does not give a timeline for the technologies or the international fieldwork. It does not say who will oversee or fund the work.

Articles.Title: Chinese archaeologists prepare for hi-tech excavations with AI and deep-sea robots

stories.Headline: Jacksonville State University to Host AI Forward Summit Connecting Education and Industry in February
stories.Summary:
Jacksonville State University will host a two-day summit on artificial intelligence in education and the workforce. The event, called AI Forward: From Classroom to Career, is scheduled for February 11-12, 2027, at Merrill Hall on the university's campus in Jacksonville, Alabama. It will bring together K-12 educators, higher education professionals, students and industry leaders. The summit aims to examine how artificial intelligence is changing teaching, learning and workplace practices and to offer chances for schools and businesses to work together.

The summit will focus on three areas: K-12 education, higher education and student success, and business and industry. Planned activities include keynote presentations, breakout sessions, panel discussions, an AI Exhibitor Expo, an AI Showcase poster session and networking. Anthony Robbins, a Jax State alumnus and former vice president at NVIDIA, will be the featured keynote speaker and will discuss AI's influence on education, industry and workforce development. Representatives from Coca-Cola UNITED, Honda, AmFirst Credit Union and other industry organizations are expected at featured sessions.

The university is accepting presentation proposals, with a deadline of November 9, 2026. Proposals can be for 30-minute presentations, 10-minute presentations or the AI Showcase poster session, and will be judged on relevance, clarity, practical application, audience value and alignment with the summit's goals. Selected presenters are expected to be notified in early December and will receive complimentary registration. President Dr. Don C. Killingsworth Jr. said AI is already reshaping classrooms and workplaces and that higher education has an important role in helping students use these tools thoughtfully and responsibly.

Registration is free but advance registration is required, with early registration through January 9, 2027, and final registration closing January 27. The first day, Thursday, February 11, will include the expo, opening keynote, breakout sessions, cross-sector discussions and the AI Showcase. Programming continues Friday, February 12, with more breakout sessions and presentations, and optional post-conference workshops are available Friday afternoon. The event is open to K-12 teachers and administrators, college faculty and staff, students, business professionals, workforce development organizations and community partners, and more information is available at www.jsu.edu/aiforward.

Articles.Title: Jacksonville State University to Host AI Forward Summit Connecting Education and Industry in February

stories.Headline: US forces in Europe are bracing for 'Ukraine's worst day.' AI could help them fight an overwhelming flood of missiles and drones.
stories.Summary:
US forces in Europe are preparing for large-scale combat and the kind of heavy missile and drone attacks Ukraine has faced. US officials believe future battlefields could produce so much data from sensors and networks that human operators would be overwhelmed. Army soldiers are looking to software, including artificial intelligence, to help process that data and keep up with the speed and scale of the threats. At the Association of the United States Army convention in Washington, DC, last month, service leaders and soldiers spoke about using AI to help troops make decisions. Brig.

Gen. Steven Carpenter, head of Multi-Domain Command Europe, said earlier this year that US forces in Europe needed to be ready to process more than 1,500 potential targets a day while defending against as many as 1,200 incoming missiles and drones. He said that volume of targets and threats could overwhelm human analysts, and that AI could help them keep up. In a conflict, soldiers could use AI to analyze battlefield data and targets based on a commander's objectives and other parameters. The system could then assess available military capabilities and recommend responses, from conventional weapons strikes to electronic warfare or cyber operations.

Carpenter said the estimates reflect what officials think Ukraine's worst day is. Carpenter said it is important to use super intelligence for things humans are not necessarily good at, namely speed and scale, but that humans should not be taken completely out of the loop. He said the human is making the decision and the final call, looking at everything needed to prosecute a valid target within the Law of Armed Conflict. He said the intent is not to replace analysts but to unburden them so they can focus on really tough targets, such as a dual-use facility or other potential targets that need more analysis. Earlier this year, a joint US Army and NATO exercise in Europe saw troops use a homegrown AI system to consume and sort data, and Army officials said they aimed to test it on a larger scale at a future exercise.

The Army is also incorporating AI into its Next Generation Command and Control, its new warfighting system. NGC2 uses AI and machine learning to give commanders and soldiers real-time data on targeting, capabilities, ammunition levels, maintenance needs, intelligence feeds, and simulated enemy attacks. AI and autonomy are being integrated quickly across uncrewed systems, command and control processes, and other technologies. Russia's war against Ukraine has involved frequent, heavy drone and missile bombardments, with complex strike packages of ballistic and cruise missiles and one-way attack drones, more of which are equipped with jet engines that make them faster and harder to kill.

Articles.Title: US forces in Europe are bracing for 'Ukraine's worst day.' AI could help them fight an overwhelming flood of missiles and drones.

stories.Headline: Prediction: This Under-the-Radar AI Stock Could Have a Big 2030 Ahead
stories.Summary:
Marvell Technology's Data Center segment brought in $2.1715 billion last quarter, up 46%, and now makes up 79% of total revenue, according to a 24/7 Wall St. article published on October 31, 2026. The article says AI-related bookings remain exceptionally robust, according to CEO Matt Murphy. The shares are up 194.58% year to date but sit below their peak. At $249.92, the stock is 24.2% below its 52-week high of $329.73.

The article says reaching $500 by 2030 would require a gain of 100.1%. It says that path depends on three things: the custom business more than doubling year over year in fiscal 2028, non-GAAP operating margin reaching the top of its 38% to 40% target range, and Google programs ramping in fiscal 2029. Management guided Q3 non-GAAP gross margin to 57.5% to 58.5%, below Q2's 58.9%, and raised its fiscal 2027 operating expense outlook to approximately $2.55 billion. The article also notes that a small group of hyperscalers drive most of the revenue and that the Google warrant could dilute shareholders by up to 7%.

Wall Street gives the stock 40 Buy-or-better ratings with zero Sells and a consensus target of $341.44, implying about 36.6% upside, the article says. It lists 8 Strong Buy recommendations, 32 Buy ratings and 6 Holds. Murphy said there is a lot of upside bias in the numbers in fiscal 29 and beyond in custom, and he called the full potential of the hyperscaler agreement game-changing. The article's own model has a base case of $284.80, or 17.23% upside, within a one-year range of $218.43 to $352.54, and its 2030 bull case reaches $509.10 by October of that year.

The article says the biggest risk is hyperscalers cutting capital spending or bringing more chip design in-house. It says a sharp slowdown in AI infrastructure spending would disrupt the plan. At today's price, the article says, Marvell trades at 41x forward earnings, which it calls reasonable for a company guiding to roughly $12 billion in fiscal 2027 revenue. It says the stock has run from $70.62 to $329.73 over the past 52 weeks and has returned 1943.93% over 10 years.

Articles.Title: Prediction: This Under-the-Radar AI Stock Could Have a Big 2030 Ahead

stories.Headline: The Nasdaq 100 Briefly Fell Into a Correction as the AI Trade Cracks
stories.Summary:
The Nasdaq 100 briefly fell into correction territory on Friday, October 30, 2026, then climbed back above the line before the close. It dropped 3.46% to close at 28,384.85, after an intraday low of 28,093.24. That low was 10.0% below the October 6 record close of 31,224.47, so the index crossed the 10% line during the session. It closed 9.1% below the record, meaning it never finished a day in correction.

The selling started in chip stocks. Intel fell 28.6% after guiding fourth-quarter revenue to $15 billion to $16 billion, below the $16.5 billion it had just reported. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 7.2%, its worst day since June 23, and lost 15.4% for October. Invesco QQQ Trust closed at $690.49, down 3.47%, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 2.86% to 25,437.00, its lowest close since July 31.

Joe Tigay, a portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, said the AI trade was moving out of the hopes and dreams phase and into what he called the show me phase. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said the company still expected 2026 cash capital expenditures of approximately $220 billion. On Intel's call, management said data center demand exceeds supply, but guided fourth-quarter gross margin to 38%, compared with 44.1% in the third quarter, and warned of a PC slowdown linked to memory prices. Apple slipped 1.23% but at $5.03 trillion became the most valuable company, ahead of NVIDIA, which fell 4.2% to $204.64 and was worth $4.94 trillion.

This was the third time in 2026 that the index fell more than 10% below a record, after March 27 and July 29, and both earlier times it later set new records. The VIX hit 23.93 during the session but closed at 19.41, up 12.91%. The next tests come quickly: Apple is expected to report after the close on November 2, though it has not confirmed the date, the midterm elections follow on November 3, the October jobs report comes out on November 6, and NVIDIA reports in mid-November. The key level to watch is a Nasdaq-100 close below the October 30 intraday low of 28,093.24, which would put the index in correction on a closing basis.

Articles.Title: The Nasdaq 100 Briefly Fell Into a Correction as the AI Trade Cracks

stories.Headline: Israeli AI founders bring Jigso team to Placer.ai in push beyond traditional analytics
stories.Summary:
Or Shani and Tomer Naveh, co-founders of the Israeli artificial intelligence startup Jigso, are joining the U.S. location analytics company Placer.ai along with a team of AI and machine learning specialists. The two founders have spent 16 years developing AI and machine learning products. They will work with Placer.ai's existing teams on technology designed to identify patterns, detect unusual activity and generate business recommendations from location data. Placer.ai provides information about foot traffic and activity at physical locations, including stores, shopping centers, hotels and commercial properties.

Placer.ai's platform is used by more than 5,000 organizations, including Fortune 500 companies, to assess consumer behavior, compare locations and track changes in market activity. The company wants to move beyond conventional analytics, where customers examine data and draw their own conclusions, toward systems that automatically identify developments that may require attention. These could include unexpected changes in visitor numbers, shifts in consumer patterns or other indicators relevant to business decisions. Shani and Naveh previously co-founded Albert.ai, an early AI platform for automating digital advertising decisions, which went public and was later sold. They then established Jigso, which built an AI platform that connected to enterprise systems and analyzed business information to identify anomalies, surface insights and support automated actions.

Noam Ben-Zvi, CEO and co-founder of Placer.ai, said the company's ambition was never to be just an analytics platform. He said Placer.ai had already invested in AI development and that the incoming team would work alongside its existing specialists. Shani said Placer.ai's data resources were a central factor in the decision to join, adding that great AI needs great, unique data. The announcement did not specify how many Jigso employees are joining Placer.ai or disclose any financial arrangements. It also did not detail which new products or features the team will be responsible for developing.

The move comes as businesses increasingly experiment with AI systems that can do more than respond to questions or produce reports. Placer.ai is pursuing a similar approach using its proprietary location data, though it has not provided a timetable for introducing new capabilities resulting from the team's arrival. For Placer.ai, the immediate significance is the addition of an experienced Israeli AI team to an existing development operation. Whether that translates into substantial changes for customers will depend on how effectively the company integrates the new expertise and turns its ambitions for automated analysis into working products.

Articles.Title: Israeli AI founders bring Jigso team to Placer.ai in push beyond traditional analytics

stories.Headline: The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a benchmark experiment by Nolan Lawson, published on November 1, 2026, on his blog Read the Tea Leaves. Lawson built a small Pokémon app using the PokéAPI and had AI agents build it with different JavaScript frameworks and meta-frameworks, including Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, Angular, React Router, Hono with htmx, Gracile with Lit, TanStack Start, and plain Vite. He gave the spec to Opus 5.5 with high effort and told it to use the latest version of each framework, with each agent running in a sandbox. He took the median of five runs per framework, except Angular, which failed to create a working app twice, so he used three iterations. He measured development time, tokens spent, lines of code, and Lighthouse performance and accessibility scores.

The results showed that SvelteKit, Gracile with Lit, and Angular were more expensive to build than the other frameworks. Lawson said SvelteKit's cost may be because agents read the SvelteKit v3 migration guide in every run, likely because it is too new to be in Opus 5.5's training data, and that Gracile agents did not know the framework well and either cloned its repo or read its compiled source from node_modules. For Angular, he said the cost seemed to be a function of total code size. He also noted that not every agent used an MCP, skill, or Claude Code plugin, and not every framework had one: TanStack Start's agent only found its skill files in two of five runs, Nuxt's MCP was never used, and Next.js agents read the skill file in one of five runs and the AGENTS.md in two of five. He said the plain Vite setup underperformed several frameworks, which seemed to show that having some framework can be better than nothing.

Lawson said the experiment is not perfect and that everything he measured is very stochastic, since LLMs are random-word generators and Lighthouse itself can give inconsistent results, for example picking a different largest element for Largest Contentful Paint on different runs. He said he did not over-specify the architecture, such as SSR versus CSR, and did not tell agents the app would be tested in Lighthouse, though they were given a conformance test suite. He avoided Tailwind, Bootstrap, and other component frameworks and used spec tokens for visual consistency, and he tested against a conformance suite based on the accessibility tree rather than the raw DOM. He said the Pokémon app is small and does not represent a large, complex real-world application, and that Lighthouse and Core Web Vitals are biased against SPAs, so MPA frameworks are almost guaranteed to win on metrics like Total Blocking Time and JavaScript bytes. He reported only the home page scores, and said Performance, Accessibility, and CLS scores were nearly saturated and did not vary much by framework, so he looked at other metrics, with JavaScript bytes sent being the most reliable.

Articles.Title: The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks

stories.Headline: Axios C-Suite: The 6 dimensions of AI leadership
stories.Summary:
Jim VandeHei wrote in the Axios C-Suite newsletter, published on October 31, 2026, that AI is not a choice but an urgent enabler of revenue, growth and cost. He said he had heard from two companies deeply involved in AI tutoring of CEOs that at best 15% of CEOs are AI-savvy, and that most board chairs know even less about the technology. He argued that leaders of AI-enabled companies need six new layers of AI leadership and expertise. He said he would outline the six layers in that newsletter and use future editions to help readers master each one.

The six layers he listed are: understand AI, use and explain it, govern it, implement and measure it, restructure teams and companies to exploit it, and make sure companies and products show up inside it. On governance, he wrote that 71% of directors named AI as the top skill their boards need to strengthen, and 82% said information on AI's link to risk and business performance was fair, poor or unavailable. He said the technology changes weekly and that implementation is a living, never-ending project. He described the coming companies as human/agent hybrids operating at a speed never seen before, and said he is three years into this work and tinkers with structure constantly.

On responsibility, he said the CEO cannot outsource understanding AI, and that it will soon be a vital part of every decision. He said he hired a personal AI savant to work with him outside the company's formal structure, and that leadership on using AI must come from the CEO, at least broadly, because staff are desperate for reassurance that it will be unleashed smartly and safely. He said the CEO decides who owns AI and what is off-limits, while specifics fall to the CTO or CIO. He said boards are largely flying blind on AI, and that CEOs need to flatten their organizations fast and rethink the CIO, CTO and CPO roles to find one person responsible for proprietary data, the tech and security stack, and AI enablement companywide.

He said most CEOs are clueless about showing up inside AI, and that all companies need to restructure content, marketing and messaging to surface inside large language models and agents. He noted that the CEO of Profound, which he called the leading company monitoring this dynamic, recently gave C-Suite readers tips on fixing this fast. He said consultancies including Accenture, Teneo, Thoughtworks and FSG are helping CEOs with some pieces, but that everyone needs a holistic solution. He invited CEOs and their teams to ask to join the newsletter for deeper coverage of the six dimensions in the weeks ahead.

Articles.Title: Axios C-Suite: The 6 dimensions of AI leadership

stories.Headline: What Happens When AI Starts Self-Replicating?
stories.Summary:
Anthropic's Frontier Red Team published research suggesting small AI models may be only months away from replicating and spreading across insecure devices, creating slow but hard-to-kill autonomous botnets. The research was published on October 31, 2026, and cites the 2016 Mirai botnet, which let cybercriminals build a large botnet of IoT devices and carry out a DDoS attack. That attack broke much of the internet, knocking Amazon, GitHub, PayPal, Reddit and Twitter offline for many users across the US and parts of Europe. Sony estimated it lost about $2.7 million in net revenue.

Experts Engadget spoke to broadly agree small AI models could become capable of self-replicating in the near future. Chris Canal, CEO of EquiStamp, said the timing is maybe a little earlier than he would have predicted, and that he would have expected to worry around the summer of next year. Michael Bailey, a professor at Georgia Tech, said self-replicating models are real and will be seen, but whether they take the exact form Anthropic describes is an open question. Bailey said the framing is somewhat of a misnomer because the models do things like sharding, which is not full propagation like a worm or virus.

Bailey said what Mirai showed is that botnets could be composed of everyday devices like cable routers and IP-enabled cameras, which were thought useless to an adversary but are actually quite effective. He said adaptability itself is not new, since Mirai already worked across heterogeneous devices, but each new architecture required human work. He suggested more capable AI models will redistribute who does the work of creating botnets and change the economics between attackers and defenders. Canal said the companies are likely worried about other AI companies being reckless, and that they know those companies have the same incentives to deliver models fast for market share.

Anthropic suggests ISPs notify customers of an infection and then limit their internet access to a short list of safe websites, a strategy deployed during Mirai. It also suggests regulation, pointing to the UK, where easily guessable default passwords on IoT devices are now banned under the PSTI Act. Bailey argues the appropriate response looks a lot more like what has been done in systems security for a very long time, and that even misbehaving agents will have a hard time against hardened devices. Canal said it would be difficult to add safeguards to an open-weight model to prevent it acting as a worm, and that nothing robust exists so far.

Articles.Title: What Happens When AI Starts Self-Replicating?

stories.Headline: Self-learning AI releases NFL picks, score predictions for every Week 8 game
stories.Summary:
SportsLine's self-learning AI released picks and score predictions for every Week 8 NFL game, in an article published on October 31, 2026. stories.Headline: Charles Schwab (SCHW) Expands AI Tools For RIAs, Is The Stock Still 25% Undervalued?

Charles Schwab has moved artificial intelligence from concept to real tools for advisors, according to a Simply Wall St article published on October 31, 2026. stories.Headline: Circle Internet Group (CRCL) Showed AI Agent USDC Payments With Verified Identity At Money20 20
stories.Summary:
Circle Internet Group and Proof presented an AI agent-based payments and identity protocol at Money20/20 in late October 2026. The partners used USDC to show AI agents completing verified, identity-gated purchases without exposing underlying personal data. The demo integrated the x401 identity framework with the x402 payment protocol to support automated on-chain transactions by software agents. Circle runs a blockchain based platform for stablecoins and digital payments, giving it a direct role in how USDC moves across applications that rely on programmable money.

The showcase matters for Circle because it goes straight at a concern raised by Mizuho, that AI assistants could steer users out of USDC and into higher yielding products. By wiring x401 identity and x402 USDC payments into agent workflows, Circle is trying to make USDC the default rail that those same agents use for verified spending. The article ties this to the narrative around Arc and onchain payments becoming an economic operating system, and to USDC's role in payments and collateral rather than just as a yield carrying reserve asset. Circle had a market cap of $20.4b as of October 2026.

The practical test comes when Circle's agent wallet, x402 and Arc show up in live merchant traffic. The article says to watch for disclosed volumes of agent initiated USDC transactions, the number of merchants and identity providers using x401 and x402, and any commentary in upcoming filings or product updates that breaks out usage or revenue tied to these agent based payment flows. It also says readers can add Circle Internet Group to a watchlist and get alerts as these catalysts play out. The article is general in nature and is not intended as financial advice.

stories.Headline: Is AI your new wingman? How chatbots are transforming dating
stories.Summary:
A survey of 3,000 British singles, published in October 2026 by Match Group, the owner of Tinder and Hinge, found that 39% had used AI in their dating lives. The figure rose to 66% for gen Z and 53% for millennials. Sam, a 27-year-old from Stoke-on-Trent, turned to Google Gemini after his ex joked that her sister found him ugly, and the chatbot politely disagreed with the photo. He has used AI as a wingman ever since, for pep talks and for vetting his messages.

The most common uses of AI, according to Match, are getting advice about someone a person is talking to, planning date ideas, practising conversations, writing profiles or messages, and checking whether profiles or photos are genuine. Using AI to alter a photo is a no-no for most singles. About a third of UK singles said they would end a date if they found out AI had been used to write a potential partner's messages. More than a quarter liked the idea of two people's assistants talking to each other before the people speak, even though a majority called the idea unacceptable.

Match's head of trust and safety, Yoel Roth, said the company takes a hard stance against bot-to-bot dating. He said that in a world where people feel more alienated and hungrier for connection than ever, having robots talk to each other does not bring anyone closer to human connection. Sam said relying on AI is bad and he would rather begin dating in person, but he described a paradigm shift in which everything is expected to start online. He also said that if he replaced his humour with AI, he would have died as a person.

A single mother from New Zealand, who asked to remain anonymous, said she set up ChatGPT to coach her to become more secure, to not panic about delays in messaging and to not rush into anything. A 51-year-old man from Melbourne, who began dating after his 20-year marriage ended, said AI made finding his current partner faster by assessing his matches and testing his responses. When he told his partner, she admitted she had used Anthropic's Claude to analyse his responses, and she joked that the two Claudes were probably chatting behind the scenes. Dec, 31, from London, said he uploaded his dating conversations to ChatGPT and asked it to spot red flags, but he worries his brain feels like it is rotting because everything is offloaded to AI.

Articles.Title: Is AI your new wingman? How chatbots are transforming dating
