stories.Headline: FRE 707 and AI-Generated Evidence: Where the Proposed Rule Stands
stories.Summary:
A proposed federal rule on AI-generated evidence, known as Federal Rule of Evidence 707, was published for public comment in August 2025. The Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules approved it for comment in May 2025, and the Standing Committee on Rules of Practice and Procedure followed in June 2025. The comment period closed on 16 February 2026, after two public hearings and 59 written comments. The published version said machine-generated evidence offered without an expert, which would be subject to Rule 702 if a witness gave it, could be admitted only if it met Rule 702(a) to (d).

At its 7 May 2026 meeting, the Advisory Committee did not recommend final approval of the rule as published. It preferred a revised draft, known in the minutes as Version 2, titled "Evidence Produced by Artificial Intelligence and Presented at Trial Without an Expert." That draft covers "a product of artificial intelligence," writes out the four Rule 702 factors, presumes an expert is ordinarily needed, and adds a notice requirement. It also drops the exception for simple scientific instruments and takes its definition of artificial intelligence from the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020. The committee agreed that any revised rule would need a new round of public comment.

The committee's May 2026 report states that it does not recommend action on the proposed Rule 707 at this time. Its reporter, Professor Daniel Capra, told the Standing Committee in June that this was the first time in his experience that a rule published for comment had not gone forward. The Standing Committee received an information report only in June 2026, and the Judicial Conference took no action in September 2026. The Department of Justice raised continuing concerns about how the rule would work in practice, according to the minutes, and favoured considering it alongside the deepfake draft.

Rule 707 is not law and has no effective date, so it cannot take effect on 1 December 2026. Under the Rules Enabling Act, the Supreme Court must send a new rule to Congress by 1 May for it to take effect no earlier than 1 December of that year. To take effect in December 2027, the rule would have needed Judicial Conference approval in September 2026, which it did not get. The committee has said the revised version must be republished, and on the usual annual cycle a revised rule published in August 2027 could not take effect before 1 December 2029, which the article describes as its estimate rather than a date the committee has set. The committee held expert panels on AI evidence and deepfakes on 15 October 2026, and a separate draft Rule 901(c) on deepfakes is being held in reserve.

Articles.Title: FRE 707 and AI-Generated Evidence: Where the Proposed Rule Stands - Legal Desire

stories.Headline: OpenAI Highlights Legal Briefs Arguing AI Training Can Qualify as Fair Use
stories.Summary:
OpenAI on Friday, Oct. 30, highlighted legal briefs arguing that fair use can cover some AI training, adding third-party arguments to an unsettled U.S. copyright debate. The excerpts came from briefs filed by creators, academics, accessibility advocates and legal experts. Those filers argue that fair use can support some AI training and innovation. OpenAI's post did not announce a new court ruling. In June 2025, federal district courts accepted fair-use arguments for model training in Bartz v.

Anthropic and Kadrey v. Meta, based on the evidence in each case. The Bartz decision treated pirated books kept in a central library separately from its finding on model training. Neither decision established a nationwide rule. A May 2025 U.S. Copyright Office report said AI training can be transformative.

It also identified unlawful acquisition, model functionality, deployment and effects on markets for original works as relevant factors. The article does not name who at OpenAI is responsible for the post or what any OpenAI official said about it. It says the excerpts came from briefs filed by creators, academics, accessibility advocates and legal experts. Those filers argue that fair use can support some AI training and innovation. The article does not paraphrase any statement from those filers beyond that position.

The article says earlier district court decisions addressed fair use on the evidence in specific cases. It notes that TokenPost previously covered OpenAI's fair-use position in a summary-judgment memorandum and the Justice Department's separate filing backing that defense. The article does not say what happens next in any case. It does not say whether further filings or rulings are expected.

stories.Headline: Tech Leaders Kiss the Ring and Refuse to Call It "AI" After Trump Told Them Not to
stories.Summary:
After President Donald Trump ordered that artificial intelligence be called "Super Intelligence," or SI, technology executives complied. An analysis by CNBC found that Microsoft, SpaceX, Meta, Tesla and IBM used the term in official documents and communications during this earnings season. One SpaceX filing referred to SI 85 times. Microsoft used the phrase "Super Intelligence era" in an annual report letter. The push began last month, when Trump launched a poll on Truth Social asking supporters to choose a better name for AI.

Days later, Trump told the UN General Assembly that all US government documents would drop the term AI in favor of SI, and he made the change official with an executive order. This week he said he would be "officially BANNING" the term AI in government documents and "everything else." Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella wrote in the annual report letter that the central question in this Super Intelligence era is not just how big the opportunity becomes but how the company delivers real-world outcomes. SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk has insisted on using SI in all his public appearances and posts, with occasional slip-ups, and rebranded his AI company SpaceXAI as SpaceXSI. Musk recently admitted he has "SI psychosis."

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman called Super Intelligence a "more accurate" term than artificial intelligence but rejected rebranding OpenAI as OpenSI. He has generally sounded skeptical about the rebrand's usefulness. He told Politico that people are going to keep calling it AI. The article describes the tech leaders' embrace of SI as extraordinary toadying toward Trump since he returned to the Oval Office, including from those he once saw as enemies.

Articles.Title: Tech Leaders Kiss the Ring and Refuse to Call It "AI" After Trump Told Them Not to - Futurism

stories.Headline: Here's why an AI-generated campaign ad depicting Gov. Shapiro is allowed on the air in Pennsylvania ahead of the 2026 election
stories.Summary:
A campaign advertisement paid for by Pennsylvania treasurer and Republican gubernatorial candidate Stacey Garrity features an AI-generated version of Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro, 6abc.com reported on Friday, October 30, 2026. The commercial opens with the AI-generated Shapiro saying hello and that he has been very busy, then goes on to admit to a variety of alleged scandals and claims. The ad discloses its use of artificial intelligence about 40 seconds into the spot, saying it was created with AI thanks to big beautiful data centers. Some viewers said they quickly recognized the ad as artificially generated, and one called it something that should not be legal.

There are currently no Pennsylvania laws prohibiting the use of AI-generated content such as the ad. Pennsylvania Senator Lisa Boscola issued a memo in May announcing plans to introduce legislation that would prohibit AI deepfakes targeting candidates during election season. Delaware already has a similar law, making it illegal to distribute a deepfake of a candidate within 90 days of Election Day unless it is disclosed that the content was created using AI. Under federal broadcasting rules, stations cannot censor or reject campaign advertisements paid for or sponsored by legally qualified candidates, though stations might be able to reject the ad if a third party had submitted it.

A spokesperson for Shapiro's campaign described the ad as cheap and dishonest in a statement to Axios. Matt Beynon, a spokesperson for Garrity's campaign, said it is telling that Shapiro's only complaint with the new ad is that he was depicted using AI, and that he has never refuted a single criticism made in the ad because he knows they are all completely accurate. Lindsay Hoffman, a communications professor at the University of Delaware, said the ad's obvious use of AI may help alert viewers to the technology and its growing capabilities, and that legal frameworks often lag behind technological developments. She said people should already be skeptical when they see political ads, but that this makes it even more important.

Hoffman said she hesitates to claim AI uniquely changes the game, arguing new technologies have historically been used to influence public opinion and create confusion. She said people will find a way to manipulate any technology to change the conversation, the climate of opinion, or to cause chaos and make it difficult for people to understand what they are voting for. She also said the technology could further disengage voters who are already disconnected from the political process, possibly pushing them further away. The article does not say what happens next beyond Boscola's planned legislation and the possibility that laws will catch up to the technology at a slower pace.

Articles.Title: Here's why an AI-generated campaign ad depicting Gov. Shapiro is allowed on the air in Pennsylvania ahead of the 2026 election - 6abc Philadelphia

stories.Headline: Why AI is boosting Meta's ad business while hurting Google search
stories.Summary:
In the third quarter, Meta's advertising business grew 26% in revenue to $63.1 billion, up from $50.1 billion a year earlier, while Google's search division grew 12% to $63.4 billion, according to CNBC. That 14-point gap is the widest in Meta's favor since 2021. The divergence comes as chatbots such as ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude and Meta's recently launched Muse assistant become alternatives to search, leading consumers to click fewer links. Meta's gains back Mark Zuckerberg's claim that its AI investments are producing better targeting tools for brands on Facebook and Instagram.

After Alphabet's disappointing third-quarter earnings report on Wednesday, its stock plunged more than 12%, its worst day ever, wiping out about $500 billion in market cap. Meta's stock fell 14% in October, its worst month since October 2022, after a 27% surge in September. Google projects up to $205 billion in capital expenditures this year, while Meta expects up to $145 billion. Ads now account for less than two-thirds of Google's revenue but 98% of Meta's sales. Google's cloud division reported over 100% growth to $31 billion in quarterly revenue, and YouTube added $11 billion in third-quarter revenue.

Meta CFO Susan Li said on the earnings call that advertisers adopting the Meta AI business assistant's recommendations drove almost 5% more conversions and increased their advertising investment by 9% compared with similar non-adopters. She cited syrup producer Simply Organic Maple, which saw a 57% increase in purchases and a 36% decrease in cost per purchase, and said almost 10 million advertisers used at least one of Meta's AI tools in the quarter. Google chief business officer Philipp Schindler said the company is deploying its Gemini models across its entire ads infrastructure. Emarketer analyst Nate Elliott said changing search habits could be potentially catastrophic for Google's ad business. UBS analysts wrote that search cannibalization fears are back at the forefront, and Wedbush analysts wrote that Google shares are unlikely to work until the search narrative changes, which will likely require new ad products and proof points.

Articles.Title: Why AI is boosting Meta's ad business while hurting Google search

stories.Headline: TCAI’s Jai Jaisimha on artificial intelligence and mental health: How should AI be used?
stories.Summary:
Jai Jaisimha, co-founder of the Transparency Coalition, spoke with Rachel Harrison, host of the podcast The Mental Health Evolution, about how artificial intelligence is affecting health care. The interview was published on October 30, 2026, in an article written by Bruce Barcott. Jaisimha discussed the factors driving this year's surge in state AI legislation and the ways AI tools are appearing in clinical settings. The article includes an excerpt of the conversation and a link to the full episode.

The coalition's mid-year report found 84 new AI laws in 27 states in the first six months of 2026. By October 15, that figure had risen to 115 new laws in 30 states. Jaisimha said constituents are speaking up more than ever about their fears, hopes and concerns about AI. He also said legislators have climbed a learning curve through years of education efforts, and even lawmakers whose bills failed in 2025 said they wanted to try again this year.

Jaisimha said a small body of legislation focuses on mental health, especially chatbots used for patient-facing therapy, and the American Psychological Association is actively involved. He said this past year was largely about general-purpose consumer chatbots, with concern that people sometimes treat a chatbot like a trusted person and that its outputs can be confusing, misdirecting or worse. He said AI is widely used for clinical note-taking and transcription, which is not patient-facing. He said future legislation will likely address health care data handling, privacy and patient opt-in, along with questions about clinician supervision, transparency and when a clinician is alerted.

Jaisimha said stakeholders may differ on review, with some preferring clinician review, others some other human-in-the-loop review and others no review at all. He said those questions will be debated alongside the limits of AI technology to ensure legislation protects everyone in the ecosystem. He said he expects more legislation on mental health chatbots next year. The article also links to the coalition's 2026 AI Legislation Report, which found 115 new laws in 30 states as Congress declined to act.

Articles.Title: TCAI’s Jai Jaisimha on artificial intelligence and mental health: How should AI be used? - Transparency Coalition

stories.Headline: Column: Cybersecurity in the age of AI
stories.Summary:
The article is a column by Sandy Wagner, the Central Oregon Regional Manager for SELCO Community Credit Union, published on November 1, 2026. It says headlines about artificial intelligence are everywhere and that the future role of AI is an increasingly important debate. It also says people should be aware of how AI is used today, including by scammers. The column states that AI has given fraudsters powerful new tools, such as polished phishing emails and text messages and deepfake technology that can clone voices and make a video call appear to come from someone trusted.

The column says October is Cybersecurity Awareness Month and that financial institutions work with government agencies, technology companies, security firms, and law enforcement to combat attacks. It names tools like AI-driven voice authentication, anti-money laundering and fraud-prevention platforms, advanced cybersecurity tools, and built-in digital banking protections. It says these tools are getting better every day. It also says one of the most important defenses is low-tech, namely slowing down.

Wagner says old fraud tactics and new AI schemes share a sense of urgency meant to pressure people into bad decisions. She says people should verify a request through a separate channel, such as calling back on a number they already have or asking a question only the real person could answer. She says anyone feeling pressured should pause, step away, and take a breath, and that legitimate companies will not penalize you for taking time. She says people should contact a company directly using a trusted number, website, or app rather than a link or number in a suspicious message, and should ask a friend, loved one, or trusted business for help.

The column says these steps are easy to remember with B.A.C.K., which stands for Breathe, Ask, Confirm, Keep others safe. It says cybersecurity is sometimes viewed as a battle between sophisticated criminals and sophisticated technology, but some of the most effective defenses are surprisingly simple. It says AI may be changing the tools scammers use but does not change the ability to be cautious, ask questions, and look out for one another. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: Column: Cybersecurity in the age of AI

stories.Headline: Vision-language AI agent could help radiologists interpret ultrasounds faster and more accurately
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine have created a vision-language AI agent that reads right upper quadrant ultrasounds, which show organs such as the liver, the gallbladder, the right kidney and part of the pancreas. The work was published in Nature Communications, and Harrison Bai, M.D., M.S., a visiting associate professor in the Department of Radiology, is the senior author. The agent combines visual ultrasound data with written clinical data from the lab. It can diagnose common conditions affecting these organs and suggest logical next steps.

The team tested the agent on roughly 11,000 RUQ ultrasounds from Stanford University, the University of Colorado and Johns Hopkins University. They then manually reviewed 100 AI-generated reports, and the agent identified the correct diagnoses in each ultrasound 99.6% of the time. The agent made some mistakes in the overall reports, but radiologists who reviewed and edited them found the errors easy to catch. In a blinded evaluation, experts could usually pick out unedited AI reports, but most of the time they could not tell radiologist-edited AI reports apart from reports written by radiologists. The agent was designed to scan for 16 common diagnoses, estimate each patient's prognosis and autogenerate reports.

Bai said the goal is not to replace the physician and that the team is not trying to build an AI radiologist. He said that if the agent can write preliminary reports, it saves radiologists time. He also said he does not expect AI to replace the need for human supervision in medicine and that it will take time for doctors to adapt. He said he can see the technology playing a huge role in how medicine is practiced and that he is excited to see it incorporated into daily practice to help patients and doctors.

The researchers say radiologists face extra pressure from an aging U.S. population and rising demand for medical imaging, and that as of 2022 radiologists were leaving the field at twice the rate they were in 2014. Bai said the team is trying to address the increasing workload, that there are not enough people or radiologists to do the work, and that Medicare reimbursement is decreasing. The researchers say the technology needs to be evaluated in real-world emergency care before it can be widely adopted. They say it will also be critical to study how physician-AI collaboration affects diagnostic accuracy, efficiency and patient well-being.

Articles.Title: Vision-language AI agent could help radiologists interpret ultrasounds faster and more accurately

stories.Headline: Elementary, my dear… So... what can all of us ‘little’ people do about the looming AI problem?
stories.Summary:
The article is a first person column by a writer who taught first, second and third grade for 39 years and whose maiden name was Little. She describes asking an AI tool to generate a childlike crayon drawing of a robot, then asking for a smile when the first result looked too grim. She also writes that she Googled current concerns about AI and got an AI generated list including job loss and automation, fake news and misinformation, scams and cyber security, bias and discrimination, privacy and data sourcing, and loss of human oversight. She says two of her cousins are university professors who told her incoming undergraduates lack the ability to think and no longer know how to research simple problems or judge whether information is true.

She writes that her publisher asked about a year ago whether her book content could be used for AI training, and she agreed, partly because a tidy sum of money was offered. She says she reasoned that if AI could improve its vocabulary or simplify its language she would feel satisfaction like she did when third graders began enjoying story problems. She adds that she doubts she will ever get feedback on whether her contributions were useful. She also recalls arguing with a human copy editor over the term weather beach, which he said was not real, and says she sent examples of its use in local publications dating to earliest settlement.

She says she does not mind being one of the little people, meaning ordinary working class citizens, and that she does not want to confuse contentment with complacency. She argues that the more people rely on AI, the less they solve problems for themselves, and she recalls opening third grade story problems by telling students that life is a series of problem solving situations. She says she will keep taking chances to teach, keeps her sense of humor about arguing with a robot, and notes there is always the delete button. She writes that mainstream media and the internet are full of concerns from medicine, technology, finance and job displacement, and that ultimately she believes it will be up to us little people to use our innate good sense and instincts for survival to find the solutions.

Articles.Title: Elementary, my dear… So... what can all of us ‘little’ people do about the looming AI problem?

stories.Headline: Innocent People Are Being Accused of Shoplifting by Faulty AI-Facial Recognition Systems at an Alarming Rate
stories.Summary:
In the United Kingdom, AI facial recognition systems used in retail stores have led to a rise in customers being wrongly accused of shoplifting, according to TechRadar cases highlighted by Futurism. One woman identified as Mary said her husband was socially isolated after a Home Bargains store system flagged him as a shoplifter during a quick trip to buy vitamins. The couple was forced to leave by management, seemingly without any chance to refute the accusation. The man told TechRadar that he was scared to go into a shop.

Another man was said to be shaking from head to toe after his wife was removed from a Budgens chain store over an accusation of stealing loads of meat days earlier. That accusation was complicated by the fact that they had not set foot in the store for months. The publication reported a maze of corporate bureaucracy and vague insinuations that leave innocent people unable to access their local businesses. Those people have little recourse to clear their name.

In the UK, individuals can file Subject Access Requests, or SARs, which are like US Freedom of Information Act requests but for private companies. The avenue technically exists for those wrongly accused of shoplifting, but it is a massive undertaking just for the hope of clearing your name. It also requires handing over even more private information to private companies. Jack Coulson, head of advocacy at civil liberty group Big Brother Watch, told TechRadar that being trapped in a maze of bureaucracy and forced to hand over even more personal data just to be told the accusation is the stuff of Kafkaesque nightmares.

The article describes AI facial recognition security systems as a common sight from New York City to Tokyo and says the tech is nowhere near ready for live use. It points to the troubling rise of false-positive matches as evidence. The piece also links to other reports, including an innocent man freed after spending over 50 days in jail due to inaccurate AI facial recognition tech. It does not say what happens next for the people accused in the UK cases.

Articles.Title: Innocent People Are Being Accused of Shoplifting by Faulty AI-Facial Recognition Systems at an Alarming Rate

stories.Headline: CoreWeave and Neocloud Stocks Face a Tougher Test as AI Spending Mounts
stories.Summary:
Sara Awad, an analyst at Tech Contrarians, said on an Investing Experts podcast published Tuesday that the next phase of the AI trade may depend less on demand for computing power and more on which companies can afford to build it. She expects the AI boom to face a potential bubble burst in 2027, with funding pressures posing a greater risk than weakening demand. She favors semiconductor equipment and optical-networking companies over capital-intensive AI infrastructure operators. She said ASML continues to benefit from demand for its extreme ultraviolet lithography systems, even though investors sold the stock after a strong quarter and improved guidance.

ASML expects to ship 65 EUV units in 2026, with targets of 85 in 2027 and potential for 110 in 2028. Awad urged caution on AI cloud providers CoreWeave, IREN and Hut 8, whose heavy infrastructure spending leaves them exposed to financing constraints. She said CoreWeave has fallen more than 50% from its highs. She characterized the recent technology pullback as a correction following the April-to-June rally rather than a broad deterioration in earnings.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC's Brian Sullivan on Wednesday that rising debt yields in the AI sector are not a concern, describing neocloud companies as a minor part of the broader market. He said he does not think it is problematic at all because the neoclouds are a small component of the overall ecosystem. He noted that capital continues to flow into the technology sector despite rising borrowing costs, with financing and deals still getting done. He added that some companies, such as Meta Platforms, are choosing to finance with equity.

The comments came alongside mounting financial pressure on CoreWeave, an Nvidia-backed neocloud company. The yield on CoreWeave's $2.75 billion bond maturing in 2031 rose to a record 15.76%, according to last week's report. Shares of CoreWeave have declined about 44% in the past six months, and the stock fell about 6.92% to $59.50 premarket on Thursday. Bessent also expressed support for Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh and said he expects a strong GDP number for the third quarter.

Articles.Title: CoreWeave and Neocloud Stocks Face a Tougher Test as AI Spending Mounts - Yahoo Finance
